articles.title: 2 vessels barred from sailing after Cagayan, Bohol mishaps
articles.summary: M/B Rose Marie 1 and MV Ocean Jet 788 are barred from operating pending safety inspections and technical assessments.

blocks.text: November 1, 2026 | 1:21pm
The fast craft MV OceanJet 788 as seen in a company promotional video posted in November 2022.
OceanJet

MANILA, Philippines — The Maritime Industry Authority (MARINA) has ordered the immediate suspension of the safety certificates of motorized banca M/B Rose Marie 1 and fast craft MV Ocean Jet 788 following separate maritime incidents in Cagayan and Bohol.
In a statement on Sunday, November 1, the Department of Transportation (DOTr) said the incidents occurred on October 31.
The vessels are prohibited from operating while their certificates are suspended and must undergo safety inspections before they can be cleared as seaworthy.

Initial reports indicated that rough sea conditions and uncontrolled movement of livestock caused M/B Rose Marie 1 to partially submerge in waters between Dalupiri and Fuga islands in Cagayan at around 8:15 a.m.
All eight people aboard, including the captain, survived the incident. Six of the 11 livestock animals aboard died.
Hours later, at around 10:57 a.m., MV Ocean Jet 788 encountered an electrical failure while maneuvering to dock at the Port of Tagbilaran in Bohol.
According to the DOTr, the power disruption affected the vessel's bridge engine remote control and throttle system, temporarily compromising its maneuverability.
Both vessels remain barred from operations pending safety inspections and technical assessments by MARINA.

articles.title: VP Sara Duterte visits memorial for Super Typhoon Yolanda victims
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte paid respects to the victims of Super Typhoon Yolanda, which hit Tacloban City in 2013, a few days before All Saints' Day.

blocks.text: Published November 1, 2026 1:17pm
Vice President Sara Duterte paid respects to the victims of Super Typhoon Yolanda, which hit Tacloban City in 2013, a few days before All Saints' Day.

Duterte visited the Holy Cross Memorial Gardens on Friday where the victims of the calamity were laid to rest. She was joined by personnel of the Office of the Vice President-Eastern Visayas Satellite Office.
"Nag-alay tayo ng bulaklak at nagsindi ng mga kandila, kasabay ng ating mga panalangin para sa kapayapaan ng kanilang mga kaluluwa," she said in a Facebook post.
(We offered flowers and lit candles, along with our prayers for the peace of their souls.)
The vice president also encouraged the public to pray for the souls of those who died from calamities.

"Sa ating paggunita sa Araw ng mga Patay, isama natin sa ating mga panalangin ang mga kababayan nating biktima ng kalamidad at sakuna, gayundin ang kanilang mga naiwang pamilya," said Duterte. "Patuloy tayong maging matatag sa gitna ng mga pagsubok sa ating buhay."

(As we commemorate All Saints' Day, let us include in our prayers our fellow countrymen who were victims of calamities and disasters, as well as the families they left behind. Let us continue to stay strong amid the trials in our lives.)
Yolanda was the worst storm to hit the Philippines, with thousands of lives killed and 1.14 million houses damaged.
Roxas Night Market bombing victims
On October 30, Duterte also honored the lost lives in the Roxas Night Market bombing in Davao City last 2016, which killed more than 10 individuals.

"Binisita ko ang memorial ng ating mga kababayang nasawi sa pambobomba sa Roxas Night Market noong 2016. Sa banal na paggunita na ito, nag-alay tayo ng panalangin para sa kanilang mga kaluluwa. Nawa’y matagpuan nila ang walang hanggang kapayapaan sa piling ng ating mapagmahal na Maykapal," she said in another Facebook post.

(I visited the memorial of our fellow countrymen who perished in the Roxas Night Market bombing in 2016. In this holy commemoration, we offered prayers for their souls. May they find eternal peace in the presence of our loving Almighty.)
—Vince Angelo Ferreras/KG, GMA News

articles.title: On Bangladesh’s temporary islands, Runa Khan helps families stand with dignity
articles.summary: Social entrepreneur Runa Khan receives the 2026 Ramon Magsaysay Award for her work in providing health care, education, and climate solutions to remote island communities in Bangladesh

Profile
Social entrepreneur Runa Khan receives the 2026 Ramon Magsaysay Award for her work in providing health care, education, and climate solutions to remote island communities in Bangladesh
By Jelo Ritzhie Mantaring | Published November 1, 2026

Along the Brahmaputra River in Bangladesh, some communities live on land that is constantly shifting. They are situated on sandbar islands called char, formed by sediment deposition from major river systems.
These areas, which are continuously reshaped by erosion and flooding, are home to up to 20 million people, according to some estimates.
Runa Khan was introduced to char communities in 1997 while doing her work in preserving traditional boat-building skills.

During her visits, one moment stayed with her: a woman feeding her sick child with only two meals to save money for lamp oil. The second meal, rice and onions, was the child’s early dinner, given in hopes that he would forget his fever and sleep throughout the night.

Khan, who came from a privileged, wealthy family, said she saw the injustice and poverty that had become the reality for those living on these temporary, shifting river islands. Residents there are at risk of displacement as river erosion threatens to wash away their villages. Families have to constantly relocate even with their unstable income, trapping them in extreme poverty.
Her sadness turned to anger — and it might have been anger that pushed Khan to search for answers to help these communities.
“Realization, as I keep saying, leads to a responsibility. The fact that you can do something, then it becomes your responsibility,” she said in a virtual roundtable discussion last September.
In 2002, Khan founded the social purpose organization Friendship and established a hospital ship along the Jamuna River, a branch of the Brahmaputra River, in northern Bangladesh.
HOSPITAL SHIP. The Lifebuoy Friendship Hospital, the organization’s first floating hospital. Photo courtesy of Friendship/Ramon Magsaysay Award Foundation
Over two decades later, Friendship has expanded its services to include education and livelihood, as well as programs for climate resilience, for 7.5 million people annually.

“I started the work because I just couldn’t leave or not be responsible for what was staring at me in the face, which was incredible poverty. Twenty-five years ago, these areas were totally untouched,” the 67-year-old humanitarian told journalists.

Khan earned the 2026 Ramon Magsaysay Award, considered Asia’s Nobel Prize, for her “profound empathy for the poorest of the poor in her country, and her courage, vision, and tenacity in building and leading Friendship to accomplish her mission.”
Her work is not over yet, however, as char communities become more vulnerable because of the worsening climate crisis.
INITIAL REACTION. Runa Khan thanks the Ramon Magsaysay Award Foundation for naming her a 2026 Ramon Magsaysay Awardee on August 31, 2026. Photo by Jelo Ritzhie Mantaring/Rappler
Better access to health care
Char dwellers find it difficult to access healthcare services and be properly diagnosed with their diseases. Their communities are low-lying, flood-prone areas as they sit across rivers.

Residents frequently suffer from common infectious and water-borne diseases amid floods triggered by the monsoon season from June to October. Mothers and children could also have elevated health risks. If they get sick, they have to cross rivers to reach hospitals on the mainland — or rely on alternative medicine.

This did not sit well with Khan, who believes the first thing a person needs is good health. So, through Friendship, she converted a river barge into a hospital ship for these temporary river islands.
“Without access to health, you can’t provide…any kind of empowerment to a person or any kind of hope to a person, nor give them dignity,” Khan said.

“Impossible” was a comment she would hear about the floating hospitals. But those hospital ships now provide surgeries to treat cataracts, clubfoot, and other common but debilitating conditions; give pediatric, gynecological, dental, and eye care; and supply free or cheap consultations and medicines.

It’s part of Friendship’s three-tier health care system. The organization trained local women to become medic aides, who handle door-to-door check-ups, provide maternal care, and gather patient data through a mobile app.
Meanwhile, roving medical teams give primary healthcare services in mobile and satellite clinics. If patients need major interventions and specialized care, they are referred to the hospitals.
Today, the organization has seven hospital ships and two land-based hospitals, 550 mobile clinics, and 700 medic aides.
TOGETHER. Runa Khan participates in a discussion with char communities. Photo courtesy of Friendship/Ramon Magsaysay Award Foundation
Khan valued regular visits to the char communities because they informed the organization about how to expand its services.
“I’ve not been reading books on development or reading economics of development…. It all came from the needs of the community,” she said of their work.

“I listened to what people said, and I listened to what they did not say. Because it’s in what they don’t say, there is the pain, the suffering. And from there, you have to understand what it is they need.”
Runa Khan
Empowerment through education, employment
Friendship was not Khan’s first social work.

She was a passionate educator. In 1979, she pushed for an educational system that promoted critical thinking and veered away from repeated memorization. She also introduced “user-friendly, goal-oriented” textbooks to improve student performance in Bangladesh.
For this, she was named a fellow of Ashoka, a United States-based nonprofit organization, in 1994.
This advocacy also led Khan to reach remote areas, including char communities, in Bangladesh. Education then became part of Friendship’s work.

Friendship trained locals to teach primary school, while secondary schools have pre-recorded video classes by trained facilitators. It also rolled out a literacy program for adults in char communities.
EDUCATION. Runa Khan with children studying in Friendship’s schools. Photo courtesy of Friendship/Ramon Magsaysay Award Foundation
“Even the remotest person knows that education is hope — not for themselves, but for their children, for their family, [so] that they can survive,” Khan said.
“When you do all this, you need to ensure that there is empowerment, and empowerment can [give] the people sustainability when you’re not there.”
Students in the adult literacy program, especially women, are connected to different income-generating trainings, such as homestead gardening, livestock rearing, and vocational weaving and tailoring.
Friendship also employs char dwellers as medic aides, teachers, paralegals, skilled birth assistants, solar technicians, and para-vets, among others.
“The people [whom] we have served so far, we have to now turn them into becoming…more self-sufficient and…how they are going to use the money that they earn,” Khan said.

HUMANITARIAN. Runa Khan, a 2026 Ramon Magsaysay Awardee, wears a sari, a traditional attire in Bangladesh made by women living in char communities, during a virtual roundtable discussion in September 2026. Zoom screenshot
Changing climate
Because char communities rely heavily on agriculture, they’ve adapted the timing and kinds of crops they plant to expected storms and floods.

That slight predictability has been erased by worsening climate change. In the latest Climate Risk Index, Bangladesh was among the countries that had recorded the most people affected by extreme weather events in 2024.
In a 2025 study, residents reported prolonged and swift floodwater accumulation, as well as substantial floodwater height. Add to that the threat of sea level rise.
“With the heat, ice melts became heavier, the flow of the river became extremely strong…. All built of silt, land damage and erosion absolutely skyrocketed,” Khan said.
The climate crisis also affected Friendship’s education solution. The organization builds prefabricated schools, which can be easily assembled, dismantled, and relocated amid shifting land.
LEARNING. Friendship’s prefabricated primary school in Bangladesh. Photo courtesy of Friendship/Ramon Magsaysay Award Foundation
For instance, Khan said that from 2012 to 2015, they moved just one or two schools per year. By 2018, they had to move 16 schools.
Friendship is currently operating 43 primary schools and 17 secondary schools in char communities in northern Bangladesh.
“I don’t even need a rocket scientist to come and evaluate what the trouble is. I can see it daily,” she said.

As part of its climate adaptation work, Friendship implements a mangrove afforestation program. It also introduced “plinth housing,” where permanent houses are constructed on elevated land to accommodate displaced families and their possessions during floods. Families are also given access to low-cost solar-powered lighting.
CLIMATE SOLUTIONS. Runa Khan plants mangrove saplings with women living in char communities. Photo courtesy of Friendship/Ramon Magsaysay Award Foundation

Friendship believes in local climate solutions. It also empowers the char people to survive and thrive without the organization, as displacement amid the climate emergency will be inevitable for them.

“We started preparedness, relief work, and then rehabilitation, and then how to get back to income. And when they migrate from one place to the other…they [need to be ensured] that even if they’re out of our reach, they can reach the government…that they [have] the dignity and they [have] courage to be able to continue their lives,” Khan said.
Through its work called “integrated climate adaptation solutions,” Friendship won the Earthshot Prize in the “Fix Our Climate” category in 2025.
Forging the future
Given the climate risks Bangladesh and other countries face disproportionately, it’s apparent that Friendship’s climate solutions are also much needed elsewhere.

Khan said they will launch the Friendship Academy to expand their services and models, especially the “spirit” of their designs so other communities and countries can replicate it. She said these are “easily scalable.”
AT WORK. Runa Khan talks with international guests visiting char communities. Photo courtesy of Friendship/Ramon Magsaysay Award Foundation
Their Community Initiated Disaster Risk Reduction model will also be taught as a course at University of Dhaka. Khan hopes the course will also be disseminated internationally.

She believes she should not follow an “old-fashioned, colonialistic” way of amplifying solutions. She would rather share the ways of Friendship with the world rather than put human dignity at stake with her mandates.
“You are the person. You will say what you need for your country and your people…. This is, for me, respect.”
During September’s virtual chat, this journalist asked Khan whether the anger she felt over two decades ago ever went away.

The Ramon Magsaysay awardee immediately recalled potential donors who would allot only two hours to visit Friendship’s projects. She would tell them the communities were kilometers away from Dhaka, Bangladesh’s capital city, and that they should really see the social work.

“Sparks happen because I deal with it,” Khan said, answering Rappler’s question. “I make sure that there is a solution for that anger, you know? Because anger and injustice move hand in hand.”– Rappler.com

articles.title: Marcos visits dad, sends flowers to Cory, Noynoy on Undas
articles.summary: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. visited the tomb of his late father and namesake as the country observes the annual Undas in remembrance of departed loved ones.

blocks.text: Published November 1, 2026 12:13pm
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. visited the tomb of his late father and namesake as the country observes the annual Undas in remembrance of departed loved ones.
"Though they are no longer with us, the memories we shared and the values they taught us continue to bring our families closer together," he said in a Facebook post on Sunday, All Saints' Day.

In his post, the President can be seen together with his mother, former First Lady Imelda Marcos, and his younger sister, Irene Marcos as they paid their respect to their patriarch at the Libingan ng mga Bayani in Taguig City.

"Let us honor those who have passed not only through our prayers, but also through the way we care for those who remain. May these solemn days bring peace to those who mourn and remind us to cherish the people we hold dear," he said.
Aside from his father, Marcos also honored members of the Aquino family, including former presidents Corazon Aquino and Noynoy Aquino, as well as former senator Ninoy Aquino.
It must be noted that the Marcoses and the Aquinos were political rivals.
According to Super Radyo dzBB's Mao dela Cruz, Marcos sent flowers to the tombs of the departed Aquino members at Manila Memorial Park in Paranaque City.
Supporters of the Aquino family were also reportedly seen at the burial site to pay their respects.
In 2013, then President Noynoy Aquino said that he did not want to continue the revival of the Marcos family who at the time had assumed several political posts.
Marcos Jr. was a senator, the former first lady was a congresswoman, while Imee Marcos was a provincial governor.
But Marcos Jr. later said that the rivalry between their families is only limited to politics.

Kris Aquino, the youngest daughter of the assassinated senator and sister of the late president, recently shared that Marcos Jr.'s wife and First Lady Liza Marcos helped handle her annulment to basketball player James Yap in 2012. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: 8 crew rescued after banca partially submerges off Cagayan
articles.summary: All crew members were brought to safety after their banca partially submerged.

blocks.text: November 1, 2026 | 12:04pm
Philippine Coast Guard personnel conduct a seaborne patrol off Barangay Alegria in Ormoc City on Oct. 31, 2026, as part of maritime safety and security operations.
Philippine Coast Guard / Released

MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine Coast Guard rescued eight crew members, including the captain, after their motorized banca partially submerged off Dalupiri Island in Cagayan on Saturday, October 31.
In a statement on Sunday, November 1, the coast guard said its search and rescue teams in Calayan deployed after receiving reports that M/B Rose Marie 1 was in distress.
Upon reaching the area, responders confirmed that all eight crew members were accounted for.
Five crew members were initially brought to the shoreline of Barangay Magsidel and taken to the Calayan Rural Health Unit. Medical personnel found all five to be in good physical condition.

A second search and rescue team aboard M/B Lagadan 1 assisted in towing operations and brought the remaining three crew members to shore. They were also taken to the Calayan health unit for medical evaluation.
One crew member sustained a laceration on the right knee and was evaluated for suspected hypertension.
The other two crew members were also treated for suspected hypertension, according to the coast guard.

The "Benteng Bigas, Meron Na!" program provides subsidized rice to vulnerable sectors, including senior citizens, persons with disabilities, solo parents, minimum wage earners, public transport workers, indigents, and registered farmers and fisherfolk.

articles.title: Marcos on Undas: Extend devotion to helping others
articles.summary: The president says devotion to the departed should extend to people who are struggling.

blocks.text: November 1, 2026 | 11:16am
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. speaks during the National Correctional Consciousness Week celebrations at New Bilibid Prison in Muntinlupa City on Oct. 28, 2026.
PCO / Released
MANILA, Philippines — President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. called on Filipinos to extend the devotion shown during All Saints' Day and All Souls' Day to acts of kindness and concern for others.

In his Undas message, Marcos encouraged the public to draw inspiration from the selflessness of saints and the sacrifices of those who came before them, and to reflect these examples in how they care for one another.

"Across the country, families return to cemeteries, offering prayers and celebrating the lives and legacies of departed loved ones. Some travel great distances for these visits, finding an opportunity to reunite with relatives and recall the moments they once shared," Marcos said.
He said the memories of departed loved ones continue to strengthen the bonds of Filipino families and communities.
Marcos also urged Filipinos to extend the same care shown in honoring the departed to people who are struggling.
"If we can make time to revere those who have passed, we can also make room to listen to those who struggle, and let that same concern guide our society and the work of government," Marcos said.
He ended his message by wishing peace to those who mourn and reminding Filipinos to cherish those who remain.

articles.title: Trump grants visa to mother of Ghanaian boy killed in NYC — Mamdani
articles.summary: Javits Frimpong was killed on his way to school in the Bronx. He was 15 years old.

image.caption: Zohran Mamdani said he spoke with President Donald Trump on SaturdayImage: NDZ/STAR MAX/IPx/picture alliance

blocks.text: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Saturday that US President Donald Trump had agreed to grant a visa to the mother of a 15-year-old boy who was killed in a neighborhood in Bronx earlier this week.
Javits Frimpong moved to New York from Ghana last year to be with his father and begin a new life in the US, according to Representative Ritchie Torres, a Democrat from the Bronx.
Frimpong was shot in the abdomen on Thursday morning on his way to school and later died in the hospital, according to New York City police.
There have been no arrests in the case so far, with police investigating the shooting.
Mamdani says he spoke to Trump
"I just got off the phone with President Trump and he has agreed to grant her visa immediately," Mamdani posted on X.
"The murder of a child is a pain no parent should have to endure, let alone from thousands of miles away," he wrote. "Javits Frimpong's mother deserves to say goodbye to her son in person."
The killing led to an outpouring of grief in New York, with Torres writing, "Our entire borough is mourning a young man who should have had his whole future ahead of him."
The White House is yet to comment on the Trump-Mamdani phone call.
Teen was bullied in school, father says
Thomas Frimpong remembered his son as a quiet boy and said he was bullied in school by two boys.
Ghana's Foreign Minister Sam Okudzeto Ablakwa also thanked Mamdani and Trump in a post on X.
He said Ghanaian officials were coordinating with Javits Frimpong's mother to assist her with the visa application process.

articles.title: [Two Pronged] A cross-dressing husband seeks a chance to reply
articles.summary: A cross-dressing husband — who may be the subject of an earlier Two Pronged column — responds to 'half-truths' raised in that earlier column

blocks.text: Rappler’s People section runs an advice column by couple Jeremy Baer and clinical psychologist Dr. Margarita Holmes.

Jeremy has a master’s degree in law from Oxford University. A banker of 37 years who worked in three continents, he has been training with Dr. Holmes for the last 10 years as co-lecturer and, occasionally, as co-therapist, especially with clients whose financial concerns intrude into their daily lives.
Together, they have written two books: Love Triangles: Understanding the Macho-Mistress Mentality and Imported Love: Filipino-Foreign Liaisons.
Dear Dr Holmes and Mr Baer:
I refer to your column of Oct 10, 2026.
I do not intend to sue you for publishing the half-truths of my wife, but I insist on (the) right of reply. This column allows that, I presume?
I have every reason to believe my wife (or former wife, as she insists although divorce is yet to be legal in our country) wrote the letter you published the 10th of October, 2026.
All the details she mentions are accurate, although there are other facts she forgets to mention:

items: Yes, I used to cross dress and it is my eternal regret that instead of sharing this voluntarily with her, she discovered this on her own. I immediately promised never to do it again.
She said it explained many things that did not seem right in a marriage between two people who loved each other. I love her — and still do, despite the years we have been separated.

I gave her many books and research articles to read unequivocally stating that my being a cross dresser did not translate to being gay and/or being transgender. After a while she stopped reading them. I cannot understand such denial of logic.

How could she refuse such undisputed data? My wife is also an attorney, but working for a non profit. She has a good heart but no business sense. Her final decisions are guided by heart, not a hard core mind.
Each time she discovered I broke my promise never to cross dress again, I could feel her love for me diminish.
I will never forgive myself for this, but each time I failed, there was a very good reason that I did.
When she finally left me, I stopped cross dressing for the next few years in an effort to win her back.

She has always refused my attempts at reconciliation, so can you blame me for going back to cross dressing every now and then? I am not gay, I do not hate women, and I don’t think I am a woman trapped in a man’s body. I just enjoy doing so. It provides much needed relief from a job that is full of pressure.

blocks.text: Any thoughts? – Andrew
Dear Andrew,

Thank you for your email. This column welcomes all responses of whatever nature, positive or negative. In this case, there is just one caveat – we will answer your letter without treating your wife as a party to this exchange since we have not verified any connection between you.

Your letter states that you regret that rather than hearing about it from you, your wife discovered your cross-dressing for herself. You also acknowledge that your broken promises diminished her love for you and eroded the trust between you. However, regarding the broken promises, you claim that there were ‘very good reasons’ for them, unfortunately without revealing what these were and thus forestalling any analysis of your reasoning.
It seems clear that despite your concealment of your cross-dressing, it was not the cross dressing per se, but the continuous breaches of promise that drove your wife from the marriage.

This was no doubt exacerbated by your decision to conceal the supposedly ‘very good reasons’ from her, since how was she to be expected to understand you if you consistently failed to explain yourself?

Perhaps it is also significant that you have done exactly the same in your letter to us — claimed that there were ‘very good reasons’ without any further explanation. How are we then expected to evaluate this situation, much less your wife?

Your refusal to explain yourself, together with your efforts to deflect by deluging your wife with information to prove that cross-dressing did not mean you were gay or trans, suggesting that reason alone should convince her, are thus what drove her away and you seem to make it clear that you never altered these tactics, despite claiming you wanted to win her back.

So, to answer your question, no one can blame you for going back to cross-dressing now that you have alienated the only person whose opinion you actually wanted. As for further thoughts, perhaps it is time to recognize that your marriage is over for good, regardless of the law.
Further efforts to win her back will simply confirm what she already believes, namely that your promises are hollow.
All the best – JAF Baer
Thank you very much for your letter. There are two points Mr Baer brings up in his answer above that I would like to expound on.

First, it was not your cross dressing per se that caused your wife to leave you. If it were, she would have left you the first time she discovered it… or the second… or, at the very most, perhaps the third or fourth. It was how you promised repeatedly that you would stop doing so and never did.

How exhausting that must have been for her! And yet… AND yet… I see no attempt on your part to understand how she must be feeling. Instead, I read rationalization after rationalization about why you behaved the way you did, and why you have gone back to cross dressing. And even then, you rationalize why you went back and manage to blame her for it!

Besides, for a lawyer who seems to place logic above all else, is it not ironic that you “immediately promised” never to do it again. This belies your statement that you find nothing wrong with cross dressing. I feel it is only when you finally reach point #8, your last point, that you seem to give the actual reasons you cross dress: “I just enjoy doing so. It provides much needed relief from a job that is full of pressure.”
Why in God’s name did you not share this with her? Why did you not open your heart to her, trusting her to believe you (or, at the very least, hoping she would believe you)?

There seems every reason to think she would have. After all, she believed your promise to stop cross dressing (even if you felt there was nothing wrong with it, as all the research articles and books you insisted she read confirmed).

I realize that, with the quick razor-sharp mind you pride yourself on having, you will accuse me of merely projecting my own feelings when I share another reason for your wife’s refusal to believe you. But clinical experience says otherwise.

Many — though admittedly not all — people who pride themselves on, and convince themselves that, their intellect is what makes them who they are; that it is their formidable mind that makes them not just admirable, but also lovable.

Not so. I have yet to hear a wife say the major reason she loved her partner was their IQ. Many — and admittedly not all — women who love their partner do so for inner qualities that usually cannot be measured by simple metrics. Most women love their partners basically for how their partners make them feel: cherished but also safe.
I can’t help feeling it was your behavior and your arrogance, both during your marriage and after it ended, that was the nail that finally ended your marriage.
Here’s hoping you find the courage to discover some truths — and not mere data — about yourself
– MG Holmes
Life got complicated? Write to our Two Pronged duo at twopronged@rappler.com.

articles.title: Valkyries defeat Dream in historic Game 7 to capture 1st WNBA title in 2nd season
articles.summary: Gabby Williams scored her team's final 11 points of the third quarter and dazzled through the fourth on the way to 30 points, and the Golden State Valkyries captured a championship in just their…

image.caption: Members of the Golden State Valkyries celebrate after defeating the Atlanta Dream 68-63 in Game 7 of the WNBA Finals on Saturday at Chase Center in San Francisco. (Thearon W. Henderson/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Basketball·Breaking

Gabby Williams scored her team's final 11 points of the third quarter and dazzled through the fourth on the way to 30 points, and the Golden State Valkyries captured a championship in just their second season by beating the Atlanta Dream 68-63 in a sensational first WNBA Finals Game 7 Saturday night in San Francisco.
Gabby Williams leads Golden State to 68-63 victory
· The Associated Press
· Posted: Oct 31, 2026 10:48 PM EDT | Last Updated: 11 minutes ago
Jordin Canada scored 18 points, Allisha Gray 16 and Angel Reese eight points and 12 rebounds for the Dream, denied another championship in the franchise's fourth try.
Gray made two free throws with 11 seconds left then Atlanta forced a jump ball — Gray against Williams — and Veronica Burton corralled it and converted two free throws with 5.1 seconds to go.

Rhyne Howard's layup tied it at 57 with 2:41 left only for Williams to answer once more by making a clutch three-pointer. She converted two free throws with 1:40 remaining, then Kiah Stokes scored a late basket. She pulled down 13 rebounds and blocked two more shots to cap her spectacular post-season.

items: Dream force Game 7 of WNBA Finals with convincing victory over Valkyries

blocks.text: Williams left Seattle with a great feeling about joining Golden State and its close-knit culture, returning to the Bay Area where she played youth basketball to build something special with the Valkyries — and she's now done that. Fans chanted "Gabby! Gabby!" throughout the fourth quarter.
When the final buzzer sounded, the violet-clad sellout crowd at Chase Center went into a frenzy as players sprinted onto the floor to hug and celebrate as confetti fell from the rafters.

"Ballhalla" had become "Boohalla" for this far-but-haunted Halloween night in the raucous arena. Now, with a women's championship to its name right alongside the one earned by the Golden State Warriors in 2022.

articles.title: Binance says 90% of losses from $6.3bn hack covered as FBI says North Korea behind attack
articles.summary:
Cryptocurrency exchange says withdrawals expected to resume on Sunday as FBI blames North Korean state-sponsored group TraderTraitor

Cryptocurrency exchange Binance says it has…

blocks.text: Cryptocurrency exchange Binance says it has replaced 90% of the ⁠amount stolen after a record $6.3bn hack of its platform by a group the FBI identified as being backed by North Korea.

The remaining 10% of tokens are less liquid, meaning they ⁠may take ​longer to buy, the company said in a post on X on Saturday. Co-CEO Richard Teng said separately that the company was “committed to covering the ⁠remaining 10%” and that “users will not bear the financial impact of this incident”.
Binance suspended user withdrawals after the hack, but said in its latest update that it was on track to resume them on Sunday.
The announcement came as the FBI on Saturday confirmed earlier suspicions from private investigators and analysts that a North Korea-affiliated group called TraderTraitor was behind the hack.

TraderTraitor is believed to be part of the Lazarus Group, which gained notoriety in 2014 when it was accused of hacking into Sony Pictures as revenge for The Interview, a film that mocked North Korean leader Kim Jong-un.

“The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is releasing information advising the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (North Korea) was responsible for the theft of more than $6 billion USD in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, on or about October 29, 2026,” the law enforcement agency said in a statement.

The FBI added that it had observed “TraderTraitor actors” converting stolen assets into Ethereum, and expected those assets to be laundered further by converting them using decentralised finance and instant swap services.
It said it was urging private sector entities “to block transactions with or derived from addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder these stolen assets”.

Teng said on Friday that the breach was a “complex attack” involving a compromised laptop and malicious software designed to delete evidence of its activity, making it ‌harder to trace and investigate.
Binance said it had set aside around $6.34bn of company funds to cover the losses.
“Our commitment remains the same: Binance will fully cover the financial impact of the funds stolen in this incident,” the company said.

The money spent re-buying tokens came from using part of its $1bn Secure Asset Fund for Users, a bitcoin reserve it holds to protect customers in the event of security breaches, as well as some ⁠of its Futures Insurance Fund, and the company’s own corporate treasury, it said ​on X.
The attack on Binance came as many observers express worries that the ever-expanding capabilities of artificial intelligence models could compromise cryptography and IT security protocols.
Bitcoin plunged nearly 5% after the news of the hack, while Ethereum dropped nearly 6% and BNB, native to Binance, tumbled nearly 10%.

The sheer scale of the hack has put a spotlight on the capacity of North Korea – which faces extensive international sanctions over its nuclear and missile programmes – to find illicit means to capture revenue.

articles.title: How chefs Kevin Uy and Gabriel Ong steered FLOW to one Michelin star
articles.summary: For Filipino chefs Kevin Uy and Gabriel Ong, returning home isn't just a culinary homecoming — it’s a humbling, emotional rediscovery of the country they thought they knew

blocks.text: The hardest thing chef Kevin Uy had to unlearn after returning to the Philippines was not a cooking technique. It was how to speak.

Abroad, Uy said, he could communicate directly with colleagues and express his thoughts without much hesitation. But after becoming a boss at FLOW, the Makati restaurant he co-leads with fellow chef Gabriel Ong, he realized that straightforwardness alone was not enough.
“What I had to unlearn was being more diplomatic, because I’m not a very diplomatic person,” Uy told Rappler.
The adjustment revealed an unexpected lesson from his years in international kitchens: Professional experience does not automatically translate into knowing how to lead in a different environment.

The 32-year-old chef spent years training and working in Barcelona and Peru before returning to the Philippines. His experiences abroad helped shape his culinary perspective, but building a restaurant at home required him to reconsider how he worked with people and dealt with constraints he had not encountered in quite the same way overseas.

For Filipino chefs who leave to learn, the journey home is not simply about bringing back recipes or techniques. It can also mean discovering how much they still need to understand about the country where they grew up.

Uy graduated from Enderun Colleges in 2016 with a degree in International Hospitality Management, specializing in Culinary Arts. He completed an internship at Hotel Arts Barcelona in Spain, later studied at the Basque Culinary Center, and spent years working with the group behind Peruvian restaurants Central and Mil and research initiative Mater Iniciativa.
His five years in Peru, much of them spent working under chefs Virgilio Martínez and Pía León, helped him approach food through the environments, ingredients, and people behind each dish.
But returning to the Philippines presented challenges beyond the kitchen.

One was sourcing. Uy said he had worked in prestigious restaurants abroad where obtaining supplies seemed relatively easy. Starting out in the Philippines made him realize that getting ingredients was not always as straightforward as he had expected.
View this post on Instagram A post shared by Restaurant FLOW (@restaurantflow.mnl)
Although he said his own suppliers had been accommodating, he had heard from other chefs who struggled to obtain particular ingredients.
Ong, who also worked abroad before returning to the Philippines, said logistics can affect the quality of produce by the time it reaches a restaurant.
“Some of the produce being so nice, the raw materials being so nice, gets through a three-hour traffic,” Ong said. “[Of] course, at the end, it ends up in your restaurant, it’s not the same quality.”

For chefs accustomed to working in established international kitchens, the challenge is not simply finding ingredients. It is learning to work with the quality, availability, and consistency of what reaches their kitchens locally.

Ong sees this contrast as both a limitation and an opportunity. International exposure gives returning chefs a reference point for the standards they want to achieve, while working in the Philippines shows them how much room there is to improve sourcing and distribution.
“The learning is the contrast,” he said.

Managing people posed another steep learning curve for Uy. Despite prior experience in Europe and Latin America, this was his first time leading a local team as an employer — not to mention his first job in the Philippines.

FLOW’s staff of about 18 came from different parts of the country, including Leyte, Bacolod, Antipolo, and Laguna. Uy said working with people from different backgrounds taught him that communication involves more than giving instructions.
“It’s not just all about saying things and people follow,” he said. “It’s making sure that they understand it and that they respect you for it.”

It was the same group of people that helped push FLOW to the periphery of the Michelin Guide’s anonymous inspectors, who felt that the fine dining concept deserved to receive its own highly coveted Michelin star.

During the 2027 Michelin Guide ceremony, FLOW became the latest addition to the Philippines’ mighty roster of one-star restaurants. Uy and Ong were present to receive the glass trophy on stage, while their 18 staff members were at FLOW preparing for the upcoming dinner service.
While the recognition had come as a shock to the two chefs, they knew it had all been made possible by their hardworking team.
“I think just working hard every day,” Uy told Rappler just after the ceremony when asked what they think FLOW was doing right to have earned a star.

blocks.caption: How chefs Kevin Uy and Gabriel Ong steered FLOW to one Michelin star

blocks.text: “And the team is behind us. So they understand, and they work just as hard, and it’s because they care as much as we do. So that’s something that I think that they recognize as well.”
“It’s our team who deserves all of this award. We could not have done it without them,” Ong added.

The accolade had clearly come as a surprise to the two chefs. Anytime a member of the press would ask how they were feeling about it, they would answer that they were still processing the fact that they had received a Michelin star, but were nonetheless grateful for it all.

Perhaps one of the first things you would notice about Uy and Ong is that they are of Filipino-Chinese descent. Culinary is not a common path for the people in their community to take, but it was something both chefs were willing to gamble on — all the more now that FLOW finally has a Michelin star to its name.

“I think more than anything, for Filipino-Chinese in particular, [we have] perseverance, perseverance in the fact that we are able to push and prove to our families who really are skeptical about this entire industry, that we can manage to make it. And that’s something very important to us,” Uy told Rappler.

Uy and Ong take perseverance seriously in their work. Evolution is expected in the world of gastronomy, and the two know that by heart. A chef’s original vision must be tested against sourcing, preparation, consistency, and the experiences of the people expected to bring it to life.
For Uy and Ong, adapting also means learning from one another. Uy contributes much of FLOW’s creative direction, while Ong helps translate those ideas into a working kitchen.

Ong said chefs returning from abroad have a responsibility to use their experience to help improve the industry around them. Rather than demanding that local colleagues adopt the same standards or methods they encountered elsewhere, they must find ways to communicate what they learned.
“For me, I think it’s about being the bridge,” Ong said.

Asked to compare his years abroad to a television show or film, Uy settled on Emily in Paris. The comparison, he explained, was not about glamour but about a person finding her way in an unfamiliar place and building a life in an industry she wanted to join.
It is a fitting description of the experience he and Ong now encourage other Filipino chefs to embrace: being willing to learn even after gaining experience in prestigious kitchens.
Uy said chefs returning home should be flexible enough to absorb lessons from the people around them, rather than assuming their overseas experience has prepared them for everything.
“The only difference is what they were doing is where they were doing it,” he said, referring to Filipino chefs who built their careers locally while others trained abroad.
Uy said working overseas does not mean that a chef knows more than everyone who stayed, nor does growing up in the Philippines guarantee that returning professionals understand the local industry.
“Just because you grew up here doesn’t mean you know everything, and just because you worked there doesn’t mean no one else knows everything,” Uy said.
His advice is simple: “Be humble.”

The value of going abroad, for Filipino chefs, may lie not only in what they learn elsewhere, but in how they use those lessons when they return. The work at home is not simply to recreate an international kitchen; it is to understand the people, ingredients, and constraints around them, then find ways to build something that belongs here. – Rappler.com
Dominique Astucia is a Rappler intern studying BA Journalism at the University of Santo Tomas.

articles.title: Shops looted as German cost of living protests turn violent
articles.summary: Police in Frankfurt say "violent riots" took place in the city centre, with unrest also reported in Berlin, Hamburg and Cologne.

blocks.text: Rioters looted shops in central Frankfurt late on Saturday and clashes erupted with police there and in other German cities after largely peaceful mass protests over the cost of living.

Besides Frankfurt - Germany's financial hub - there were incidents of violence in Berlin, Cologne and Hamburg, with police saying they used water cannon to disperse protesters who targeted emergency workers with fireworks, stones and bottles.

Thousands earlier joined the demonstrations organised by the campaign group Gen Z regelt - meaning "Gen Z takes charge" - to protest against underfunding in schools, the high cost of living, public spending cuts and military service.
The unrest in Germany follows similar youth-led mass protests in France, where more than 320,000 people also demonstrated on Saturday.
A large section of Frankfurt's main shopping street was closed off by police, AFP news agency reported. A police spokesperson said many arrests were made in the city.
Authorities in Frankfurt, Munich and Berlin reported as many as 18,000 protesters, roughly half of what the organisers had estimated on their website.
Gen Z regelt spokesperson Lina Friedrich said the demonstrations were "to fight for peace and freedom, rather than for war and coercion".
She said: "What matters most to us is better support for the health and education systems. We are against compulsory military service and we are in favour of a fairer distribution of the burden."

articles.title: CHR urges child-centered emergency response, preparedness amid National Children's Month
articles.summary: The Commission on Human Rights (CHR) on Sunday urged government and stakeholders to ensure that disaster preparedness and response measures are inclusive, accessible, and responsive to the needs of…

blocks.text: Published November 1, 2026 9:59am

The Commission on Human Rights (CHR) on Sunday urged government and stakeholders to ensure that disaster preparedness and response measures are inclusive, accessible, and responsive to the needs of children.
With the theme “Manindigan! Tumugon at Kumalinga: Sa Batang Handa, Mas Ligtas ang Bansa,” CHR said preparedness and response must uphold children’s rights before, during, and after emergencies.

The commission cited the country’s exposure to typhoons, floods, earthquakes, armed conflict, and other crises can disrupt children’s access to essential services and increase their risk of abuse, neglect, and family separation.

“Child-protection measures must be inclusive, accessible, and responsive to the needs of all children, particularly children with disabilities and those in disadvantaged situations,” CHR said in a statement.

“Equally important, children must be recognized as rights-holders whose experiences, perspectives, and recommendations should inform preparedness plans, the continuity of essential services, and recovery efforts,” it added.
Protection vs exploitation

CHR further called for stronger protection against online sexual abuse and exploitation, including accessible and child-sensitive mechanisms for reporting, rescue, rehabilitation, and access to justice.
Following the school shootings across the country, the commission urged stronger school safety and preventive measures, psychosocial and mental health support, and protection of children’s privacy.
In March, CHR welcomed the Philippines’ removal from the United Nations’ list of situations involving grave violations against children in armed conflict after 22 years.
Based on its monitoring and interviews with 14 government agencies in Regions II and XII, CHR reported that there has been a decline in the number of working children and child laborers.
However, the commission said there should be sustained action to address the issue’s root causes.
2026 National Children’s Month
CHR will begin its month-long observance of National Children’s Month on November 3.
In partnership with the NORFIL Foundation, CHR will consult children and youth with disabilities and their parents on barriers to inclusive and accessible education on Nov. 14.

CHR will also hold a "Children’s Dialogue with Legislators" with the Child Rights Network and the House Committee on the Welfare of Children on November 24 to let children share their experiences and recommendations directly with policymakers.
Meanwhile, the Department of Justice will hold the Children’s Summit and the 20th Juvenile Justice Week celebration from 23 to 27 November 2026.

CHR Regional Offices will also conduct Kabataan Karapatan Caravans in selected schools and child- and youth-serving facilities to raise awareness of children’s rights and available protection mechanisms.

“We want you to know how to protect yourselves, how to recognize harm, abuse, and situations that may put you at risk–and, most importantly, where and how to seek help when your rights or the rights of your peers are violated. A child who is informed, empowered–a batang handa—plays a vital role in building a safer and more caring nation–a mas ligtas na bansa,” CHR Commissioner Beda Epres said. —Mariel Celine Serquiña/RF, GMA News

articles.title: FBI says North Korea behind $6 billion Binance crypto theft
articles.summary: The FBI said the theft was tied to "malicious cyber activity" by an entity known as TraderTraitor, the same actors behind a $1.5 billion Bybit hack last year.

image.caption: The theft, which happened within a matter of minutes, is believed to be the biggest cryptocurrency heist in historyImage: Romain Doucelin/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: The FBI said Saturday that North Korea was behind the theft of more than $6 billion (€5.36 billion) in virtual assets from the cryptocurrency exchange Binance.

"The Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea) was responsible for the theft of more than $6 billion USD in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, on or about October 29, 2026," the US law enforcement agency said in a statement.
The theft, which happened within a matter of minutes, is believed to be the biggest cryptocurrency heist in history.
The stolen assets included bitcoin, ethereum and stablecoins such as tether and USD Coin, whose values are pegged to traditional currencies.
News of the cyberattack caused the prices of most major cryptocurrencies to slump on Friday.
Cryptocurrency giant Binance hit by $6.3 billion hack
What did the FBI say?
The FBI said the theft was tied to "malicious cyber activity" by an entity known as TraderTraitor, the same actors behind a $1.5 billion Bybit hack last year.
The agency said it had "observed TraderTraitor actors converting stolen assets" primarily into a cryptocurrency called ethereum.

"It is expected these assets will then be further laundered by converting them using DeFi [decentralized finance] and instant swap services as they prepare them for further laundering stages," it added.
The FBI asked crypto exchanges, blockchain analytics companies and others to block transactions linked to various addresses to ensure the money is not laundered to cover up its origins.
Crypto boosts Trump family fortune since White House return
What did Binance say about the heist?
Binance is the world's largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes.
The exchange said on Saturday it was using company funds worth over $6.34 billion to buy tokens to replenish about 90% of the assets stolen in the attack.
The remaining 10% consisted of tokens that were less liquid, meaning they may take longer to buy back, the company said.
"Our commitment remains the same: Binance will fully cover the financial impact of the funds stolen in this incident," the company said on X.
The heist came amid growing worries that the ever-expanding capabilities of artificial intelligence models could compromise cryptography and IT security protocols.

articles.title: Rainy All Saints' Day expected in parts of Luzon
articles.summary: Parts of Northern Luzon may see scattered rains and isolated thunderstorms on All Saints' Day.

blocks.text: November 1, 2026 | 9:38am
Aerial photos taken at around 4 p.m. on Saturday, Oct. 31, 2026 shows generally orderly conditions at several cemeteries in Lucena City, ahead of the expected influx of visitors for All Saints' Day.
The STAR / Michelle Zoleta
MANILA, Philippines — Rains are expected in parts of Northern Luzon on All Saints' Day, November 1, state weather bureau PAGASA said.

In its Sunday weather forecast, PAGASA said a shear line is affecting the eastern section of Northern Luzon, while the northeast monsoon, locally known as *amihan*, is affecting the rest of the region.
Mainland Cagayan, Apayao, Kalinga and Isabela may experience cloudy skies with scattered rains and isolated thunderstorms due to the shear line.
PAGASA warned of possible flash floods or landslides in these areas due to moderate to, at times, heavy rains.
Meanwhile, the *amihan* may bring partly cloudy to cloudy skies with isolated light rains to Batanes, Babuyan Islands, Ilocos Norte, Abra and Benguet.
Metro Manila and the rest of the country may experience partly cloudy to cloudy skies with isolated rain showers or thunderstorms due to localized thunderstorms.
PAGASA warned that severe thunderstorms may still trigger flash floods or landslides in affected areas.
Typhoon outside PAR
PAGASA is also monitoring Typhoon In-Fa outside the Philippine area of responsibility (PAR).
As of 3 a.m., the typhoon was located 2,290 kilometers east of Extreme Northern Luzon.
It had maximum sustained winds of 155 kilometers per hour near the center and gusts of up to 190 kph.
In-Fa was moving east-northeastward at 10 kph.

articles.title: These firms you've never heard of are feeding fears the AI bubble could burst
articles.summary: The amount of debt held by data centres is measured in the tens of billions of pounds.

blocks.text: Neocloud firms often finance themselves by signing long-term lease contracts with major tech customers who need quick access to computing power.
Firms can then borrow money using those contracts – plus the AI chips they purchase – as collateral, explained analyst Cory Johnson of "The Quiet Period" IPO research outfit.
He said debt is common across neocloud firms because the hardware has to be paid for up front.
Take the industry leader: CoreWeave. It's a fraction of the size of some of the Big Tech companies it serves.
But Johnson believes lenders sometimes consider the creditworthiness of CoreWeave's customers, like Microsoft or Meta, more than the company's when they lend.
"This helps explain how CoreWeave accumulated $35.1bn (£26.3bn) in debt," he said.
Some jittery investors appear to be having second thoughts.
CoreWeave stock has lost a quarter of its value over the past month, and it's not alone.
Shares in other neocloud firms like Nebius, IREN, and Applied Digital have all shed about that much if not more during the same period.
Debt investors also appear spooked, and are demanding ever-higher returns from several firms in the sector.

CoreWeave's CEO Mike Intrator has said that the market is acting "irrationally" and has expressed confidence in its business model. Some of the world's most consequential companies are queuing up for CoreWeave's infrastructure and other AI services.
Several neocloud firms have their roots in the volatile crypto mining industry, made of companies that generate cryptocurrencies, like Bitcoin.
Crypto miners use some of the same kind of physical infrastructure that is used to develop AI.
CoreWeave was founded in 2017 with a focus on mining Ethereum.
IREN, Core Scientific and Applied Digital also started in crypto mining.
Their infrastructure left them well-positioned when AI exploded in 2022 with the introduction of OpenAI's ChatGPT.
One outlier is Nebius, which was known as Yandex NV when it was part of Russia's version of Google before splitting off and changing its name in 2024.
Now, the success of these firms hinges on the fate of major AI developers and hyperscalers – even larger data centre operators which neocloud firms often count as key customers.
"There is just an enormous amount of spending getting injected into the system," said Melissa Otto, head of Visible Alpha Research at S&P Global. "It's an arms race."
And neoclouds have benefitted.
But the trade-off of their model is "greater financial risk" in the face of change, said Forrester VP and principal analyst Charlie Dai.
That includes any adjustments that their Big Tech customers might make to their spending plans.
This past week, when Microsoft and Google forecast less AI spending than Wall Street analysts had projected, shares in several neocloud firms tumbled.
Much is also riding on Anthropic and OpenAI, which are both expected to start selling shares to the public in the months ahead.
If AI proves to be a bubble – and bursts – neocloud firms "are definitely going to face collateral damage," said Bradley Tusk of Tusk Ventures.
The future of the neoclouds also depend on their ability to keep borrowing, which gets more expensive as interest rates rise.
In a recent social media post, Elon Musk suggested this challenge could lead more than 200 neoclouds to "see guppy-level death and consolidation", with the smallest firms being the most vulnerable.
"Some will make it through, but not many," he added.
For now, analysts at Yorkville Ives said demand for computing power still exceeds supply, adding that neoclouds are filling an important gap that larger data centre companies cannot fill.
But to some, the neocloud sector's recent wobbles are concerning.
Microsoft recently cancelled a deal with a British neocloud outfit called Nscale amid power supply issues which could last through to 2030.
Australia's Firmus just shelved plans to start selling shares to the public.
These developments come amid a public backlash against data centres and questions about how much value AI can add to worker productivity.
"There's reason to worry," said Johnson.

articles.title: How to observe Undas in an eco-friendly way
articles.summary: As the public visits cemeteries for this year"s Undas, an environmental watchdog made an appeal to minimize waste and protect the environment while doing so.

blocks.text: UNDAS 2026
Published November 1, 2026 9:17am
As the public visits cemeteries for this year’s Undas, an environmental watchdog made an appeal to minimize waste and protect the environment while doing so.

“Every November 1 and 2, millions of Filipinos visit cemeteries to honor departed loved ones. However, the tradition also generates a surge in waste, often left behind due to inadequate waste management and weak enforcement of regulations,” BAN Toxics said in a statement.
“If not properly managed, these can contribute to plastic pollution and undermine efforts to keep public spaces clean and safe,” it added.
According to BAN Toxics, the Manila North Cemetery and Manila South Cemetery recorded a combined 278 metric tons of waste, equivalent to more than 45 truckloads, on the first day of Undas last year.
Among the most common types of waste found in cemeteries are single-use plastic bottles, food wrappers, discarded candle packaging, and other disposable materials.
Here are some tips to observe an eco-friendly Undas:

1. Bring reusable items such as food containers, water bottles, and utensils. Avoid styrofoam, disposable plastics, and other single-use items, such as plastic straws, cups, and plates, that contribute to plastic pollution.
2. Segregate waste properly by placing trash in designated bins and observe cemetery rules on hygiene.
3. Bring enough food and drinks to avoid spoilage and unnecessary leftovers.
4. Offer candles and flowers responsibly. Avoid lead-core candle wicks to prevent potential exposure to toxic chemicals and choose flowers without plastic wraps.
5. Choose lead-safe paint when painting or repairing tombs.
6. Take your waste at home if bins are full and dispose of it properly. Help prevent waste from accumulating in walkways, burial areas, and surrounding communities.
BAN Toxics said honoring the dead should also mean caring for the living and protecting the environment.
“Let us not allow the resting places of our departed loved ones to become dumping grounds for garbage,” it said.
“This Undas, let remembrance go hand in hand with responsibility. Let us commemorate with environmental care, practice waste reduction, and make 𝘡𝘦𝘳𝘰 𝘞𝘢𝘴𝘵𝘦 #Undas2026 a shared commitment,” it added.
On Sunday morning, November 1, around 400 visitors were initially reported at the Manila South Cemetery in Makati City, which is open from 6 a.m. to 9 p.m.
Meanwhile, the Manila North Cemetery, the largest cemetery in the country, located in the City of Manila, has so far recorded 2,800 visitors as of early Sunday.
Over 111,000 policemen are deployed to enforce security across the country for the observance of All Saints' Day and All Souls' Day from Nov. 1 to 2. —Mariel Celine Serquiña/RF, GMA News

articles.title: [Time Trowel] Ube is taking over the world. So why are Filipinos still obsessed with rice?
articles.summary: While the Philippines remains heavily reliant on rice despite being a major importer, recognizing and investing in alternative root crops like ube and taro can enhance food security and agricultural…

blocks.text: A trowel (/ˈtraʊ.əl/), in the hands of an archaeologist, is like a trusty sidekick – a tiny, yet mighty, instrument that uncovers ancient secrets, one well-placed scoop at a time. It’s the Sherlock Holmes of the excavation site, revealing clues about the past with every delicate swipe.

Long before ube became fashionable in cafés from Los Angeles to London, Filipinos had already given it a place in halo-halo, one of our most beloved desserts. The combination of shaved ice, sweetened fruits, beans, and milk has long included ube halaya, sometimes accompanied by ube ice cream for those who believe one serving of ube is never enough. Now, the rest of the world has discovered this purple yam, transforming it into lattes and pastries that sometimes contain more food coloring than actual ube.

The enthusiasm has attracted investment. The United States Department of Agriculture has committed $34.1 million to develop the Philippine ube industry through a five-year program expected to support 12,500 Filipino farmers. This is welcome news, particularly if it increases farmers’ incomes. Still, I find it amusing that a crop cultivated in the Philippines for generations is suddenly attracting millions of dollars because international consumers have developed an appetite for purple desserts. More importantly, the investment raises questions about how we value crops and determine agricultural priorities, especially in a country where food security has become almost synonymous with rice production.

Filipinos have an enduring love affair with rice. Someone who has eaten bread for breakfast and noodles for lunch might still complain about not having eaten rice all day. Government agricultural policies reflect this preference, with billions of pesos allocated to rice production. Yet the Philippines is the world’s largest rice importer. According to the Philippine Statistics Authority, Filipinos consume approximately 329 grams of rice daily, or 120 kilograms annually per person. That is a considerable amount of rice for a country struggling to meet domestic demand.

Root crops, meanwhile, are frequently associated with poverty or food shortages. Kamote has even become a term for incompetence, an unfortunate reputation for a crop that has fed generations of Filipinos. Our preference for rice has influenced how we value other staples, including those cultivated long before rice became central to Philippine diets.

Archaeology offers another perspective on Philippine food history. There is no securely established archaeological evidence of wet-rice cultivation in the Philippines earlier than approximately 700 years ago. For much of Philippine history, communities relied on other food sources, including taro and yams, which played important roles in early Philippine agriculture. Our ancestors had more options on their plates than our contemporary obsession with rice might suggest.

Our archaeological research in Ifugao has challenged the popular claim that the Cordillera rice terraces represent 2,000 years of continuous wet-rice agriculture. Evidence indicates that intensive wet-rice cultivation expanded approximately 300 to 400 years ago, partly in response to Spanish colonial intrusion. Earlier agricultural systems included taro cultivation, supported by Indigenous knowledge of land management. Ifugao communities were producing food long before rice terraces came to dominate the landscape. Their agricultural history extends beyond the terraces that tourists photograph today.

This history has implications as the Philippines confronts climate change. Typhoons can destroy rice crops within hours, while drought threatens irrigation supplies. Certain varieties of yams and sweet potatoes tolerate periods of limited rainfall, while underground storage organs may survive wind damage. Although root crops are also vulnerable to flooding and prolonged drought, cultivating different crops could reduce dependence on rice. Given our annual encounters with typhoons, placing so much of our food security in one crop seems an unnecessary gamble.

items: Think ube’s just ube?
Purple harvest: Safeguarding the future of the ube industry
[Time Trowel] Ube: History you can eat
Trend Intel: Here’s why we’re not done talking about ube, the world’s latest craving

blocks.text: Root crops contribute to household nutrition in several ways. Ube provides carbohydrates and dietary fiber, while orange-fleshed sweet potatoes contain beta-carotene, which the body converts into vitamin A. Including these crops in everyday meals can improve dietary diversity and provide an alternative to rice. Their nutritional benefits, however, depend partly on how they are prepared. Ube ice cream and sugar-laden lattes are hardly substitutes for nutritious meals. Adding ube to a dessert does not turn it into health food, regardless of what social media influencers might claim.

Indigenous communities have maintained knowledge of root crop cultivation that agricultural institutions could learn from. Across the Philippines, farmers cultivate varieties of taro and yams adapted to local environments. Some communities also maintain knowledge of wild yams requiring processing before consumption. These practices developed through generations of experimentation and have supported households during periods of scarcity, often without the institutional recognition afforded to rice cultivation.

Commercialization raises questions about the future of this agricultural diversity. Export markets favor varieties selected for yield or processing characteristics. Farmers may consequently abandon cultivars that do not meet commercial requirements, including those adapted to particular environmental conditions. It would be ironic if ube’s international popularity eventually contributed to the loss of varieties.

The Philippine government’s decision to restrict exports of fresh ube and planting materials reflects concerns about protecting domestic production. Protection should also extend to farmers who have maintained these resources. Communities should participate in commercialization decisions and benefit from the use of their agricultural knowledge.

Agricultural research could use the enthusiasm for ube to investigate root crops beyond export markets. Universities and government agencies could document varieties maintained by farming communities and assess their responses to changing climatic conditions. If millions of dollars can be mobilized because people abroad enjoy purple pastries, perhaps we can also invest in crops that could address food insecurity at home.

I am certainly not proposing that Filipinos abandon rice. Anyone who has attempted to replace a Filipino household’s rice with boiled kamote knows how that conversation might end. Some might rather skip the meal entirely. Our preference for rice, however, should not prevent us from recognizing crops that sustained Philippine communities long before intensive rice agriculture became widespread.

For now, I will continue enjoying halo-halo with a generous serving of ube halaya. Perhaps the next time someone pays six dollars for an ube latte in Los Angeles, they might consider the Filipino farmers whose agricultural knowledge has sustained its cultivation for generations. I hope the international enthusiasm improves their livelihoods and encourages investment in other crops that have long fed Filipino communities. Taro and other root crops may never achieve ube’s celebrity status, but they were feeding people long before anyone thought of putting a yam in a latte. – Rappler.com

Stephen B. Acabado is a professor of anthropology at the University of California, Los Angeles. He directs the Ifugao and Bicol Archaeological Projects, which emphasize communityengagement in archaeological research. He grew up in Tinambac, Camarines Sur. His latest book, Stirring the Pot and the Past: Food Stories and Philippine History, co-authored with John Sherwin Felix, explores how centuries of cultural exchange have shaped Filipino cuisine and identity.

articles.title: How the downfall of Serbia's Vučiċ mirrored that of Hungary's Orbán
articles.summary: Defeat for Serbia's Aleksandar Vučiċ in last weekend's vote was a carbon copy of Viktor Orbán's fall in Hungary.

blocks.text: Mobilisation of voters, and the role of election monitors, played a big role in the opposition victory in both countries.

Last weekend, the DE civic action group in Hungary sent 70 election monitors to Serbia, to work with students' movement representatives, visiting polling stations in the northern Serbian province of Vojvodina.
During the summer, even before the election was called, they held workshops to share their experience and methods from the Hungarian election with the Serbian students.

A key technique was to identify "infected" polling districts in advance - places where the surprisingly high number of votes for the governing party at previous elections suggested that voter intimidation or "chain voting" techniques were used.

"From around 16:00 on election day, we noticed groups of masked hooligans - Vučiċ supporters - gathering near voting stations," Péter Klemm, a student activist from Subotica, told the BBC. "So we sent mobile teams, and started filming everything."
Combined with the "stationary" monitors already in place, 20 to 30 volunteers at each threatened polling station acted as a strong deterrent, he believes, and prevented intimidation or fraud.

Orbán in Hungary, Vučiċ in Serbia, both looked invincible. Both were powerful leaders, in office for 16 and 14 years, who had taken over state institutions and established business empires overlapping the two countries.
Orban chose cheese, Vučiċ meat, when they sat down to a quick lunch of traditional burek pastries at a small, popular town centre bakery in Subotica almost a year ago.

They continued to a local winery, to talk about oil and other business deals - the planned Hungarian purchase of Serbia's Nis oil refinery. The two nationalist leaders found much in common, in business and politics, not least their friendship with Vladimir Putin in Russia and Chinese President Xi Jinping, and their strong support for Milorad Dodik, the separatist leader of the Bosnian Serbs.
A high-speed railway between Belgrade and Budapest is being built with Chinese finance and know-how.

The parallels between the fall from power of the two men are extraordinary. Aleksandar Vučiċ admitted defeat at exactly 21:30 on Sunday evening, just as Viktor Orbán did on 12 April. Few observers expected either leader to concede peacefully.

There has been speculation this week that Vučiċ spoke to Orbán twice on Sunday night to ask his advice - once before he conceded, and again at 23:15. And that Orbán convinced his Serbian ally not to use force.
Vučiċ denies that he spoke to Orbán before he made his announcement, but acknowledges the later conversation. Viktor Orbán, contacted by the BBC, declined to comment.

An hour before polls closed in Serbia, masked and hooded vigilantes took up position in central Belgrade. During voting, similar groups were photographed at many polling stations, and blocked by election monitors.

There is another strange numerical similarity. The Student List will have 140 seats in the 250-seat Serbian parliament, the same number Péter Magyar's Tisza party won in the 199-seat Hungarian parliament.
Magyar was the only European leader to ring the students directly to congratulate them that evening - and probably the only one who had their number.
"It is always good to hear that the story of Tisza could provide an inspiration for other nations," the Hungarian prime minister told the BBC.
"The result of the Hungarian election clearly showed us that what we are doing here is right," the head of the Student List, Ilija Srdanoviċ, said on the eve of the vote.
Srdanoviċ was one of those Péter Magyar spoke to that Sunday evening.
Orbán, 63, and Vučiċ, 56, may now both face prosecution for corruption and abuse of power.

The judicial machinery in both countries is similar. Serbia's special prosecution service for organised crime, JTOK, and Hungary's brand new special prosecutors, known as NVVH, have similar powers. They could prove useful to each other.

Hungarian companies close to Orbán were also involved in the Novi Sad railway station construction project. The collapse of the station's canopy on 1 November 2024 - blamed on corruption, as well as negligence - killed 16 people, and acted as the catalyst for the Serbian student movement.
"There was a perception in Europe that the longer the Orbán and Vučiċ regimes stayed in office, the stronger they got," Áron Timar, founder of the DE civic action group in Hungary told the BBC.
"In fact they got weaker. And once society found its voice and rose up, there was no way of stopping it."

articles.title: Filipinos flock early to cemeteries on All Saints' Day
articles.summary: Many Filipinos all over the country went early to visit departed loved ones in cemeteries on Sunday morning, November 1.

blocks.text: Published November 1, 2026 8:22am
Many Filipinos all over the country went early to visit departed loved ones in cemeteries on Sunday morning, November 1.
The Manila South Cemetery in Makati City opened at 6 a.m. to the public. Around 400 visitors were initially reported on a drizzling morning, according to Super Radyo dzBB's Mao dela Cruz.
As part of security protocols, there were separate lanes for men and women. There were also designated lanes for persons with disabilities and senior citizens.
The cemetery will be open until 9 p.m.
Meanwhile, the Manila North Cemetery, the largest cemetery in the country, located in the City of Manila has so far recorded 2,800 visitors as of early Sunday.

Although there was no influx of visitors yet at Bagbag Public Cemetery in Quezon City, several barangay personnel and law enforcers are on standby at the entry and exit points to ensure safety and order.
But according to Super Radyo dzBB's Allan Gatus, there was a slight increase in visitors on Saturday. Authorities are expecting more people to arrive at the Novaliches cemetery later in the day.
Over 111,000 policemen are deployed to enforce security across the country for the observance of All Saints' Day and All Soul's Day from Nov. 1 to 2.
Aside from cemeteries, there will also be cops stationed at bus terminals and other transportation hubs amid the expected exodus of travelers. —RF, GMA News
