articles.title: India's opposition set to hold mega rally seeking election chief's resignation
articles.summary: It comes amid growing protests over a voter roll revision exercise feared to leave 130 million voters off rolls.

blocks.text: India's opposition set to hold mega rally seeking election chief's resignation

blocks.caption: Image caption, Rahul Gandhi has called on people to gather at the protest site in large numbers

blocks.text: Image source, Hindustan Times via Getty Images
Rahul Gandhi has called on people to gather at the protest site in large numbers
ByGeeta Pandey and Nikita Yadav
BBC News, Delhi
Tens of thousands of people are expected to gather in the Indian capital, Delhi, for a mega opposition rally, seeking the resignation of chief election commissioner and electoral reforms.
The rally, called by the main opposition Congress party, will begin around noon at the famous Ramlila Maidan grounds, with leaders claiming a million people could attend.
Several top leaders of the Congress-led INDIA alliance have said they would attend and the influential Gen Z-led pressure group Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) has also pledged support.
The rally comes amid growing criticism of a voter-list revision exercise that has removed 130 million names from the draft rolls across India.
The Election Commission of India (ECI) says the exercise is aimed at updating the voters' list by purging names of people who have died or moved away from their registered addresses.

But opposition parties allege that the exercise - known as the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) - could benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) by removing eligible voters from the rolls. They accuse the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) and the BJP of "vote chori (theft)". Both the BJP and the ECI have denied the allegations.

The controversy intensified in September when The Indian Express newspaper in its investigation, external reported that the CEC, Gyanesh Kumar, made key decisions related to the exercise without the agreement of the two other election commissioners, who had raised objections on more than a dozen occasions.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Protests have been going on for weeks seeking CEC Kumar's resignation and electoral reforms

blocks.text: Image source, NurPhoto via Getty Images
Protests have been going on for weeks seeking CEC Kumar's resignation and electoral reforms
The Election Commission said differences of opinion were normal in any institution and did not affect its functioning.
But concerns over the revision process have continued, with the opposition parties, the CJP and student groups organising a number of protests in Delhi and other Indian cities.

Last month, Congress MP and leader of the opposition Rahul Gandhi led tens of thousands of protesters in a march from Connaught Place in central Delhi to the Supreme Court, seeking the CEC's resignation.
"The march was just the trailer," a party leader told the BBC, adding that "Sunday's rally will be several times bigger than that".

Ahead of the rally, Gandhi said their protest was against "the demolition of Indian democracy", adding that "all the opposition parties and everybody who wants to come, political or non-political, is welcome".
"There is huge anger, huge emotional pain because millions are being disenfranchised," he said.
"We are all standing together because we are defending the Constitution. We are defending the idea of India. We are defending the vote, which is the expression of all Indians."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Thousands gathered for the last Congress rally in Delhi on 12 October

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Thousands gathered for the last Congress rally in Delhi on 12 October

Delhi police have given permission to hold Sunday's rally, but it comes with several conditions. Media reports say the rally must end by 5pm, CCTV cameras must be installed at the venue and no marches will be allowed outside the designated protest site.
The planned mega rally has also divided opinion among traders in Chandni Chowk, one of Delhi's oldest and busiest markets, located less than a kilometre from Ramlila Maidan.
Earlier this week, a group of traders said the protest could hurt business during the festive season, coming just a week before Diwali.
But a rival group of traders said they supported Gandhi's rally and criticised the BJP for taking out a march through the market on Thursday, saying that disrupted the festive season more.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Leaders of the ruling BJP party also carried out a march in Chandni Chowk market on Thursday

blocks.text: Image source, Rekha Gupta/X
Leaders of the ruling BJP party also carried out a march in Chandni Chowk market on Thursday
Authorities have deployed thousands of police and paramilitary personnel across the city, including the roads leading up to Ramlila Grounds, Sunday's protest venue.
The opposition, which has been preparing for the rally for days now, has accused the government of trying to stop people from travelling to Delhi to take part in the protest.

Rahul Gandhi has appealed to people to turn up in large numbers. "Don't worry about the police, don't worry about lathis [batons] - the BJP will not have the guts to try any of their antics," he wrote on X.
His comments come amid growing concerns about the policing of recent protests in the capital.
On 10 October, thousands of security personnel were deployed and large parts of the city were shut down to thwart protests called by the CJP against CEC Gyanesh Kumar.

All of the top CJP leaders were detained and many demonstrators were beaten and dragged through the streets to break up their protests. BBC reporters covering demonstrations saw, external police dragging away protesters and using batons on some of them.
The CJP has publicly backed the INDIA bloc rally, but it is unclear whether its senior leaders will attend.

articles.title: They came home to the Cordillera and found more than they expected
articles.summary: For Cordillerans returning from overseas, a four-day journey becomes a chance to rediscover their roots, meeting the people who keep the region’s culture, farms, and communities alive

blocks.text: BAGUIO CITY, Philippines – At 27, Izadee Nabunat has spent much of her life in Australia knowing she is Cordilleran. But she still has questions about the ancestral homeland she calls home.
Three days into a journey across the Cordillera, she stood before fellow travelers, tourism officials, and cultural performers at Mount Data Hotel, struggling to put the experience into words.
“Being a Cordilleran who grew up overseas, there has always been curiosity within me in regards to our culture and history,” she said.
The journey had answered some of those questions, she explained, but had also made her want to learn more. Then she turned to the Department of Tourism (DOT) officials who had organized the trip.
“DOT, if your target was our hearts, I can confirm you’ve captured ours completely.”

blocks.caption: Izadee Nabunat, a Cordilleran from Sydney, Australia, treks through the UNESCO-listed Nagacadan Rice Terraces in Kiangan, Ifugao, on October 18, 2026, reconnecting with her heritage during the Discover More to Love Homecoming Caravan. All photos by Mia Magdalena Fokno/Rappler

blocks.text: Nabunat was among the overseas Cordillerans who joined the Discover More to Love Homecoming Caravan from October 17 to 20.

The four-day journey brought balikbayans, tourism stakeholders, and media partners through Ifugao, Kalinga, Mountain Province, and Benguet, beginning with a festival in Baguio City and ending at a flower farm in Atok.

For participants returning from overseas, it was an opportunity to reconnect with their heritage. For the communities hosting them, it was also a chance to show what tourism could contribute to local livelihoods and the considerable work involved in preserving cultural traditions.

The journey opened on October 17 with the fifth Cordillera Festival of Festivals, when more than 500 performers representing the region’s six provinces and two cities brought their respective celebrations to Baguio’s Session Road.

From the thanksgiving traditions of Apayao’s Say-am and Benguet’s Bindiyan to the cultural presentations of Ifugao, Kalinga, Mountain Province, Abra, Baguio, and Tabuk City, the performances introduced visitors to the region’s diverse communities.
It was a lively beginning, with the rhythms of gongs, colorful traditional clothing, and stories expressed through music and dance.
But the following days would take the participants beyond staged performances and into the communities where many of those traditions continue to be practiced.
Their first provincial destination was Kiangan, Ifugao.
On October 18, the caravan visited the Nagacadan Rice Terraces, one of the five terrace clusters inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List as the Rice Terraces of the Philippine Cordilleras.
The terraces were in their post-harvest period, far from the lush green landscape often featured in travel advertisements.

blocks.caption: When the Ifugao rice terraces rest

blocks.text: Community guides explained the agricultural cycle, irrigation, heirloom rice, and the work required to maintain the fields.

Among them was Johntrey “Dandan” Dinamling, a young resident who had put his schooling on hold to help his family farm and was gaining experience as a tourism guide. It was one of his first experiences guiding visitors.

His story offered a glimpse of the choices facing young people in farming communities. Maintaining the terraces requires labor and traditional knowledge, while families must also find ways to earn enough to meet their needs.
Tourism presents another source of income, particularly when visitors engage local guides, purchase community products, and spend time learning from residents.
The caravan also encountered traditional Ifugao houses, weaving, and local food, including binakle, a rice cake wrapped in banana leaves.
At one traditional house, visitors joined their guides in singing the Tuwali folk song “Itetem ta humgopak,” meaning “Put the ladder down so I can enter.”

blocks.caption: Threads of tradition take shape on a loom at Mabilong Weavers Village in Lubuagan, Kalinga.

blocks.text: For Nabunat, the experience in Kiangan proved especially memorable.
She recalled how the group’s guide later asked participants to identify their favorite part of the journey.
They could not choose.
“Simply there was no way to choose a single moment,” she said.
From Ifugao, the caravan traveled to Tabuk City on October 18, before continuing to Lubuagan, Kalinga, the following morning.
At Mabilong Weavers Village, visitors watched artisans create traditional Kalinga textiles, observing the intricate work behind patterns that carry cultural meaning.
The group later visited Awichon Cultural Village, established by the late National Living Treasure Alonzo Saclag and his wife, Rebecca Saclag.
Recognized in 2000 for his contributions to Kalinga performing arts and dance traditions, Saclag devoted much of his life to promoting the culture of his people.
His wife continues to share that work with visitors.

blocks.caption: A craftswoman demonstrates traditional beadmaking at Awichon Cultural Village in Lubuagan, Kalinga.

blocks.text: Rebecca Saclag personally guided the caravan through traditional houses, weaving and beadmaking activities, and other features of Kalinga community life.
She explained that their family had helped recreate traditional houses so younger generations could see the forms of architecture that have become less common as households build modern homes.
“Ginawa namin para makita ninyo (We did it for you to see),” she told the visitors.
She also showed the group wild fruit trees she had planted during the COVID-19 pandemic, recalling the difficulty of finding fruits rich in vitamin C.
Her stories brought an intimate dimension to Awichon. Cultural preservation involves the efforts of families who spend years building, collecting, teaching, and sharing what they know.
The visitors also enjoyed local dishes prepared by the Pasil Slow Food Community, accompanied by cultural performances.
Later that afternoon, the caravan reached Bontoc, Mountain Province, where the Bontoc Museum offered another encounter with the region’s history.

A cultural welcome preceded the visit, which included traditional houses, rice granaries, and displays explaining Bontoc customs and community institutions such as the ato, historically a gathering place for elders and community affairs.

blocks.caption: Traditional stone-and-thatch structures and a sculpted figure are among the outdoor displays at the Bontoc Museum.

blocks.text: By evening, the group arrived at Mount Data Hotel in Bauko.
It was there that Nabunat, representing a Philippine Cordillera organization based in Sydney, expressed her gratitude for the journey.
“We truly felt at home in every city and barangay across the provinces,” she said.
She also spoke of responsible tourism and the possibility of helping promote the Cordillera to overseas communities.
Her enthusiasm was evident. But beyond the warm welcomes and cultural experiences was a question that tourism destinations across the region continue to confront.
How can growing visitor numbers translate into lasting benefits for residents while protecting the resources, traditions, and everyday life that make these places worth visiting?
The caravan’s final stop offered a practical example.
On October 20, the participants arrived at Northern Blossom Flower Farm in Atok, Benguet.
The farm’s sweeping mountain views were familiar to many visitors through photographs and social media, although its famous flower displays were not yet at their peak.

Owner Mellany Ganayan explained that the main blooming season generally runs from December to June. The farm grows more than 30 varieties of flowers, including hydrangeas, carnations, snapdragons, and calla lilies.
Before becoming a tourist attraction, Northern Blossom was primarily a commercial flower farm.
That changed after photographs circulated online and television programs featured the property in 2018, attracting visitors eager to experience Atok’s landscape.
“We were known as a stopover before,” Ganayan said, referring to Atok’s former role as a place travelers passed through on their way to Bontoc or Sagada.
“But now we’re not just a stopover. We are a destination.”
The growth in tourism has brought employment and business opportunities.

blocks.caption: Even between peak blooming seasons, Northern Blossom Flower Farm in Atok, Benguet, offers sweeping views of the Cordillera mountains.

blocks.text: Ganayan said the farm once had around seven workers, but now employs more than 30. It also provides seasonal opportunities for student guides and workers.
She recalled that Atok had about 11 lodging establishments and homestays in 2023, compared with approximately 47 at the time of the visit.
As more tourists began arriving, she said, residents saw opportunities to improve their houses and offer accommodation.
The figures reflect Ganayan’s account of local tourism growth.
Yet increased visitor numbers also mean greater demands on resources, particularly water.
Ganayan said warmer daytime temperatures and dry periods have increased the farm’s irrigation needs, while tourists add to water consumption.

She illustrated the problem with a simple calculation. If 1,000 visitors each used three liters of water for a toilet flush, that would mean 3,000 liters consumed. Two flushes per visitor would require 6,000 liters.
For a farm whose primary business still depends on growing flowers, that is a considerable amount of water.
Ganayan said they are exploring additional water tanks, water-saving toilets, and the reuse of wastewater for irrigation.
Northern Blossom also closes on Sundays, partly to give workers and the surrounding community time for church and other personal activities.
The farm’s experience shows both sides of tourism growth.
More visitors can mean more jobs, homestays, and income. But sustaining those benefits requires planning, investment, and consideration for the community’s needs.
By the time the caravan ended in Benguet, the participants had spent four days meeting people whose daily work sustains the places that attract visitors.

They had walked through rice terraces maintained by farmers, watched weavers at their looms, listened to cultural workers share their knowledge, and learned how a flower-growing community was adapting to increasing tourism.
For Nabunat and the other overseas Cordillerans, the journey was particularly personal.
They had returned to familiar mountains but encountered stories and traditions they had not fully known.

blocks.caption: Traditional Kalinga dishes prepared by the Pasil Slow Food Community are served in clay pots lined with banana leaves at Awichon Cultural Village in Lubuagan, Kalinga.

blocks.text: At Mount Data, Nabunat said the experience had deepened their interest in their heritage and strengthened their desire to help promote the region overseas.
She also expressed hope that tourism could create opportunities while respecting the culture and way of life of host communities.
The enthusiasm of returning Cordillerans is an opportunity for the region, although turning it into lasting benefits will depend on how communities are supported and how tourism develops.
Back in Atok, Ganayan and her workers were preparing for another flowering season, with irrigation, maintenance, and water conservation among their concerns.
The next blooms were still weeks away.
For the balikbayans, meanwhile, the journey had ended with new memories, more questions about their heritage, and reasons to come home again. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Abdul El-Sayed’s campaign disinvites Haley Stevens from events to limit ‘distractions’
articles.summary:
A public spat has cast Democratic tensions in the spotlight as the close US Senate race draws to a head

Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for Michigan’s tightly fought US Senate race,…

blocks.text: Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for Michigan’s tightly fought US Senate race, has asked Democratic congresswoman Haley Stevens to stay away from his campaign events.

“I don’t want any distractions,” El-Sayed told reporters after a campaign rally, according to the New York Times. “It seems as though other folks are more interested in making this race about things that it’s not about.”
The two had planned to appear together on Sunday at a church service in Detroit.

The public rupture between the progressive El-Sayed and the more moderate Stevens, whom he defeated in a bitter primary, has cast Democratic tensions into the spotlight in one of the most consequential elections in the party’s campaign to retake control of the Senate.
Stevens endorsed El-Sayed shortly after he won the primary election in August, and planned to campaign with him on Sunday.

But Stevens had until now avoided appearing publicly with her former opponent, whom she has criticized publicly for weeks. Her fiance, Jason Turkish, has campaigned on behalf of Republican candidate Mike Rogers.

And just two days before they were scheduled to campaign together this weekend, Stevens demanded that El-Sayed denounce an outside group’s political ad that blamed higher prices on US support for Israel’s war in Gaza.

“Congresswoman Stevens seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago,” El-Sayed shot back in a statement, which noted that the American Israel Public Affairs Committee spent heavily to defeat him in the primary.

“Let’s all focus on the task at hand: that’s beating Mike Rogers, holding Trump accountable, and getting money out of politics, putting money in pockets, and passing Medicare for All,” the statement said.
The open feuding worries many Democrats, who see the tight race as a must-win for the party to win back the Senate.

“I have no idea what the hell Haley Stevens is doing,” Michigan state senator Mallory McMorrow told CNN Friday. “This is a moment where we have to recognize the stakes. People are not talking about ads. They are not talking about Haley Stevens. They are talking about the price of gas and groceries.”

articles.title: Marcos on Undas 2026: Extend devotion for the departed to helping one another
articles.summary: President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. on Sunday called on the public to extend the same devotion they show in remembering their late loved ones to the way they treat other people.

blocks.text: Published November 1, 2026 7:54am
President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. on Sunday called on the public to extend the same devotion they show in remembering their late loved ones to the way they treat other people.
The president joined Filipino Catholics and the rest of the country in observing All Saints' Day (Undas) and All Souls' Day this November 1 and 2.
In his message, Marcos called on the Catholic faithful to be inspired by the selflessness of saints.

"We also draw inspiration from the saints, whose devotion found expression in selfless service, and from countless individuals whose sacrifices have sustained our communities. Their lives call on us to make the most of the time entrusted to us, and to find lasting purpose in every kindness we give and every burden we help carry for others," he said.
Further, the president called on everyone to give the same time devoted in honoring the departed to listening to everyone struggling.

"I invite everyone to practice the same devotion we show in remembrance into the way we treat one another. If we can make time to revere those who have passed, we can also make room to listen to those who struggle, and let that same concern guide our society and the work of government. May our efforts in nurturing a Bagong Pilipinas stand as a greater testament to our lives than any words or monuments carved in stone we leave behind," he added.
November 1 and 2 were declared as special non-working holidays.

"Even in their absence, those who have lost continue to bring us closer together, keeping alive the bonds that have made the Filipino family and all the whole nation resilient and strong through challenges," said Marcos.

Marcos earlier said the government is making the necessary preparations to ensure the safe and orderly trip for Filipinos who will head to their respective provinces or travel elsewhere for this year’s Undas. —Vince Angelo Ferreras/KG, GMA News

articles.title: I've been stuck on a tiny Pacific island for years and can't get a transit visa to fly home
articles.summary: Ruchira Ranasingha, 50, has been stranded in the Cook Islands since 2023 and wants to return to Sri Lanka.

blocks.text: I've been stuck on a tiny Pacific island for years and can't get a transit visa to fly home

blocks.caption: Ruchira Ranasingha, a 50-year-old Sri Lankan woman, faces the camera against the corner of a wood-panelled room. She is wearing a bright pink patterned top, with dark hair tied back. The photograph is a head-and-shoulders portrait taken indoors, with natural light illuminating the wooden walls be…

blocks.text: Image source, Supplied
ByAyeshea PereraAsia Digital Editor and Dinuk HewawitharanaBBC Sinhala
When Ruchira Ranasingha left Sri Lanka almost a decade ago, she could never have imagined she would end up stranded on a tiny archipelago in the South Pacific.
The 50-year-old has now been stuck in the Cook Islands for three years. She tells the BBC she is desperate to go back to Sri Lanka and has even offered to go "handcuffed, bound and gagged".
Ranasingha had been hoping to settle in New Zealand.

After seeking asylum there, she says she followed an immigration adviser's recommendation to temporarily exit the country to apply for a work visa. But once in the Cook Islands, her application was rejected. And by leaving New Zealand, she had breached the terms of her existing asylum-linked visa.
Now New Zealand is refusing to issue her a transit visa that would allow her to fly home to Sri Lanka.

Australia is refusing too. The only other international destinations she can fly to from the Cook Islands - Tahiti and Hawaii - require her to give biometric information in New Zealand before any visa can be processed.
As a result, she has no feasible way of leaving.

"My son - my only child - is getting married in November and I really want to be there for his wedding. My mother is so worried about what has happened to me that she is constantly in and out of hospital," she says through tears.
"I will do anything they ask of me - I just want to go home."

blocks.caption: Map of the Pacific Ocean showing the location of the Cook Islands in relation to surrounding countries and territories. Australia and New Zealand are labelled to the southwest, Sri Lanka to the west, Hawaii to the north-east and Tahiti to the east. The Cook Islands are highlighted in red southeas…

blocks.text: Ranasingha left Sri Lanka in 2018 after being forced to close her small T-shirt factory due to a loss of business. Struggling to repay loans, she moved to Hong Kong to work as a domestic caregiver looking after elderly people and children.
Her brother tells BBC Sinhala she had come under immense financial pressure. Her husband was a drug addict who died about seven years ago, he adds.

In December 2022, Ranasingha headed to New Zealand, where she says she lived with a cousin on a two-month visit visa. As it came close to expiring, she says an immigration interpreter helped her apply for asylum on the grounds she was facing threats from lenders in Sri Lanka.

She was granted an asylum seeker "open work visa", enabling her to work for almost any employer for a year. She found a job at a restaurant, she says, which ultimately agreed to sponsor an employment visa, which she believed would give her longer-term stability.
But as asylum seekers generally cannot apply for other visas while their applications are processed in New Zealand, it was declined.

That's when she got in touch with Immigration & Secretarial Services, a firm she claims told her a fresh application for an employment visa could be made from overseas. Email correspondence the BBC has seen shows its manager, Sylviane Gallant, saying she would initiate the process as soon as Ranasingha had left the country.
So she booked a short stay in the Cook Islands while the application was made.
It turned out to be a disastrous decision.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Cook Islands is known for its beaches and volcanic peaks - but Ruchira Ranasingha is an involuntary guest

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
Cook Islands is known for its beaches and volcanic peaks - but Ruchira Ranasingha is an involuntary guest

She was again refused the employment visa. And by leaving New Zealand, she had violated the terms of her existing visa. New Zealand authorities made it clear they would not grant her any future visas.

Gallant claimed to make various interventions on her behalf, including writing to politicians including Chris Penk, New Zealand's then-immigration minister. But ultimately, Ranasingha says Gallant admitted the situation was her fault and told her "there was nothing more she could do".
"She told me I was better off going home. There was nothing holding me there so I agreed to go."
But when she turned up at the airport with an Air New Zealand ticket to Sri Lanka in hand, she was told she couldn't board the flight without a New Zealand transit visa.
Three applications for a New Zealand transit visa were rejected. Authorities said they weren't convinced she would leave New Zealand. Four applications for Australian transit visas were rejected too.

In one of its rejections, New Zealand suggested she explore other routes. But both the US state of Hawaii and the French Polynesian island of Tahiti told her she would need to provide biometric information before any visa could be processed - and that could only be done in person in New Zealand.

Her latest application to New Zealand, which included all the details of the alternative routes she'd been trying, as well as her son's upcoming wedding and mother's failing health, was also rejected.
"I have lost so much money on tickets. For almost four years I have been just applying for visa after visa with nothing working out," she says, breaking down.

blocks.caption: Ruchira Ranasingha, a 50-year-old woman, smiles for the camera in an outdoor setting, with trees and other greenery visible in the background behind her. She is wearing a blue denim short with brass buttons, and is wearing red lipstick and a gold chain. Her dark hair is tied into a ponytail.

blocks.text: On a collection of islands known for their sweeping sandy beaches and rugged volcanic peaks, just four hours from Auckland, Ranasingha has been an involuntary guest.
She's luckier than others in her position, she says, with her hotel letting her stay free of charge in its staff accommodation and friendly locals providing her with food and clothing.
One of the hotel directors even gave her a sewing machine, she says, enabling her to make a small income.
"My mother always tells me I must have done something good, for me to be in a place like this where people have been so kind to me," she tells the BBC.
But it does little to ease the sense of being trapped.
Ranasingha says the stress is impacting her health. "I am scared something is going to happen to me," she says.
"I don't know what her solution is, to be honest," says Auckland-based immigration law specialist Alastair McClymont.

She had received "terrible advice" which "certainly" could not have come from a genuine immigration lawyer, he says, pointing to an industry of "so-called immigration consultants" who charge people to lodge applications without fully understanding the risks involved. Ranasingha says she has parted with thousands of New Zealand dollars in fees to Immigration & Secretarial Services.
The BBC reached out to Gallant but did not receive a response.

McClymont suggests New Zealand authorities will not grant the transit visa because, as far as they are concerned, she has no intention of returning to Sri Lanka having made an asylum claim saying her life was in danger there.
New Zealand co-ordinates with its neighbour Australia which means it won't want to let her transit either, he says, and France and the US are likely to reach similar conclusions.
To leave, "she is going to have to transit through somewhere and no-one will want to take the risk."

Immigration New Zealand told the BBC it had received multiple transit visa applications from Ranasingha - all declined "as we were not satisfied she has a genuine intention to transit through New Zealand".

When asked why one couldn't be granted even when Ranasingha had offered to be handcuffed and escorted, a representative of the immigration minister's office said those measures do not prevent individuals from making an asylum claim.

Australia's interior ministry said it would not comment on individual cases. It said any non-citizens travelling to Australia "must satisfy the requirements of the Migration Act 1958 (the Act) and the Migration Regulations 1994".

Meanwhile, Ranasingha's family have been trying to see if the Sri Lankan government can help. Her brother says they have tried "every possible avenue... but so far we haven't been able to get anywhere on this".

Sri Lanka's foreign ministry told the BBC it was "taking all necessary steps to facilitate her return to Sri Lanka from the Cook Islands. Officials of the Sri Lankan High Commission in Wellington, New Zealand, as well as the relevant New Zealand authorities, are working closely with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs on this matter."
But Ranasingha's brother is deeply worried.
"Her mental state is not good," her tells BBC Sinhala.
"One of the times we spoke, she told me that if they were not willing to get her back home alive, they might at least repatriate her body."
Additional reporting by Kethaki Masilamani and Julianna Khan

If you've been affected by issues involving suicide or feelings of despair, details of organisations offering advice and support for people in the UK are available from BBC Action Line. Help and support outside the UK can be found at Befrienders Worldwide, external.

articles.title: Feng shui predictions ni Master Hanz Cua para sa Nobyembre 1, 2026

articles.title: Binance says billions replaced from hack that FBI blames on North Korea
articles.summary: Crypto exchange Binance said on Saturday it has been able to replace 90 per cent of the amount stolen after a record $6.3-billion US hack of its platform. The FBI on Saturday ‌said the North Korean…

image.caption: Crypto exchange Binance said on Saturday it has been able to replace 90 per cent of the amount stolen after a record $6.3-billion US hack of its platform by using company money to buy new tokens. (Dado Ruvic/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

Crypto exchange Binance said on Saturday it has been able to replace 90 per cent of the amount stolen after a record $6.3-billion US hack of its platform. The FBI on Saturday ‌said the North Korean state-sponsored unit known as TraderTraitor was responsible for the attack.
'We've now replenished 90% of the stolen assets,' says cryptocurrency exchange
Crypto exchange Binance said on Saturday it has been able to replace 90 per cent of the amount stolen after a record $6.3-billion US hack of its platform by using company money to buy new tokens.
The remaining 10 per cent consists ‌of tokens that are less liquid, meaning they may take longer to buy, it said in a statement posted on X.

"We've now replenished 90 per cent of the stolen assets, and we're committed to covering the remaining 10 per cent. Our users will ​not bear the financial impact of this incident," co-CEO Richard ​Teng said on X on Saturday.

Crypto prices fell on Friday, while Binance — the world's biggest crypto exchange — sought to reassure customers that their funds were safe ​after losing more than $6 billion worth of crypto in a hack that ⁠analysts and the FBI ⁠blamed on North Korea.

The FBI on Saturday ‌said the North Korean state-sponsored unit known as TraderTraitor was responsible for the attack. Members of the unit were observed by law enforcement converting stolen assets into the cryptocurrency ethereum, the FBI said in a statement, adding that it expects "further laundering" of ⁠the assets through the use of related technology.
Hackers steal nearly $6.3B US in crypto

Teng said on Friday that the breach was a "complex attack" involving a compromised laptop and malicious software designed to delete evidence of its activity, making it ‌harder to trace and investigate.
After the hack, the exchange stopped allowing customers to withdraw their funds, but it said on Saturday it was still on track to reopen withdrawals on Sunday.

items: Binance says $6.3B US hacked in what could be largest cryptocurrency theft ever
Trump pardons Canadian Binance CEO who failed to stop illegal activity on crypto platform

blocks.text: Binance said it has set aside around $6.34 billion of company funds internally ​to cover the losses.

The money spent re-buying tokens came from using part of its $1 billion Secure Asset Fund for ⁠Users (SAFU), a bitcoin reserve it holds to protect customers in the event of security breaches, as ⁠well as some of its Futures Insurance Fund, and the company's own corporate treasury, ⁠it ⁠said on X.
Binance also said it ​had taken a new snapshot of assets held on its platform as of 00:00 GMT on ​Oct. 31, as part ⁠of its proof-of-reserves process.

Users holding the 10 listed tokens — BTC, ETH, USDT, BNB, SOL, USDC, XRP, USD1, RLUSD, and ZEC — would be able to verify that their assets were backed at a minimum ratio of 1:1 once the full proof was available, it said.

articles.title: Tusk defends overhaul of Poland’s constitutional court despite protests
articles.summary:
Prime minister says shake-up is vital to restore tribunal crippled by years of political disputes

Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, has vowed to see through a contested overhaul of the…

blocks.text: Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, has vowed to see through a contested overhaul of the country’s constitutional court, declaring that “in certain matters, there can be no compromise”.

In a prime-time television address on Saturday night, Tusk was defiant, despite overnight protests that saw riot police drafted to protect the court’s building, saying the shake-up was vital to restore a tribunal crippled by years of political disputes.
Paralysed for more than a decade, the court sat at the core of rule of law clashes between the rightwing Law and Justice (PiS) party and the EU during the party’s eight-year rule.

Since returning to office in 2023, the centre-right Tusk has sought to unwind those judicial changes, but his agenda has been frustrated by opposition-aligned presidents with extensive veto powers. Earlier this year, president Karol Nawrocki refused to swear in five judges approved by parliament.

The crisis flared again on Friday when a group of government-backed judges attempted to seize procedural control of the tribunal, suspending the PiS-appointed chief judge and deputy and prompting street protests.

blocks.caption: Conservative supporters assemble outside the constitutional court in Warsaw. Photograph: Agata Grzybowska/Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: Defending the action, Tusk said “there was never any doubt that the court in the form imposed by PiS was not a genuine court”, citing adverse rulings from European tribunals.
He compared the opposition outrage to “a thief snatching an elderly woman’s handbag, running off, and when he is caught, he screams that he is subjected to violence”.

Tusk said: “Let’s call things for what they are: for years, there have been organisations and politicians in Poland who seek to destroy democracy and the rule of law. It is no coincidence they find support among pro-Russian forces globally.”

He later highlighted that Russia’s former president Dmitry Medvedev had joined the opposition in an outcry over the changes, accusing Warsaw of “a constitutional coup” and “hounding the conservatives”. “And everything is clear,” Tusk said.

He also criticised opposition-aligned Nawrocki for joining the protests on Friday night and forcing his entry into the court’s building to intervene. “In a democratic state, no politician can enter a court to issue orders or intimidate judges – not even the president,” Tusk said. “We Poles have succeeded too well in building a strong state to surrender now.”
He said it was the government’s duty to ensure its security and the conditions necessary for the court to operate. “And I intend to fulfil that duty,” he said.
after newsletter promotion
The confrontation sets the battle lines before next year’s parliamentary election, with polls pointing to a close race between Tusk’s broad coalition and the nationalist right.
However, experts remain divided over whether the government’s procedural gambit at the court is lawful.
Poland’s Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights said on Saturday the legal basis for the temporary suspension was “questionable”, warning it would “not contribute” to restoring the court.

The foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, conceded that the events outside the court were “not elegant”, but insisted: “The alternative was to concede an unconstitutional transformation of Poland into a presidential republic.”

Nawrocki held some cross-party political talks on Saturday, with no apparent breakthrough. His senior aide, Zbigniew Bogucki, responded to Tusk’s address, calling the prime minister “a pathological liar, who is setting Poland ablaze”.

articles.title: Alberta woman accused of sex with 15-year-old guilty of sexual assault
articles.summary: Jurors have reached a verdict in Alexa Suitor's sexual assault trial, finding Suitor guilty of sexual assault and sexual interference.

image.caption: Jurors returned a guilty verdict Saturday in the sexual assault trial of 35-year-old Alexa Suitor. (Facebook)

blocks.text: Calgary·Breaking
Jurors have reached a verdict in Alexa Suitor's sexual assault trial, finding Suitor guilty of sexual assault and sexual interference.
Jurors returned verdict Saturday afternoon after deliberating since Friday afternoon
A Sundre, Alta. woman accused of having sex with a 15-year-old boy at a New Year's Eve party has been convicted of sexual assault and sexual interference.
Alexa Suitor, 35, did not outwardly react when the jury foreperson read the verdict Saturday afternoon after 24 hours of deliberating.
The jury began deliberations Friday afternoon after hearing closing arguments prepared by prosecutors James Molloy and Laura Somers and defence lawyer Patrick Fagan.
Justice Douglas Mah will hear sentencing arguments at a later date.
Fagan indicated to the court he will be asking for a discharge for his client, which would mean she would not serve any time in jail.

items: 'We did not have sex': Sundre woman accused of sexually assaulting teen boy testifies in own defence

blocks.text: Over the week-long trial, the jury heard that on Dec. 31, 2023, a number of teens and adults attended a New Year's Eve party at a home in the Sundre area.
The teens and Suitor spent most of the night drinking in a cabin on the property while the other adults hung out in the main house.
'We took it too far'
At the end of the night, Suitor and several of the teens worked out sleeping arrangements. Some were to spend the night on cots in the living room; others would be in the bedrooms.

The victim — who CBC News is calling C.D. to comply with a publication ban — testified that he fell asleep on a cot and woke up to Suitor touching his penis. He said this led to sexual intercourse on the cot.
C.B. said the next day, he received a Snapchat message from Suitor saying “we took it too far last night.”
Two friends of C.B.’s also testified.
Suitor denied sexual touching
One friend said that she saw the pair having sex when she went into the kitchen to get a glass of water.
The other friend said that he saw the next-day Snapchat message from Suitor.
Suitor testified in her own defence, telling jurors that the sex and sexual touching never happened.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Meghan Grant is a justice affairs reporter. She has been covering courts, crime and stories of police accountability in southern Alberta for more than 15 years. Send Meghan a story tip at meghan.grant@cbc.ca.

blocks.text: A man has been charged under the Explosives Act and Firearms Order after police searched properties in Belfast.

The 35-year-old was charged with offences including two counts of possessing explosives under suspicious circumstances, and possession of a prohibited weapon (discharge of electricity or noxious gas).
He is due to appear before Belfast magistrates court on Monday, the Police Service of Northern Ireland said.
The charges follow searches at properties in the Shankill Road and Edwina Street areas of north Belfast on Friday and Saturday.
DCI McCallum said: “Following these searches a number of suspicious devices, along with other items, were located and seized by officers for forensic examination.
“Local residents who were evacuated as a precaution have now been allowed to return home following the public safety operation conducted alongside ammunition technical officers.
“All cordons have now been lifted from the area, and we thank local residents for their patience as inquiries were conducted yesterday and into today.”

McCallum added: “As we continue to investigate the circumstances surrounding this incident, we would appeal to anyone who may have information that could assist with inquiries to contact us on 101, quoting reference number 261 30/10/26.”

articles.title: NASA telescope predicted to plunge back to Earth after failed rescue mission
articles.summary: An aging NASA telescope is barely clinging to space after a failed rescue effort left it tottering lower and lower.

image.caption: In this image provided by NASA, Spectrum Astro workers remove the final pieces of protective cover on the Swift spacecraft in Hangar AE at Cape Canaveral Air Force Station, Fla., in September 2002. (NASA/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New
An aging NASA telescope is barely clinging to space after a failed rescue effort left it tottering lower and lower.
Years of intense solar activity dragged Swift down faster than usual
The U.S. Space Force predicts the Swift Observatory will come crashing down on or around Friday.

Most of the 1.5-ton telescope is expected to burn up in the atmosphere. But a handful of pieces made of denser-than-lead tungsten and some mirror parts could survive re-entry, according to NASA's Brad Cenko, the mission's chief scientist.

Any surviving wreckage will most likely plunge into the ocean. But swaths of Africa, Australia, India, Southeast Asia, and Central and South America are within the re-entry zone. The Space Force is tracking the telescope's dwindling path.

Its cosmic cremation has the Swift team mourning yet full of gratitude for the observations the telescope made during its 22 years in orbit. Swift blasted off on Nov. 20, 2004, to search for some of the biggest explosions in the universe: gamma ray bursts and supernovas.
Workers look at the final pieces of protective cover on the Swift spacecraft that must be removed at Cape Canaveral Air Force Station in September 2002. (NASA/The Associated Press)

"We've known this day would come since before Swift was launched. At least in low-Earth orbit, what goes up must come down. And that end is catastrophic," said Pennsylvania State University's John Nousek, an astronomer who led the control team.

Intense solar activity over the past few years dragged Swift down faster than usual. NASA hired Katalyst Space a year ago to mount a rush rescue. But the company's three-armed robot named Link ran into trouble after launching in July and got no closer than 12 to 15 kilometres to the telescope. Link plunged back to Earth in September.

items: This satellite is falling towards Earth, so scientists hatched a plan to give it a lil' push

blocks.text: Swift resumed observations once the rescue attempt was called off, discovering even more gamma ray bursts and other ultra high-energy events. But by late October, the telescope was too low to remain steady for observations, and its systems were shut down.

Its final tally: more than 2,000 gamma ray bursts and 1,400 exploding stars, not to mention a slew of comets, asteroids and star-shredding black holes. The telescope's superpower was its ability to swivel swiftly — thus its name — toward erupting celestial events.

NASA considered Swift a first responder for the Hubble and Webb space telescopes and others that would follow its alerts and provide deeper investigations. Scientists are still figuring out how to fill the gap.
"Our fervent hope is that the lessons learned by the successes of Swift can be applied to new generations of space missions to accelerate our discoveries about the universe," Nousek said in an email.

A federal judge on Saturday threw out U.S. President Donald Trump's multibillion-dollar lawsuit against the Wall Street Journal and media mogul Rupert Murdoch over a story reporting on his ties to wealthy financier Jeffrey Epstein.
Judge finds U.S. president did not prove defendants made statements with actual malice
U.S. District Judge Darrin Gayles in Miami dismissed the suit with prejudice, ruling that the president did not prove the defendants made defamatory statements with actual malice.
