articles.title: A world-first focus on long-term outcomes could transform UK government – or create new spending fights
articles.summary:
Tucked away in John Healey’s budget is decision to ringfence preventative projects where future savings outweigh initial cost

It merited the briefest of mentions in John Healey’s speech and…

blocks.text: It merited the briefest of mentions in John Healey’s speech and just one paragraph in the 166-page budget document, but some believe it could revolutionise not just public spending but the very process of government itself: a new focus on long-term outcomes.

The idea in the broad sense is very simple. Any spending deemed to be “preventative” – that is, the initial outlay will be more than made up for by future savings – will from now on be ringfenced, meaning it cannot be raided for more immediate needs.

This might sound uncontroversial, but it follows many years of long-term spending being pillaged to plug day-to-day gaps, particularly so during and after the austerity measures of the 2010 coalition government, which slashed numerous prevention-based services, not least the Sure Start programme for families with young children.

But now, starting from the upcoming spending review, which kicks off next year, projects that can be shown to bring down costs in the future will be protected via a new piece of jargon – a preventative departmental expenditure limit, or PDEL.

“It could end up being quite a major change in how the government runs spending reviews, and the entire spending framework,” said Stuart Hoddinott, at the Institute for Government thinktank, which had called for such a system to be implemented. Officials in the Treasury agree, with one calling it an “important reform”.

That is, however, about as straightforward as it gets. The budget document uses Andy Burnham’s new spending to prevent rough sleeping as an example of the sort of thing that would qualify. A few other areas would seem likely: for example, public health programmes to prevent future illness, and Sure Start-type early years schemes.

blocks.caption: Andy Burnham’s new rough-sleeping prevention plan is the type of project that would qualify to be protected under the PDEL. Photograph: Leon Neal/Getty Images

blocks.text: But beyond that, no one really knows what might or might not qualify for PDEL status. Departments say they are waiting for Treasury guidance, which has not yet been drawn up. “A lot depends on the definition,” Hoddinott said. “While it sounds simple, it becomes quite difficult when you think about how it will work in practice, as you could make any argument that almost all types of spending are preventative.”

Government officials agree, with one making the point that, in theory, the Ministry of Defence could argue all its spending is preventive, given the very obvious costs to the country of fighting a war, let alone losing one.
There is therefore the potential for a new variant of the endless spending-review tussles between departments and the Treasury, as ministers try to protect their pet projects from future plunder.

But what is perhaps just as important is the symbolism. Some other governments around the world protect specific preventative budgets – public health, for example – but this is believed to be the first time one has introduced this as a blanket policy.

Government officials are billing the decision as part of a wider focus under Burnham to try to deal with knotty and neglected issues that have longer-term costs and repercussions, including rough sleeping and adult social care.
after newsletter promotion

One said: “Too often government departments have ended up raiding these types of budgets to fund short-term measures. This is an attempt to combat that as part of a wider push to transform the way the state operates.”
Those whose work revolves around trying to generate long-term benefits to the public are cautiously delighted.
“This does feel like a really good thing,” said Greg Fell, Sheffield city council’s director of public health and the president of the Association of Directors of Public Health.

“There are a lot of questions about how it will work. Is it about preventing future acute demand, or creating the conditions for communities to thrive? Those are different things and they require a different mindset and way of operating. And with some spending, it might take decades to realise the benefits.
“But as a country we have never been very good at this sort of thing, so it’s up to all of us to make sure it works.”

articles.title: Ads accusing Republican candidates of protecting Epstein fill airwaves in final midterm push
articles.summary:
But select Democrats, too, are being accused of having ties to the late sex offender as country prepares to vote

In races across the country, Democratic candidates or groups that support…

blocks.text: In races across the country, Democratic candidates or groups that support them have released ads accusing Republicans of protecting pedophiles by voting against legislation to release files related to Jeffrey Epstein.
The ads appear intended to evoke an emotional response by accusing candidates of “protecting” Epstein, a notorious pedophile accused of running a sex-trafficking ring involving minors.

An analysis from CNN found that candidates and outside groups have spent more than $35m on Epstein-related ads. Another from the Washington Post found that Democrats spent more than $40m on Epstein-related ads across six key Senate races.

In Colorado, ads targeting Republican Jeff Crank note that the lawmaker voted against releasing the Epstein files. In one, the family members of Virginia Giuffre, a woman who survived abuse at the hands of Epstein and died by suicide last year, claim Crank “covered up Epstein’s crimes to protect Donald Trump”.
Ashley Hinson, a Senate candidate in Iowa, was accused of voting to “protect her donors” by refusing to vote to release the Epstein files.
“This week I had to explain to my boys, ‘No, Mom does not protect pedophiles,’” Hinson said in a campaign ad responding to attacks over the Epstein files.

An ad targeting Mike Collins, the Republican running for a Georgia Senate seat, says “Mike Collins voted against releasing the Epstein files even after he knew Epstein’s sex-trafficking operation exploited 14-year-old girls for sex”.
Florida Republican Jimmy Patronis faced an attack from his Democratic opponent, claiming he called investigating Epstein “a waste of his time”.

A spokesperson for Crank’s campaign accused the Epstein-related ad of being “intentionally vague”, in a statement to the Washington Post, because his position was that he would vote against the file’s release until he could be confident that victim information was properly redacted. The campaign also said it was “unfortunate” that his opponent, Jessica Killin, was “preying on a grieving family with the help of the Washington Democrats”.

Crank’s staff invited and met with Giuffre’s family, though Crank himself did not meet with them in person, the New York Times reported. Crank’s campaign also said it offered to meet with Epstein victims before the vote on the legislation.

Last year, Democrats and a select few House Republicans tried to force a vote on the Epstein files through a discharge petition – a procedure used in Congress to bypass the traditional steps of legislation and force a vote on the House floor.

Donald Trump, who knew Epstein in the 1990s and early 2000s, opposed the discharge petition for the files, reversing his campaign promise to increase government transparency. House Republicans largely aligned themselves with him, prompting anger from high-profile Trump voters.

Eventually, under pressure from allies, Trump supported the legislation, giving Republican lawmakers the go-ahead to vote for it. All but one House Republican voted for the Epstein Files Transparency Act.

Many of the ads omit the fact that nearly every House Republican voted to release the Epstein files when the Epstein Files Transparency Act came to the floor, although at that point Trump had agreed to sign the legislation and release the files. Instead, the ads refer to Republicans opposing early attempts to force the legislation to the floor.
Republicans have pointed to this fact when disputing the attack ads.
after newsletter promotion

“Of course I voted to release the Epstein files,” Hinson said in a direct-to-camera ad, accusing her opponent, Josh Turek, of lying. While Hinson voted for the final Epstein Files Transparency Act, she did not sign on to the discharge petition.

Patronis, meanwhile, never called the investigation a “waste of time”, but told a local radio station that while he had “no problem getting everything all released”, the issue was a “massive energy and time suck at the end of the day”.

Melissa Stone, a spokesperson for Patronis’s campaign, highlighted his work with Trump to obtain disaster funding after Hurricane Isaias and said his opponent, Gay Valimont, was “still talking about a dead pedophile in a sad web video than helping the people of [the first congressional district] recover.”
Some Republicans and groups supporting the GOP have sought to flip the script, accusing Democrats of taking money from donors who had ties to Epstein.

During a Georgia Senate debate, Collins accused his opponent, Jon Ossoff, of accepting campaign donations from Reid Hoffman, a tech billionaire who had ties to Epstein. Hoffman has said he only knew Epstein through fundraising relationships and regrets it.
“You can claim to fight against the Epstein class, but I’m going to tell you, this call is coming from inside the house and the Epstein class is on stage right now and it’s you,” Collins said.

In New Mexico’s gubernatorial race, an outside group released an ad accusing Democratic candidate Deb Haaland of accepting a ride on Epstein’s private jet and taking “tens of thousands of dollars from Epstein businesses” and then “asking for more”.
Haaland did not fly on Epstein’s jet, but did take a flight booked by one of Epstein’s companies in 2014. Haaland has said she was unaware the chartered flight was owned by an Epstein-owned company.

articles.title: Maurene Comey ruling offers hope of check on Trump’s assault on rule of law
articles.summary:
Legal experts welcome judge’s rejection of firing of James Comey’s daughter prosecutor but warn an appeal is likely

A recent legal ruling against an effort to fire the star-prosecutor…

blocks.text: A recent legal ruling against an effort to fire the star-prosecutor daughter of a former FBI chief targeted by Donald Trump could send a strong message about politicized firings – and influence other judges weighing similar cases, legal veterans said.

Judge Jesse Furman ruled this week that the Department of Justice’s firing of assistant US attorney Maurene Comey without cause was unlawful. Comey, the daughter of former FBI director James Comey, successfully litigated numerous high-profile cases during her tenure at the southern district of New York, including guilty verdicts against Ghislaine Maxwell and Sean “Diddy” Combs.

“It looks as if Judge Furman has completely vindicated her and rejected just about all of the arguments made by the government,” said Carl Tobias, Williams chair at the University of Richmond School of Law. “And so it’s really important to have this because of the way she was essentially summarily fired, and so it sets a valuable precedent.”

The Department of Justice, which fired her without cause, had argued thatarticle II of the US constitution, which defines presidential power, imbued Trump and his attorney general with a right to fire line prosecutors – who are not political appointees.
But Furman this week rejected the department’s position, ruling Comey’s firing was not greenlighted under any law and in fact, violated the Civil Service Reform Act.

blocks.caption: Maurene Comey, then an assistant US attorney, points at Ghislaine Maxwell, far left, while she presents the rebuttal for the prosecution during Maxwell’s sex-trafficking trial in New York in 2021.  Photograph: Elizabeth Williams/AP

blocks.text: The justice department’s claim “flies in the face of nearly two centuries of Supreme Court precedent”, Furman said. “It is also without merit. Indeed, to accept Defendants’ argument would be to unsettle the very equilibrium established by this Nation’s constitutional system.”

For legal observers, Furman’s decision is cause for optimism – even if optimism of the cautious sort – amid the Trump administration’s alleged repeated attacks on the rule of law. While one judicial opinion does not a panacea make, they said, such a ruling can send a strong message and be considered by other judges weighing similar cases.
“One thing I would caution is that it’s very clear the government will appeal this,” Tobias said. The justice department would do this via the second circuit court of appeals.
“I expect that Furman would be affirmed by that court, and then I assume the administration would then appeal to the US supreme court,” he added.
Then, it would up to the US supreme court to decide whether they even want to hear the case – and if they decline, the lower appeals court decision would stand.

“You are seeing the courts step up and stop and prevent the administration when they are violating the rule of law,” said Neama Rahmani, founder of West Coast Trial Lawyers and a former federal prosecutor. Just this Monday, Los Angeles federal court judge David Carter rejected Trump’s attempt to set aside 20,000 ballots in California, Rahmani noted.

“Whether it’s the supreme court and birthright citizenship, or even individual cases like this, there have been limited, I would say, rulings by the court that have limited what President Trump can do.”

Like Tobias, Rahmani said the justice department can fight federal district and appeals court decisions. And, this kind of case does contain legal issues that might pique the supreme court’s interest – especially if different federal appeals courts were to reach different conclusions.
If the supreme court did decide to hear arguments on Comey’s case, it would by no means guarantee a check on Trump’s power.

“There are a lot of the justices on the supreme court that really don’t believe there should be much of any restrictions on what the president can do,” Rahmani said. “So this is far from the silver bullet.”
For now, though, Furman’s decision can prove influential.

“The decision can be used by other folks who do believe that they were terminated lawfully,” Rahmani said, adding, “It is not binding at all, but it’s certainly something that judges look to with similar or exact same facts.”

Elizabeth Wolstein, a partner at Schlam Stone & Dolan LLP and former Manhattan federal prosecutor in the civil division, said that a judge’s decision in one case could potentially affect how other judges’ weigh similar issues.

“It doesn’t have any binding effect on another judge, even in the same district, as opposed to how a second circuit or US supreme court case would be binding,” Wolstein said. But, “if it’s well reasoned and persuasive, it is definitely going to be persuasive to another judge faced with a similar issue.”

Comey filed suit over her ouster in September 2025. Comey said she neither received notice nor explanation of her firing. Instead, Comey on 16 July 2025 got a letter that stated “your employment with the Department of Justice is hereby terminated, and you are removed from federal service effective immediately.”
When Comey asked the then Manhattan US attorney, Jay Clayton, about this notice, he allegedly said “all I can say is it came from Washington. I can’t tell you anything else,” per court papers.
The Department of Justice has said Comey’s firing was directed by the former US attorney general Pam Bondi and subsequently “ratified” by her successor, Todd Blanche.

Comey’s lawyers and critics of the US president have claimed that she was fired because her father is longtime Trump foe James Comey. Trump’s justice department has repeatedly tried prosecuting James Comey, this week making public its third case against him; one prior proceeding was dismissed, another is pending.
The department had defended the idea that someone’s familial relations could be considered in termination proceedings.

Maurene Comey’s legal team viewed Furman’s ruling as a positive development in protecting the rule of law. Comey’s attorneys are Ellen Blain, Nicole Gueron and Deepa Vanamali at Clarick Gueron Reisbaum, as well as Margaret Donovan at Koskoff Koskoff & Bieder.

“The Court’s decision is a complete rejection of this administration’s sweeping claim to unchecked executive power, and it demonstrates that our constitutional system of checks and balances is alive and well,” the team said in a statement.

The justice department did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Furman’s decision or claims of politically driven firings. In a statement, the White House rejected allegations that Trump’s justice department is trying to punish opponents.

“Unlike Joe Biden, President Trump has not weaponized the Department of Justice against his political foes. The Department is focused on restoring law and order and keeping Americans safe,” Lauren Bis, a White House spokesperson, said in a statement. “The results speak for themselves: Under President Trump, we have seen the largest decrease in violent crime in American history.”

articles.title: More than 5,000 die from Ebola in DR Congo's deadliest outbreak
articles.summary: Government data shows that more than 10,000 people have contracted the rare virus.

blocks.text: More than 5,000 people have died from an ongoing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo, government data shows.
Eight of 26 provinces are now affected, with more than 10,300 confirmed cases.
The outbreak, which started in May, became the country's deadliest in its history in August, public health officials said. The current case fatality rate is 48.6%.

In its latest update, the health ministry said the epicentre of the epidemic remains in the Ituri province, in the north-east of the country, which is a conflict zone, making it harder to contain the virus.
Cases have also been confirmed in Kenya, Nigeria and Uganda.
This marks the 17th outbreak in DR Congo's history, according to the United Nations, and the second largest in history.
The World Health Organization (WHO) office in Africa said a "continued scale-up of key control measures, greater access to affected areas, and community outreach" is needed to end the outbreak.
Testing and treatment is under way, along with clinical trials of vaccines, it added.
The Bundibugyo species is behind the current outbreak, but there is currently no treatment or vaccine for this strain.
Ebola is a rare, deadly disease caused by a virus, and symptoms come on suddenly.
As the disease progresses, vomiting and diarrhoea develop and it can lead to organ failure. Some, but not all, patients develop internal and external bleeding.
The virus spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.
Adding to the challenge of treating the disease, some health workers and a politician have been attacked while responding to the outbreak.

Earlier this week, a nurse was killed and another health worker seriously injured in an attack when responding to an Ebola alert. Local youths had accused them of contaminating water sources and spreading the virus, according to the UN-backed Radio Okapi.

Last month, a politician was beaten to death after promoting measures to stop the spread of Ebola, while in August, the Red Cross said its volunteers had been injured and an ambulance set on fire in 11 violent incidents in the outbreak's first 100 days.
No cases have been reported in Uganda since August, but travel restrictions remain in place for those crossing into the country from neighbouring DR Congo.
In Kenya, there have been nine confirmed cases and two recorded deaths. One woman was confirmed to have the disease in Nigeria, but flown to Switzerland for further treatment.
The likelihood of infection for people in the Europe area is "very low," the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control said.

articles.title: UK charity shop profits plummet amid shift in secondhand clothes market
articles.summary:
Oxfam describes ‘exceptionally challenging’ trading after retail profit reportedly fell 23% year on year

Profits at some of the UK’s best-known charity shops have plummeted as they face a…

blocks.text: Profits at some of the UK’s best-known charity shops have plummeted as they face a number of pressures, including from online secondhand clothes platforms, prompting claims that a key part of the sector’s fundraising model could be under threat.
According to unpublished accounts seen by the Financial Times, Oxfam’s retail profit fell 23% to £4.9m in the last financial year, compared with £6.4m in the previous year.

The British Heart Foundation (BHF), which has the biggest high street presence of any charity in the country, has announced plans to close 150 stores after they made a loss in the last financial year. Cancer Research UK and Scope have also closed, or are closing, some of their shops.
But these losses come despite UK spending on secondhand clothing having quadrupled over the past decade, rising to £8.8bn a year, according to GlobalData.

The shift has come alongside the rise of websites such as Vinted and Depop, suggesting that people who might previously have donated clothes to charity shops are instead selling them directly to other consumers and profiting themselves.

blocks.caption: Oxfam’s focus on books and music means it has no plans to reduce its number of shops. Photograph: Vuk Valcic/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Alongside this change, Chinese companies are selling more clothes in developing countries, particularly in Africa, which has long been a major market for unwanted secondhand clothing.
“It has been challenging … and it is going to be painful for the sector,” Lorna Fallon, the head of Oxfam’s retail operation, told the Financial Times.

Oxfam’s latest filings reveal that for every £100 people spend in its shops, just £6 now goes towards the charity’s work on alleviating global poverty. As recently as 2022, the figure was £22, the FT reports. However, the organisation’s focus on books and music means it has no plans to reduce its number of shops.
In June, BHF carried out a major review of its retail arm, which employs almost 3,700 staff, after profits from its shops plunged from £18.8m in 2024 to £3.6m in the year to 31 March 2025.
The charity cited “an exceptionally challenging trading environment”, and said it was aiming to close 90 stores by the end of March 2027 and another 60 by the following March.

The rapid change in fortunes for charity shops also highlights their limitations in the face of greater competition. Whereas Vinted and Depop directly connect sellers with buyers, charity shops remain at the mercy of high street and warehouse rents and other associated costs and inefficiencies, including collecting, sorting, pricing and storing clothes.

Another issue hampering high street charity shops is that the clothes being donated are increasingly substandard. Speaking to the Guardian earlier this month, Tansy Hoskins, the author of Charity Shop World, described the sector as dealing with “avalanches” of poor-quality clothes across the country, as people use charity shops as convenient dumping grounds for unwanted purchases.
“Quality is the big change marker – it’s gone through the floor. You’re just fighting against the waste,” Hoskins said.
Robin Osterley, the chief executive of the Charity Retail Association, said: “Fast fashion has had an impact on donations quality, there’s no question about that.”
after newsletter promotion

But he added: “We don’t see Vinted or any of the other online platforms as an issue at all. It might be having a little bit of an effect – where people have one bag for charity shop donations and one for Vinted – but we believe these effects are significantly mitigated by two things.

“The first is that Vinted and other platforms are having a very positive effect on people’s attitudes towards secondhand shopping, and creating an environment where it’s much more normalised. A rising tide floats all ships.
“The second factor is that there are a lot of people who buy things from charity shops to sell on the online platforms. Our members get a significant income from them.”

Osterley instead suggested the November 2024 budget had had a much larger impact on bricks and mortar charity shops, in which national insurance increases and the lowering of the national insurance threshold – affecting more part-time staff – has had a “really significant” effect on the costs charity shops face, as well as inflationary pressures across the economy.

Richard Hawkes, Oxfam GB’s chief executive, said: “Whilst there is no getting away from the fact that the charity retail sector has been impacted by the cost-of-living crisis, like the rest of the high street, there is still much to be hopeful and positive about for the future.
“The growth of secondhand presents real opportunities for the whole sector, but it also means we need to think differently about the traditional charity retail model.

He added: “Our shops also offer much more than just an income. They give us a presence in communities where we might not otherwise be, while providing opportunities to engage with more than 20,000 volunteers. This wider role remains a vital part of what makes charity retail so valuable.”

articles.title: More than 100 protest against Palestine Action ban outside US embassy in London
articles.summary:
Police start arresting demonstrators with Met commander alleging they are ‘essentially meeting to purposefully commit a crime’

Police have started making arrests at the first mass…

blocks.text: Police have started making arrests at the first mass demonstration under Andy Burnham’s premiership opposing the proscription of Palestine Action.
More than 100 people gathered outside the US embassy in Battersea, south London, holding signs that read: “I oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action.”
Another demonstration was scheduled for the US consulate near Holyrood in Edinburgh.
Ahead of the London gathering, the Metropolitan police warned those taking part “that they face arrest as part of a robust policing operation”.

Commander Adam Slonecki, who is leading the policing operation, said: “All those intending on coming to this event know that supporting a proscribed organisation is unlawful – they are essentially meeting to purposefully commit a crime.

He added that “anyone officers consider to be playing a key role in organising the event, giving instructions to others and/or providing logistical support will very likely be committing an offence and face enforcement action”.
Defend Our Juries, the group behind the demonstrations, said the Met were “terrified of facilitating US embarrassment”.
More details soon …

articles.title: Ethiopian PM puts ministers through military training
articles.summary: The prime minister has previously emphasised military preparedness as central to his government's ambitions.

blocks.text: Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has put his cabinet ministers and other senior government officials through military training, saying armed forces discipline can help build stronger leaders and advance the country's development.
Photos shared by him on social media show him taking part in military exercises alongside ministers, deputy ministers and heads of government institutions at the Hurso military training centre.
The move is unusual in Ethiopia, where senior civilian government officials are rarely seen undergoing military training.
Those taking part include Speaker of the House of Federation Muferiat Kamil, Finance Minister Fitsum Assefa and Health Minister Mekdes Daba.
It is unclear when the training began or how long it is expected to last.

In his post, the prime minister, who is known as Abiy, said Ethiopia's ambition to achieve universal prosperity required its leadership to be physically fit, morally strong and intellectually capable.
He said military institutions offered valuable lessons in discipline, patriotism, teamwork, accountability and leadership.

"Soldiers have targets while civilians have goals. The objective of both is victory," he said, adding that combining military and civilian disciplines would help create a generation capable of achieving both.
Abiy argued that military training could help develop leaders with a strong sense of purpose, responsibility and the ability to work together towards common objectives.
The training comes as Ethiopia faces multiple security challenges, including continued fighting in parts of the northern Tigray region, conflict in Amhara and insecurity in Oromia.
It also takes place amid heightened tensions with neighbouring Eritrea, with concerns over the possibility of renewed conflict between the two countries.
Abiy has previously emphasised military preparedness and national development as central to his government's ambitions.

articles.title: Tovera-led La Salle wins 3rd straight as rival Ateneo falls in OT thriller
articles.summary: Super rookie Joaquin Tovera shines with a heroic performance as La Salle trumps rival Ateneo in overtime to stay undefeated in the UAAP Season 89 men’s basketball tournament second round

image.caption: Tovera-led La Salle wins 3rd straight as rival Ateneo falls in OT thriller

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – La Salle rookie Joaquin Tovera again stayed ahead of his learning curve in the UAAP Season 89 men’s basketball tournament as he led the Green Archers to a thrilling 76-73 overtime escape of rivals Ateneo Blue Eagles at the Araneta Coliseum on Saturday, October 31.

Before succumbing to a non-contact ankle roll in the final minute of a heated extra period, Tovera willed La Salle with game-highs of 21 points and 6 assists to go with 7 rebounds as the Green Archers broke a standings deadlock with the Blue Eagles to go third at 6-4.
Veteran guard JC Macalalag led a balanced scoring effort behind Tovera with 11 points in nearly 39 minutes of action, as six other La Salle players tallied at least 5 points.
“When the game went to overtime, we just reminded everybody about what we discussed before the game and we talked about our dreams,” said Archers head coach Topex Robinson.
“In every moment, the strongest dream will win that moment, so we all dream about playing in the De La Salle-Ateneo rivalry. These guys just showed up and they believed in what we prepared for.”

Ateneo young stars Jared Bahay and super rookie Kieffer Alas paced the heartbreaking loss with 18 points apiece — with all their efforts nullified as they failed to link up on a basic inbounds pass that gave the ball back to the Green Archers with 3.3 seconds left in overtime.

Shawn Tuano added 12 points and 6 rebounds, while Travis Roberts likewise scored 12 on a 5-of-17 clip, as the Blue Eagles tripped down a 5-5 slate for fifth place in a hyper-competitive field still featuring seven realistic Final Four contenders.

In the previous game of the loaded double-header, the NU Bulldogs strengthened its hold of second place with a scrappy 75-71 escape of the reeling UST Growling Tigers for a 7-3 record — half a game behind 7-2 UP.

Head coach Jeff Napa once again worked his magic on big men as star foreign student-athlete Mo Diassana tallied a huge 16-point, 19-rebound double-double, backstopped by 14 markers and 6 boards in just 15 minutes from MVP candidate PJ Palacielo.

Burly big Kenshin Padrones added his own double-double of 13 points and 12 rebounds, while Tebol Garcia topscored the NU back court with 12 points, 7 boards, and a game-high 6 assists, making up for MVP frontrunner Reinhard Jumamoy’s lackluster 6-point showing.
Amiel Acido and Mark Llemit paced the losing cause with 13 and 12 points, respectively, while star center Collins Akowe was limited to 11 points on 2-of-7 shooting with just 5 rebounds in 33 minutes.
Amid a heavily-contested elimination round, UST plummeted to a 4-6 card at seventh place with a costly third straight loss, while still being just two games behind No. 3 La Salle.

articles.title: Toronto police to provide update on Bridle Path home invasion investigation
articles.summary: Toronto police will be updating the public at 10 a.m. Saturday on the investigation into the home invasion that took place in the Bridle Path neighbourhood earlier this week.

blocks.text: Toronto·
Toronto police will be updating the public at 10 a.m. Saturday on the investigation into the home invasion that took place in the Bridle Path neighbourhood earlier this week.
Police requested public's help in identifying three suspects on Friday
Toronto police give update on home invasion probe
Toronto police will be updating the public Saturday morning on the investigation into the home invasion that took place in the Bridle Path neighbourhood earlier this week.
Officers responded to reports of a "violent home invasion" at a residence near Hyde Park Circle and Post Road Thursday morning, Toronto police said Thursday.

Police said three suspects, armed with handguns and a hammer, forced their way into the home, made demands for valuables and attacked four adults in the home — a 75-year-old father, 64-year-old mother and their 26 and 28-year-old daughters.
The news conference on Saturday will take place at 10 a.m. with updates from Insp. Kristy Smith of the Toronto police's Hold Up Squad.

David Morton, CEO of MAC Group, said three members of his family are recovering in hospital after they were shot during the home invasion. All four members of the family were also attacked with a hammer, he said in an emailed statement issued Friday.
David Morton, CEO of MAC Group, a real estate group, said his family is 'traumatized' after they suffered a violent and 'horrific' home invasion in their Bridle Path home Thursday. (macsuites.ca)
"No family should ever have to experience this," he said, adding the family is traumatized and recovering after the attack on Thursday.
On Friday, police requested the public's help to identify and locate the three suspects, who fled the area in a dark coloured SUV.
The suspects are described as men in their 20s wearing dark clothing and face masks.
All three men are considered to be armed and dangerous, police said.

articles.title: UK police should not have let US force take over airbase trial, MoD documents show
articles.summary:
According to documents obtained by the Guardian, officials accused Cambridgeshire force of breaching US-UK deal by handing over case of woman strangled by US pilot

Ministry of Defence…
articles.byline: Rob Evans, Harry Davies,Louisa Loveluck and Emine Sinmaz

blocks.text: Ministry of Defence officials have privately accused a UK police force of wrongly handing over the investigation of an American fighter pilot who strangled a British woman to the US military, according to documents obtained by the Guardian.

Cambridgeshire police allowed the US military police to quickly take control of the investigation into Capt Jacob Wulfson after he had been accused of sexually assaulting Sarah Steele in his Cambridge flat.
The decision meant Wulfson was not tried in an English criminal court. Instead he was prosecuted in a military tribunal on a US airbase in neighbouring Suffolk.

blocks.caption: An all-male jury of Capt Jacob Wulfson’s fellow air force officers convicted him of strangling an intimate partner but acquitted him of sexual assault. Photograph: United States Air Forces Central

blocks.text: Ministry of Defence officials said the Cambridgeshire force should “absolutely” not have let the US military police take over the investigation in a clear breach of a long-established agreement with the US.

The disclosure of the case by the Guardian in June provoked immediate criticism from Downing Street, which said it was “deeply distressing” and “very concerning” that the UK authorities were not involved in prosecuting Wulfson.
The government to set up a high-level inquiry to examine how and why police forces have been transferring investigations into serious crimes to the US military police.
The Ministry of Defence, which is responsible for handling the military relationship with the US, is one of the key departments taking part in the inquiry.

A batch of documents, disclosed via the Freedom of Information Act, revealed the private views of MoD officials about the Steele case, which centres on an obscure agreement signed by the US and the UK decades ago.
Under the terms of the agreement, police in the UK have the primary right to investigate alleged crimes by Americans stationed in the country.

The MoD officials made it clear the agreement was “pretty unambiguous” and only permitted the US military to acquire jurisdiction over investigations in a “narrow set of circumstances”. These circumstances are: if the offences were committed while the Americans were on duty, or if they were committed against another member of their armed forces or property.

In a memo written on 8 July, MoD officials based in Washington wrote: “The Steele case does not, on the surface, appear to meet the bar for a visiting force to be awarded jurisdiction.” In the agreement, the US military is formally known as a visiting force.

Four days earlier, the MoD officials had referred to the Steele case in an email to colleagues, saying: “The decision-making on this specific case seemed at odds with what is very clear” in the agreement.
Another MoD official agreed that “as best as we understand the facts, this should absolutely have been for the UK courts”.

An unidentified Greater Manchester police officer wrote in an email to MoD officials on 6 July that Cambridgeshire police had “wrongly, in my view” handed over the Wulfson investigation to the US military.

Cambridgeshire police said they were conducting a review of the case with what they called “the assistance of material provided” by US Air Force lawyers. The force said it “remained engaged with the victim”.
“We are working with government, wider policing and criminal justice partners to ensure greater clarity of jurisdictional decision making,” they added.
after newsletter promotion
The US military aims to prosecute as many of its personnel as possible within the boundaries of its agreement with the UK.

The Americans often ask police in the UK if they can take over the prosecution of their military personnel – requests the police agree to, even when they have primary responsibility for investigating them.

A series of cases uncovered this year by the Guardian have highlighted concerns that British victims are required to give evidence in US courts martial, an unfamiliar legal system that often does not afford the same protections as that of a court in the UK.
Wulfson was off-duty when he assaulted Steele in his Cambridge flat in December 2023 after the pair talked on the Tinder dating app.
Steele testified at Wulfson’s court martial, which was held on his airbase at Lakenheath, Suffolk in April, that her experience was “degrading and distressing”.

The verdict and sentence were decided by an all-male jury of Wulfson’s fellow air force officers. All the lawyers were American. Steele was subjected to invasive and aggressive questioning by Wulfson’s lawyer.
Wulfson was convicted of strangling an intimate partner but acquitted of sexual assault. He was dismissed from the US Air Force and confined to a military jail on Lakenheath for six months.

The cross-government inquiry, which includes officials from the Home Office, Ministry of Justice and Foreign Office, is looking at how US military personnel are not being brought to justice in British courts.
The inquiry, which also involves police chiefs, is scrutinising a series of cases uncovered by the Guardian this year.
In each case, police handed over the investigations to US military police even though the American perpetrators were off-duty and the British victims had no connection to the armed forces.

They were tried in US courts martial on American bases. Tyrion Davis allegedly raped two women in Suffolk. He was convicted of one charge of sexual assault, but cleared of 10 further counts of sexual assault and abusive sexual contact.

Hannes Marschalek allegedly exposed himself to a 16-year-old girl and four young women in Littleport, Cambridgeshire. He negotiated a plea bargain at a court martial and admitted a charge of indecent conduct. He won an appeal in a US military court that quashed his conviction on technical grounds. This ruling is now being challenged.

The US has more than 12,000 US military personnel in the UK, stationed in at least 15 bases and facilities. The two biggest bases are at Lakenheath and Mildenhall, in Suffolk. Significant numbers of American military personnel live in East Anglia.

articles.title: Starmer says UK must get closer to Europe as US relationship changes
articles.summary:
Shift in dealings with Washington not likely to reset once Trump leaves Oval Office, former PM says

The UK and other European nations must draw closer together as the US becomes a…

blocks.text: The UK and other European nations must draw closer together as the US becomes a less-reliable partner, Keir Starmer has said in his first significant political intervention since leaving No 10.

The former prime minister warned European leaders of the threat posed by Russia, among others, and said the shift in relations with Washington during Donald Trump’s presidency was not likely to reset once he leaves the Oval Office. And he accused them of being caught out by these new realities twice already.
“A stronger Europe is vital and the UK must be at the heart of it,” he told an audience at the British Irish Chamber of Commerce on Friday.

“Europe has twice been caught asleep, failing to anticipate and prepare for predictable events. First, when Russia’s attack on Ukraine exposed longstanding European weaknesses on defence and security, and second, when President Trump made clear, once and for all, that the US will no longer bankroll our European security. We have to catch up.”

Starmer had called for closer European ties before stepping down as prime minister in July. Three months earlier, amid Trump’s war with Iran and his threats to withdraw from Nato, Starmer said Europe represented a “partnership for a dangerous world we must navigate together”.

He said those ties should go further than just defence, adding that Brexit had done “deep damage” to the UK economy, and that he wanted to be “more ambitious”, including pursuing “closer economic cooperation [and] closer security cooperation”.
Starmer spoke after spending time in Dublin meeting senior business leaders and politicians, including the taoiseach Micheál Martin, with whom he established the annual UK-Ireland summit.

“I will say here what I have said to European leaders. This is about responding to a permanent change of affairs, not an aberration of the Trump presidency. Things will not go back to the way they were before.

“That doesn’t mean the US relationship is no longer important. On the contrary, the military, security and intelligence alliance is far too strong for that. But it does mean enabling Europe to take on far more responsibility for its own defence and security.”

His comments reflect a growing consensus on the left of UK politics that closer ties with Europe are essential to ensure economic and military security. Soon after taking office as Starmer’s successor, Andy Burnham said that he intended to be “bolder” about closer ties with the EU.
Next month, Burnham will attend a crucial EU-UK summit where new agreements on food standards, energy and youth mobility will be the main focus.
after newsletter promotion

Burnham has also said he wants a public debate on how the UK could move to a closer relationship with the EU after the next election. At a meeting of European defence ministers in Paris this week, defence secretary Wes Streeting said that they were “united and unwavering” in support for Ukraine in the face of Russian hostility.

Besides increased defence spending, Starmer said: “We need to build up pan-European cooperation and coordination on defence and security – a common security framework as much as a common market. The EU is changing to respond to that, but it cannot be the EU alone when Europe’s periphery is core to its defence.

“Britain must be central to that project. We are one of two nuclear powers. We are a leading Nato member. We have a viable next-generation fighter jet programme. And we are pledged to work alongside European allies to guarantee security in Ukraine.

“Ireland and the UK stand side by side in the coalition of the willing and with Ukraine, working together to guarantee and shape the security of our continent. I hope and believe that Britain’s relationship with its friends and allies can and should be strengthened by this urgent and common security project.”

articles.title: Civilians evacuated from Russian-occupied Oleshky arrive in Belarus on their way to Ukraine
articles.summary: Evacuees from Russian-occupied Oleshky in Ukraine arrived in Belarus on Saturday on their way back to Ukraine, part of a major rescue operation carried out under the most significant truce since…

image.caption: Russia's human rights commissioner, Yana Lantratova, left, and Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine's commissioner for human rights, centre, speak with journalists on Friday before departing for Oleshky to evacuate local residents to a safe area during a local ceasefire. (Office of the Ombudsman of Ukraine/The

blocks.text: Evacuees from Russian-occupied Oleshky in Ukraine arrived in Belarus on Saturday on their way back to Ukraine, part of a major rescue operation carried out under the most significant truce since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine more than four years ago.

The ceasefire in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region, which the White House says was brokered with help from U.S. first lady Melania Trump, began at 3 a.m. local time on Tuesday and is expected to continue through Sunday evening.
It was a rare joint Russia-Ukraine humanitarian effort — a brief respite in the grim war.

Civilians from Oleshky, on the Dnipro River, began the long journey out of the war-ravaged region in bus convoys on Friday. The estimated 2,000 remaining residents were offered the choice of travelling to Ukrainian- or Russian-held territory or remaining in the city with replenished food and medical supplies.

Russia's Ministry of Defence said those who chose to travel from Oleshky to Ukrainian-held territory were taken to the Russian city of Anapa and flown to the Belarusian city of Homel. They were accompanied by Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine's commissioner for human rights, it said.
"We will be home soon!" said a video post from Lubinets at Homel airport.
Melania Trump-brokered ceasefire area expands in eastern Ukraine
Four planes with the evacuees landed in Belarus and the passengers would be on Ukrainian territory "within hours," said Ukrainian lawmaker Davyd Arakhamia.
Daughters wait to see their fathers again
Relatives waited on Saturday at the border between Ukraine and Belarus, along with aid tents, coffee stands and even provisions to feed the pets the evacuees were bringing with them.
Volunteers from organizations, including the Red Cross, Doctors without Borders and the World Central Kitchen, were also there.

items: Aid operation, evacuations underway in Ukraine's stricken city of Oleshky

blocks.text: Liza Paliy, 19, who last saw her father more than two years ago, was among those waiting. Paliy, her mother and sister fled from the occupied territory at the time, while he stayed behind.
"We thought at that time that it would be a month, two maximum, and we would return, but unfortunately, two years have already passed," she said.
U.S.-brokered ceasefire begins in Russian-occupied Ukrainian town
Daria Pavlyn also waited at the border in hopes of reuniting with her father, Mykhailo, whom she had not heard from in about a month.
He had planned to flee occupied territory with his family after a nearby strike killed two neighbours but stayed behind when arrangements to care for the family's home and animals fell through.
"We realized that, well, there was no [other] way, and he walked us to the road and that was it," Pavlyn said of the last time she saw her father.

items: Russia, Ukraine team up on relief effort in Russian-occupied Oleshky
Melania Trump, Pope Leo broker humanitarian ceasefire for ravaged Ukraine city Oleshky

blocks.text: She said that since then, he had feared making the arduous journey out, particularly without Russian documents.

Russia's ombudsperson and lead representative on the mission, Yana Lantratova, said buses also transported Oleshky residents who wanted to live in Russia. Russian media outlets on Saturday showed civilians arriving at a temporary accommodation site in Simferopol on the Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea, which Moscow annexed in 2014.
A humanitarian convoy carrying residents evacuated from the Russian-controlled town of Oleshky, Ukraine, drives along a road in Armyansk in Crimea on Friday. (Alexey Pavlishak/Reuters)

Russia and Ukraine have not specified how many people chose to leave the city, but the U.S. first lady posted on social media Friday that the humanitarian convoy could safely evacuate more than 750 people.
Apart from Melania Trump, Pope Leo — the first American pontiff — also pressed Russian and Ukrainian leaders to allow aid deliveries and civilian evacuations.
U.S. approves Patriot missile sales for Ukraine

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Saturday welcomed U.S. approval of Ukraine’s purchase of 500 PAC-3 Patriot interceptors but urged partners to supply the weapons from existing stocks to protect the country this winter, warning the newly authorized U.S. sale could take years to deliver.

"Right now, the Russians are attacking our energy infrastructure every single day. In just these past two weeks of October, there have already been more than 30 Russian strikes on critical parts of our power grid," Zelenskyy wrote on X.
24 hours in Kyiv: Living through Russian drone strikes

The Trump administration said Friday that it had approved a proposed $2.1 billion US sale of Patriot air defence interceptors, after Kyiv had accused the Pentagon of delaying deliveries of the vital munition needed to stop Russian ballistic missiles.
The U.S. State Department said 500 Patriot missiles would be purchased for Ukraine with donations from Canada, Germany and Norway through a U.S. program and that no American funds were involved.
A Ukrainian drone attack kills 2 in Russia

Meanwhile, a Ukrainian drone attack killed a 30-year-old woman and a 41-year-old man in Russia's western Bryansk region, local Gov. Yegor Kovalchuk said Saturday. Another five people were wounded, he said.

Local officials also reported Ukrainian drone attacks in the Russian republic of Bashkortostan. Russian media outlets said there was a fire in the region's capital, Ufa, home to several oil refineries.

items: Russia, Ukraine begin ceasefire in city of Oleshky as deadly strikes continue elsewhere
Melania Trump, Pope Leo broker humanitarian ceasefire for ravaged Ukraine city Oleshky

blocks.text: Russia's Ministry of Defence said Saturday its forces had shot down 433 Ukrainian drones overnight.
Zelenskyy said Moscow launched drone attacks on energy and railway infrastructure across Ukraine overnight, leaving 280,000 households in Dnipro and Kyiv regions without power.

The attacks targeted combined heat and power plants in Kyiv and Sumy regions, four electricity substations and a gas distribution facility in the Dnipro region and railway infrastructure in Dnipro and Kharkiv, he said, adding that repair crews were working to restore power.
B.C. animal rescuer killed by drone on Ukraine's front lines
Zelenskyy urged partners to impose further sanctions on Russia and provide new support packages to Ukraine.
"The world sees Russia targeting civilian infrastructure every day. Everyone who does not want to see this Russian escalation spread further into Europe must help Ukraine," he said in an online post.

articles.title: France braces for 3rd weekend of discord as youth-led protests spread across Europe
articles.summary: France prepared Saturday for a third consecutive weekend of protests over living costs and education, deploying 70,000 police and gendarmes and rerouting the Paris march to the capital's edge as…

image.caption: A man stands in front of a barricaded shop of the soccer team Paris Saint-Germain before protests over living costs and education get underway in Paris on Saturday. (Emma Da Silva/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World

France prepared Saturday for a third consecutive weekend of protests over living costs and education, deploying 70,000 police and gendarmes and rerouting the Paris march to the capital's edge as youth-led demonstrations spread across Europe.
High school students began demonstrating against school conditions last month
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez warned of a "very high risk" of disorder, especially after dark on Halloween.

Paris police banned union and "yellow vest" marches through the city centre, ordering demonstrations to follow a single route along the capital's outer boulevards, from Porte de Bagnolet to Porte de Charenton. Unions and student groups challenged the restrictions in court but lost in a last-minute legal battle.
Students in France clash with riot police amid weekslong education protests
President Emmanuel Macron said on Monday that marches would stay out of city centres to protect shops.
Police also barred entry to Place de la République and Les Halles, both hit by rioting and looting on Oct. 17, Saturday night into Sunday morning.

Unaccompanied minors face a separate 9 p.m. curfew around the Champs-Élysées. A Paris court on Wednesday suspended an earlier curfew on minors as a serious and illegal infringement of freedom of movement.
Protesters scuffle with riot police during a demonstration against rising living costs, in Paris on Oct. 17. (Emma Da Silva/The Associated Press)
The movement began with high school students protesting school conditions and broadened into anger over living costs.

Authorities counted about 550,000 protesters nationwide on Oct. 17, when rioters looted hundreds of shops, and 410,000 last Saturday, when rallies were largely peaceful, but police made more than 1,300 arrests.

In Germany, a youth initiative called "Gen Z regelt" — roughly "Gen Z's got this" — urged protests in some 30 cities "for education, health, climate protection and an affordable life" and against any return of military conscription. Organizers said more than 140,000 people had signed up online.

items: What's behind the youth protests in France?
Tens of thousands march in France as protests continue over schools and living costs

blocks.text: Berlin police expected about 10,000 people at the Brandenburg Gate. Some shops on the Kurfürstendamm boulevard boarded up their windows, although authorities said they were unaware of specific threats of violence. Protests were expected to begin in the early afternoon.

In Barcelona, Catalan police planned to activate their highest-level alert after an anonymous TikTok network called Blocus urged new gatherings. Rioting in the Spanish city last Saturday led to about 130 arrests, mostly of minors.
Italian police were on alert after clashes in Milan, Turin and Bologna, and calls to protest circulated on TikTok in Belgium, the Netherlands, Austria, Switzerland and Portugal.

articles.title: Parks Canada set to slash warden detachments, officers across national parks
articles.summary: Detachments will be closing in British Columbia, Alberta, Ontario, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Yukon and Northwest Territories. The number of wardens impacted by the decision is unknown, but CBC News…

image.caption: These changes come amidst $145 million in cuts to Parks Canada over the next three years. (Parks Canada)

blocks.text: Calgary·New

Detachments will be closing in British Columbia, Alberta, Ontario, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Yukon and Northwest Territories. The number of wardens impacted by the decision is unknown, but CBC News has learned at least a dozen positions will be cut.
Federal agency spokesperson says it 'will continue to provide services across all locations'
Parks Canada is closing at least 13 warden detachments and prioritizing a regional service for law enforcement, according to multiple sources.
Detachments will be closing in British Columbia, Alberta, Ontario, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Yukon and Northwest Territories.

The number of wardens impacted by the decision is unknown, but CBC News has learned at least a dozen positions will be cut. Some detachments, such as Banff and Jasper, will each lose one warden, multiple sources told CBC News.
"We’re deeply concerned what that looks like. These aren’t just administrative changes," said Krysty Thomas, regional executive vice-president for Public Service Alliance of Canada’s Prairies region.

"We’re talking about highly trained officers who play an important role in protecting our national parks, enforcing environmental laws and providing critical support to other employees working in the field."
These changes come amidst $145 million in cuts to Parks Canada over the next three years.

Parks Canada acting CEO and vice-president of transformation Andrew Campbell wrote in an Oct. 20 email to staff that 2,917 letters went out to employees to let them know they could move to new jobs or be let go. Thomas said the union has been told Parks Canada plans to cut 517 full-time jobs.

items: Parks Canada plan to cut 500 jobs draws criticism from union

blocks.text: Among the detachments closing will be Kluane National Park in Yukon, Kejimkujik National Park in Nova Scotia, Elk Island National Park in Alberta and Point Pelee National Park in Ontario. Others are Gulf Islands National Park Reserve in British Columbia, Fundy National Park in New Brunswick and Nahanni National Park Reserve in Northwest Territories.
A new regional system will have 85 total wardens spread over western, central, eastern and northern Canada, and the Rockies.
Thomas said PSAC wants to hear how Parks Canada will “maintain these important services with fewer people in fewer locations.”

Meaghan Bradley, a spokesperson in Parks Canada’s national communications office, told CBC News the federal agency is “modernizing its law enforcement model by redistributing capacity to focus on areas of highest priority and risk.”

Bradley didn’t acknowledge the number of wardens being let go, but said “some detachments are being consolidated into higher-need areas” and "adopting a more intelligence-driven approach to enforcement," including adding three regional intelligence co-ordinator positions.

CBC News reached out via email to the leadership team in charge of the decision-making for the cuts. Campbell, executive director of transformation Hugues Michaud, transformation communications Stéphane Rondeau and senior strategic adviser Laurie Wein didn't get back to CBC News.
Multiple other requests for interviews were also declined.
Some of the 34 national park wardens who received the Peace Officer Exemplary Service Medal in Banff on Oct. 21, 2025. (Parks Canada)
'You just get burned out'
When a detachment in a national park is closed, it means there's no on-the-ground law enforcement. The new system will rely on bringing in regional wardens to enforce federal law.

Mike Henderson was a warden in the Canadian Rockies for more than 30 years until retiring in 2022. He said a regional plan could contribute to staff burnout, especially if they’re thinly stretched to cover vast territories.

If a warden in the Lake Louise, Yoho, Kootenay field unit were to get a call on the Icefields Parkway, for instance, it could take more than half a shift to respond and get to another call, Henderson said.

“If you’re relying on the bigger national parks to fill the holes required in smaller national parks, you’re still pulling somebody from a bigger place,” he said. “You still don’t have enough staff. It’s not really a Band-Aid solution. It’s a way to muddle your way through.”

items: Parks Canada ends search and rescue dog program

blocks.text: He noted the majority of warden work is a one-person job in remote areas — a mixture of front country and back country work.
“You go to these calls and you know you’re by yourself. … You just get burned out,” he said.
“That’s the weird thing with wardening: it’s pretty smooth sailing until it’s not.”
Thomas said “one of the most troubling things they’re hearing” is staff may be without backup in remote locations.
“Worker safety cannot be an afterthought in the workforce reduction exercise,” she said.
The former warden cabin near the Iceline Trail in Yoho National Park on Oct. 4, 2026. (Greg Colgan/CBC)
'Parks Canada has a responsibility to protect these places for future generations'
Parks Canada’s executive director of conservation Tamaini Snaith presented the changes in an Oct. 22 virtual meeting with wardens across the country, according to multiple sources.
Multiple sources told CBC News that people in some of the positions being cut will be offered roles in the new regional enforcement areas.

items: Parks Canada not laying charges after Banff National Park superintendent admits to violating federal law

blocks.text: Parks Canada did an evaluation of the law enforcement program in 2023. The report states it has an annual budget of about $10 million, with roughly 80 per cent allocated to salaries.

It notes there were about 100 wardens in 2022. Through surveys and interviews, it found “there is also agreement that available resources have not kept pace with the increasing needs of the program” since new national parks have been created and laws have increased responsibilities.

Parks Canada administers more than 450,000 square kilometres of land and water in 37 national parks, 11 national park reserves, five national marine conservation areas, one national urban park and 171 national historic sites.
Bradley said some positions will be relocated, and the warden service “will continue to provide services across all locations.”
Thomas said the union has been asking Parks Canada about impacts to response times, increased travel distances and what happens when a warden needs immediate backup.

“These are occupational health and safety concerns and not just financial savings. ... Parks Canada has a responsibility to protect these places for future generations," she said. "That responsibility doesn’t disappear because budgets are being reduced.”
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Greg Colgan is a journalist for CBC in the Bow Valley. He was previously the editor of the Rocky Mountain Outlook in Banff and Canmore. He has also worked for media outlets in Ontario and has experience covering topics such as sports, politics, housing and development, courts and arts and entertainment. He joined CBC in 2025. He can be reached at greg.colgan@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Undas 2026: Flooding hits Iloilo cemetery; flower prices surge in Cotabato
articles.summary: A day before All Saints" Day, Filipinos have begun visiting cemeteries across the country to pay their respects to departed loved ones, with some areas reporting flooding and higher flower prices…

blocks.text: Published October 31, 2026 7:44pm

A day before All Saints’ Day, Filipinos have begun visiting cemeteries across the country to pay their respects to departed loved ones, with some areas reporting flooding and higher flower prices ahead of the Undas observance.

According to a social media report by Zen Quilantang-Sasa of GMA Regional TV Ratsada Balita, the Tanza Public Cemetery in Iloilo City was partially flooded on Saturday following heavy morning rainfall.
To help visitors navigate the flooded pathways, several men were seen placing concrete debris and rocks to create makeshift elevated walkways.

PANOORIN: Nagtulungan ang ilang kalalakihan upang malagyan ng madadaanan ng mga bumibisita ang Tanza Public Cemetery sa Iloilo City matapos bahagyang bumaha sa sementeryo dahil sa pagbuhos ng ulan kaninang umaga, Oct. 31. Ayon sa mga bumisita sa kanilang mga yumaong mahal sa buhay, taon-taon nila itong nararanasan tuwing Undas. Umaasa silang kaagad itong mabigyan ng atensyon ng Iloilo City LGU. | via Zen Quilantang-Sasa/GMA Regional TV Ratsada Balita Bisitahin ang https://t.co/bAMF9JOAN0 para sa pinakabagong balita. Other Stories — GMA News (@gmanews) October 31, 2026
Some visitors appealed to the Iloilo City local government for an immediate solution, saying the flooding has been a recurring problem during Undas whenever it rains.
Flower prices rise in Cotabato City
In Cotabato City, prices of flowers sold at PC Hill in Cotabato City had doubled, Efren Mamac of GMA Regional TV One Mindanao reported.

PANOORIN: Presyo ng bulaklak sa PC Hill, Cotabato City, dumoble ngayong bisperas ng Undas. Ayon sa mga florist, nagkulang daw ang suplay ng mga bulaklak dahil sa mataas na demand ngayong #Undas2026. | via Efren Mamac/GMA Regional TV One Mindanao Bisitahin ang https://t.co/bAMF9JOAN0 para sa iba pang updates.— GMA News (@gmanews) October 31, 2026
Florists attributed the increase to high demand and limited supply.
“Medyo tumaas at dumoble ang presyo ng mga bulaklak natin ngayon, Sir,” said florist Jay Agan.
(Prices of our flowers have increased, nearly doubling today, Sir.)
Agan added that their flower stocks had already sold out on Friday, October 30.
According to Mamac's report, a pot of chrysanthemums that normally sells for around P150 now costs about P300.
Prices are expected to triple on All Saints’ Day, November 1.
Cemeteries in other provinces
Visitors also flocked to the Baguio City Public Cemetery, where the police recorded more than 700 arrivals as of 10 a.m. on Saturday.
In a report by Jasmin Gabriel-Galban of GMA Regional TV One North Central Luzon, the number of visitors was expected to exceed 5,000 by the end of October 31.

PANOORIN: Aabot na sa mahigit 700 katao ang bumisita sa Baguio City Public Cemetery as of 10 AM ngayong umaga, Oct. 31, 2026, ayon sa Baguio City Police Office. Gardening tools at maging mga alagang aso at pusa, hindi pinayagang makapasok sa loob ng sementeryo. | via Jasmin Gabriel-Galban/GMA Regional TV One North Central Luzon Bisitahin ang https://t.co/bAMF9JOAN0 para sa pinakabagong balita.— GMA News (@gmanews) October 31, 2026

Police officers were stationed at the cemetery entrance to inspect visitors’ bags. Among the items confiscated were cleaning materials, including hard brooms, as the period for cleaning gravesites had already ended.
As of 10 a.m., no traffic buildup was reported on nearby roads, while the situation inside and outside the cemetery remained orderly.
Taxi and jeepney stands were also set up outside the cemetery to accommodate commuters heading home after visiting their departed loved ones.

Residents of El Salvador City, Misamis Oriental, have begun visiting the graves of their departed loved ones at the Our Lady of the Snow Cemetery ahead of All Saints’ Day, according to GMA Regional TV One Mindanao's Cyril Chaves.
However, several graves remain uncleaned, while some tombs are still damaged, as relatively few visitors have arrived to prepare the gravesites.
—VBL, GMA News

articles.title: France and Germany braced for unrest with hundreds of demonstrations planned – Europe live
articles.summary:
French interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, warned earlier this week of a ‘very high risk of public disorder’

In Germany, a loose alliance of groups called Gen Z regelt (Gen Z is sorting it)…

blocks.text: Key events

items: 33m agoFrance braces for third weekend of protests as 70,000 police deployed

blocks.caption: Jon Henley

blocks.text: Jon Henley

In Paris, two separate marches planned by unions and gilets jaunes through the city centre have been banned. Instead, police have authorised a single march in the far south-east. An appeal by organisers against the decision to exclude them from the centre was rejected late on Friday night.

The interior ministry has said 410,000 people marched last Saturday, when a strong police presence mostly prevented a repeat of the widespread violence and looting that swept French cities during a first wave of mass protest on 17 October.

Unions and the gilets jaunes movement protesting over low wages, the cost of living and deteriorating public services have joined school and university students calling for better learning conditions, with a nationwide ​strike called for 5 November.

Government measures to address the students’ demands – including replacing a creaking university admissions platform and providing loans to local authorities for school renovations – did not go far enough, student leaders said.

blocks.caption: Deborah Cole

blocks.text: Deborah Cole

In Germany, a loose alliance of groups called Gen Z regelt (Gen Z is sorting it) has called for supporters to turn out in more than 30 cities demanding more spending on schools, climate protection and housing, and against any plans to return to mandatory military service.

Alexander Throm, of the ruling conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) parliamentary group, wrote in the Handelsblatt business newspaper: “Scenes like those in France must be prevented at all costs.”
But Felix Banaszak, the co-leader of the opposition Green party, cautioned against attempts to place the youth protests under general suspicion in advance.

“The [CDU’s] rhetoric, which seeks to criminalise these protests pre-emptively and paint them as the work of marauding gangs, may even drive people towards radicalisation,” he told the RND media group.
Berlin’s police chief, Barbara Slowik Meisel, said she would deploy an additional 1,500 officers in the capital, though she had little reason to fear that people or property would come under attack.
“We have no concrete evidence of any coordinated looting operations being planned,” she said.
France braces for third weekend of protests as 70,000 police deployed
France is bracing for a third weekend of protests, with police deploying 70,000 officers in an effort to prevent a repeat of the riots and looting that have swept the country in recent weeks.

Nationwide protests over the rising cost of living and the deteriorating education system have drawn hundreds of thousands of people onto the streets. Some demonstrations have descended into violence, with widespread looting and vandalism reported on 17 October.

Ahead of this weekend’s planned demonstrations, shops and businesses across France have boarded up their storefronts. Police have restricted access to Place de la République and Les Halles between 11pm and 6am on Saturday and Sunday and unaccompanied minors face a separate 9pm curfew around the Champs-Elysees.

blocks.caption: French gendarmerie and police officers gather near the Arc de Triomphe ahead of planned demonstrations on Halloween in Paris. Photograph: Pedro Nunes/Reuters

blocks.text: The French interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, warned earlier this week of a “very high risk of public disorder”, saying demonstrations would be permitted but not in city centres, where authorities are concerned about the potential for violence and damage to property. The interior ministry said around 150 demonstrations were scheduled to take place nationwide.
Nuñez said authorities had identified social media posts for Halloween gatherings urging protesters to spark a “revolution”.
“Everyone is on deck to ensure an extremely firm response to any trouble,” he added.

The largely peaceful protests, which began in late September by students angry over the state of school facilities, overcrowded classrooms and what they regard as an unfair university admissions process, have since been joined by the gilets jaunes (yellow vests) activists and and trade unionists. Government pledges to overhaul the education system and reduce fuel costs have done little to quell public anger.

blocks.caption: Workers board up storefronts and entrances of shops in Berlin ahead of the announced Gen Z regelt protests. Photograph: dts News Agency Germany/Shutterstock

blocks.text: The protests have sparked a wave of youth-led demonstrations across Europe, with protests scheduled in more than 30 German cities today. An alliance of groups called Gen Z regelt (Gen Z is sorting it) has urged supporters in cities including Berlin, Frankfurt, Munich and Cologne to take to the streets to demand greater investment in education, climate action and housing, as well as opposition to proposals to reintroduce compulsory military service. Organisers said they are expecting more than 160,000 people to take part in the demonstrations.

articles.title: Evacuated Ukrainians from Russian-occupied Oleshky arrive in Belarus
articles.summary: Residents were taken out from the devastated city on Friday during a local ceasefire.

blocks.text: Residents evacuated from the devastated Russian-occupied city of Oleshky have arrived in Belarus and are expected back in Ukraine later on Saturday, authorities have said.
They were taken out on Friday during a local ceasefire brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump.
Planes carrying Oleshky residents landed in the city of Gomel on Saturday morning, according to Belarusian state media and a senior Ukrainian official.

"The last, fourth plane landed in Gomel (Belarus). In a few hours, all Ukrainian citizens evacuated from Oleshky, together with the Ukrainian delegation, will be on Ukrainian territory," said David Arakhamia, a key Ukrainian official.
The state-owned Belarusian news agency Belta reported a bus convoy of Oleshky residents had left Gomel airport and was heading towards the Ukrainian border.
A humanitarian ceasefire took force across the frontline region of Kherson on Tuesday, providing the first few days of peace in the area in four years, following Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
The ceasefire allowed the road out of Oleshky to be demined and will remain in place until the end of Sunday 1 November.
Residents had a four-hour window to leave before a convoy of 25 buses, with space for 750 people, left the town on Friday afternoon - along with ambulances for people with limited mobility.
Several hundred people are understood to have decided to stay in the war-torn city, despite widespread devastation and a lack of gas, electricity and running water.
Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said on Friday morning that those who decided to stay "will receive all the necessary humanitarian assistance".

blocks.text: Former German Chancellor Angela Merkel has called for a woman to succeed President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, pointing out that no woman has held the office in the country's 77-year history.

articles.title: PH, Germany sign climate resilience agreement
articles.summary: The Philippines and Germany have signed an agreement for a project that focused on bolstering cooperation for climate resilience, biodiversity conservation, and low-carbon development.

blocks.text: Published October 31, 2026 6:46pm
The Philippines and Germany have signed an agreement for a project that focused on bolstering cooperation for climate resilience, biodiversity conservation, and low-carbon development.

An Implementation Agreement was signed for the Transformative Actions for Climate and Ecological Protection and Development (TRANSCEND) Project. The project is supported by €32.702 million in funding from Germany’s International Climate Initiative (IKI).

“TRANSCEND does not carry these national commitments on its own. Its contribution is focused: work in selected landscapes and sectors that connects local activity with national priorities,” Climate Change Commission (CCC) Vice Chairperson and Executive Director Robert E.A. Borje said.
“The point is not to add a climate label to work already under way. It is to make climate risk, ecosystem condition, and emissions part of how development choices are made,” he added.

Borje said that the project would help connect local activities with the Philippines’ broader climate commitments, as climate considerations needed to be integrated into public investment, infrastructure, enterprise, local planning, and livelihoods.

Apart from Borje, the agreement was also signed by Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) Undersecretary Analiza Rebuelta-Teh, German Development Cooperation (GIZ) Country Director Immanuel Gebhardt, and TRANSCEND Program Manager Johanna Sibbert.
“The unique selling point of TRANSCEND is that it works across adaptation, mitigation, and biodiversity conservation,” Sibbert said.
“It also supports the government at the national and subnational levels, working with development partners to advance the country’s climate and biodiversity commitments,” she added.

TRANSCEND will operate in Luzon, Panay, and Northern Mindanao, with interventions planned in ecosystem conservation and restoration, urban ecosystem-based adaptation, and more, with the goal of incorporating climate and environmental concerns into development planning and implementation.

“That is the most important project for Filipino-German cooperation and for GIZ. TRANSCEND is the biggest program of its kind, bringing together multiple sectors and partners to address climate change and biodiversity loss,” Gebhardt said. —VAL, GMA News
