articles.title: France braces for fresh unrest, government vows tough response
articles.summary: Some 150 gatherings are planned across France, the interior ministry says

blocks.text: POLICE PREPARATIONS. French gendarmerie and police officers gather near Arc de Triomphe on the day of a demonstration organized by labor unions as part of nationwide protests called by the 'Yellow Vests' movement joined by French high school and university students against the cost of living and rising fuel prices, in Paris, France, October 31, 2026.
Pedro Nunes/Reuters
Some 150 gatherings are planned across France, the interior ministry says

items: France has deployed 70,000 police to manage expected protests on October 31, driven by public anger over living costs and President Macron's government.
A ban on a major march in Paris has been enforced, with authorities concerned about potential rioters using Halloween masks to hide their identities.
The unrest has led to significant economic losses and has bolstered far-right political sentiments ahead of upcoming elections.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

PARIS, France – France deployed a 70,000-strong police presence to contain a widely expected bout of fresh unrest on Saturday, October 31, in the latest nationwide protests driven by anger over living costs, public services and President Emmanuel Macron’s government.

The demonstrations, which fall on Halloween, come two weeks after riots and looting caught security forces off guard, leaving damaged shops, public buildings, and businesses in cities across France. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez has vowed not to let a repeat happen.

“Everyone is on deck to ensure an extremely firm response to any trouble,” Nunez told a news conference earlier this week as he set out details of security arrangements for a day he described as carrying “a very high risk” of unrest.

France’s top administrative court confirmed on Saturday a march between the emblematic Paris squares of Republique and Bastille will be banned, rejecting a challenge by unions. Demonstrations will instead have to be held on boulevards on the eastern fringe of the city, away from the main shopping areas in central Paris.

Authorities are also alert to the possibility that rioters could use Halloween masks to conceal their identities. Nunez noted that laws already allow police to ban face coverings when public order is at risk.
Some 150 gatherings were planned across France, the interior ministry said.
The US Embassy advised travellers to avoid areas where demonstrations or large gatherings are planned.

The protests gathered pace in late September as Macron’s minority government launched 2027 budget talks. Facing public debt approaching 120% of economic output and rising borrowing costs, the government is under pressure to rein in spending, narrowing its room for manoeuvre.

Students angry at the dilapidated state of many schools, crowded classes and a university admissions system widely seen as unfair, have been joined by trade unions and a re-emergent “Yellow Vest” movement demanding action on the cost of living.
The protests have inspired youth-led protests across Europe, with demonstrations planned in more than 30 German cities on Saturday.
The French government’s promises to reform education and ease fuel costs have failed to calm discontent.

“When I was little, I was told young people were the future,” said Aaron Berthier de Grandry, a 15-year-old high school student in the Paris suburb of Nogent-sur-Marne who plans to join his third consecutive weekend of protests.
“Well, if we, as the future of France, lack resources, that means France will end up collapsing.”

The unrest has handed a political boost to far-right leader Marine Le Pen, who leads opinion polls ahead of April’s presidential election, while potential centrist successors to Macron remain divided.
The troubles are the latest blow to an economy which, data on Friday showed, was already shrinking in the third quarter.
The Chamber of Commerce estimates losses to retailers exceed €1 billion ($1.1 billion). Other estimates put the total at double that when including uninsured damage and lost revenue.

Along Paris’ main shopping boulevards, early Christmas lights glow around boarded-up windows and security grilles. Among the shops targeted in previous unrest were outlets belonging to luxury brands including Hermes, Louis Vuitton, and Burberry.

The government is pushing ahead with a controversial law making rioters liable to pay up to €10,000 for damage caused either by themselves or by groups they are deemed to be part of. Rights groups and some lawyers say the measure risks undermining the right to peaceful protest. – Rappler.com

articles.title: ‘Hope and help’: How the Philippines fights to lower breast cancer deaths
articles.summary: While treatments for late-stage breast cancer have reached the Philippines, medical professionals point out that making them available is vastly different from making them affordable and accessible

items: Global cancer research aims to eliminate breast cancer as a cause of death, with advancements making metastatic breast cancer more manageable.
In the Philippines, breast cancer is often diagnosed at advanced stages due to misconceptions and lack of awareness, leading to poorer outcomes compared to countries like the US.
Efforts are being made to improve early detection and access to treatment through government programs and community initiatives, but significant gaps remain in awareness and accessibility.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – There’s a bold ambition in global cancer research to eliminate breast cancer as a cause of death.

And it’s this goal that has transformed cancer treatment over the years, even making Stage 4 or metastatic breast cancer — when the cancer has spread to distant organs like the bones, lungs, liver, or brain — more manageable.

“It’s important for people to know that metastatic breast cancer is not a death sentence,” said Dr. Marvin Mendoza, head of medical oncology and ambulatory infusion therapy unit of the National Kidney and Transplant Institute.
“It’s really very different from before, like the ’90s. We now have a lot of options.”
“The medical advancement in cancer is really fast. There’s a lot of investment in innovative medicine,” added Dr. Kriska Lim, medical affairs head of oncology for AstraZeneca Philippines.

“Most people think when it’s metastatic breast cancer, they won’t get treatment anymore. But even people with this cancer can live meaningful lives if they get the right treatment and the right support.”
But there are still a lot of hurdles doctors and breast cancer advocates face when dealing with Filipino patients.

For instance, some patients diagnosed at advanced stages abandon standard treatment and turn to alternative remedies, believing these will cure them. Others refuse biopsy on a suspected tumor, fearing the procedure will cause it to spread.

blocks.caption: Why are more Filipino women getting breast cancer?

blocks.text: Kara Magsanoc-Alikpala, co-founder of the ICanServe Foundation — which helps breast cancer patients by connecting them to medical specialists, educational resources, and support groups — said there are many misconceptions in local communities.
“Common ‘yung nakakahawa ang breast cancer (The belief that breast cancer is contagious is common). A lot of husbands distance themselves, it’s so common in communities,” she shared.
“There’s also the use of underwire bra and deodorants, we still get that. And the biopsy, ’pag ginalaw, kakalat (if moved, it might spread), it’s so common.”
The lack of breast cancer awareness and education remains one of the reasons the Philippines ranks poorly in global breast cancer statistics.

In the US, around 66% of breast cancer patients from 2019 to 2023 were “diagnosed at a localized stage, meaning the cancer had not spread outside the breast.” This early detection results in a higher survival rate, according to the United States Cancer Statistics.
Unfortunately, that isn’t the case in the Philippines.
“We’re so far from that. We’re the total opposite,” said Magsanoc-Alikpala. “Around 65% of breast cancer here is diagnosed at an advanced stage, Stage 3 or 4.”
Breast cancer remains the most common occurring cancer among Filipinos, according to the 2024 statistics of the International Agency for Research on Cancer of the World Health Organization (WHO).
It’s the second highest cause of death among Filipino cancer patients in both sexes at 12.9%, just behind lung cancer (13.6%).
In Asia, the Philippines also ranks in the top six for both breast cancer incidence and mortality in 2024, according to WHO.
“We really want breast cancer, and all cancers in general, to have enough attention. In AstraZeneca, our bold ambition is to eliminate breast cancer as a cause of death,” said Lim.

“Recently, breast cancer is no longer the top cause of death. For it to happen, there’s a lot of things we have to look into. We recognize that it’s not enough that we bring the medicines in, it’s not enough that we invest. We’re supposed to work with like-minded organizations and really help the country move forward.”
“We do have advanced lines of treatment for metastatic breast cancer. It’s not just chemotherapy. There are a lot of targeted therapies now made available,” added Mendoza.

“Of course, made available is different from made affordable and accessible. But it’s one thing that they’re already here. We have to do the work to make it affordable for more patients, because treatment can take years or even a lifetime.“

blocks.caption: Rappler Talk: From breast cancer survivor to cancer exercise specialist

blocks.text: Medical professionals and advocates admit there are still many gaps even as the government expanded the PhilHealth Z Benefit, the health package that covers catastrophic and high-cost medical conditions.
“The biggest program is the PhilHealth Z Benefit package, but the sites and hospitals that offer it are still limited. That’s why the lines are so long,” said Magsanoc-Alikpala.

Other government programs to help alleviate medical costs include the YAKAP program, which covers cancer screening tests, and the Cancer Assistance Fund under the National Integrated Cancer Control Act, which covers specialized treatments and palliative care.
“There are many initiatives from the government, medical society, and private institutions, but it has to reach the communities. That’s the main barrier,” said Mendoza.
“If people don’t know about the program and initiatives, how to access them, it doesn’t complete the loop. There are still many people who haven’t been reached.”

While a lack of awareness about government programs often leads to late diagnosis and poorer outcomes, navigating the required paperwork once assistance is found presents an entirely different challenge.
“Kailangan pa rin ng kumpas ng gobyerno para mas ma-improve pa (The government needs to provide direction to improve it),” said Mendoza.
For now, some private institutions try to fill in the gaps, with the ICanServe Foundation, for instance, running its Ating Dibdibin (Take Your Breast Care to Heart) flagship program.
“We partner with local government, usually a city, then we institutionalize the program. It’s a community-based breast cancer control program with the aim of saving lives,” said Magsanoc-Alikpala.

“We bring services to the barangays instead of expecting them to go to the hospital. It’s proactive, going house to house, checking on women, because sometimes they don’t know where to go. We make sure there’s a clear pathway, there are patient navigators to hand-hold the patients.”

Lowering breast cancer deaths in the Philippines through early detection remains the key message among advocates, who hope that conversations would go beyond the Breast Cancer Awareness Month every October.
“The government should really have a national campaign. It’s the same message every year — early detection,” said Magsanoc-Alikpala.
“We really need to be intentional in the way we promote our message, not only early detection, but there’s hope even if your cancer is diagnosed at a later stage.”
“I want everyone to know there’s hope and help,” she added.

“There’s the medical world, their supportive care. The government has some help — it’s not enough, but it’s a big help as well. There are foundations willing to help patients. But take charge of your health. Get screened. When you’re young, that’s the best time to find out.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: Drug runner? Arms dealer? The Adeline-C made waves in Halifax and beyond
articles.summary: The Adeline-C arrived in Halifax on Oct. 31, 1981, filled with state-of-the-art equipment, but it was soon abandoned by its crew. It would be years before its role in a complex U.S. drug smuggling…

image.caption: The Adeline-C arrived in Halifax on Oct. 31, 1981. 'It was a really interesting story full of ... international intrigue and dope smuggling and big money," says Rob Gordon, a journalist who covered the ship. (www.newspapers.com)

blocks.text: Journalist Rob Gordon was at the courthouse on Upper Water Street in downtown Halifax one day in 1981 when he overheard a sheriff say something that piqued his interest.
"Oh, we were just on a boat, you know, and we seized a couple of guns and stuff," said one of the sheriffs.
Gordon, who later retired as a CBC News journalist, was covering courts then for the Chronicle-Herald newspaper.

On his lunch break, he headed down to the waterfront to check out the Adeline-C. The 32-metre trawler with a maximum width of seven metres had arrived in Halifax on Oct. 31, 1981, and was abandoned by most of the crew.

But it would be years later that the Adeline-C's role in a complex U.S. drug smuggling operation worth as much as $200 million US became fully known. Based out of the small coastal city of Newport, R.I., it involved purchasing around 100,000 pounds of marijuana and hash from the Middle East and Far East.
The operation was financed by a fraudulent bank loan in the Channel Islands that paid for the drugs, ships and manpower needed to run the scheme.

This Sept. 3, 2013, photo shows Guernsey, one of the Channel Islands in the waters between England and France. A loan was obtained from there due to the territory being an offshore tax haven. (Charmaine Noronha/The Associated Press)

Gordon found the ship tied up near Historic Properties. On board were two shady characters who had joined the ship in Florida and travelled north with it. Gordon knew them and they welcomed him aboard to have a look around.
Underneath the floorboards of the engine room were rolled-up marine charts for places like the Mediterranean, Florida and Lebanon, a major player in global hash production in the 1980s.
"This is a dope smuggling ship and they're hiding the charts," Gordon realized.
He later interviewed U.S., Canadian and British police to piece together Adeline-C's origins for some stories in the Chronicle-Herald.
Retrofitted to smuggle drugs

Other features advantageous for drug smuggling that had been retrofitted on the 1963 trawler were high-capacity fuel tanks and winches, elevators and cranes that made it easier for the mother ship to carry out hefty cargo transfers to smaller ships at sea. The smaller vessels then smuggled the drugs into ports along the East Coast, targeting the U.S. and possibly Canada.
With its countless isolated bays and inlets, Nova Scotia has long been a popular destination for smugglers, be it rum or drugs.

items: How a $500M Cape Breton drug bust helped inspire the film Little Lorraine

blocks.text: A spokesperson for the Halifax sheriff's department told the Toronto Star in 1982 he was perplexed by the situation.
"She has a 1,000-horse diesel [engine] aboard and that would drive her right smart through anything," he said. "No one in his right mind would walk away from something like that."
But abandoning a valuable ship was just a minor business expense for the people who owned the Adeline-C.
"What they were making was so much more," said Gordon.

The Federal Court ordered that the Adeline-C be sold in late 1982, with the sale planned for January 1983, but the Toronto Star reported another round of bids might take place because the highest original bid was $76,000 "from a bargain-hunting local fisherman."

An article in the Sept. 14, 1986, Chicago Tribune included a photo of Robert Christopher (Chris) Murray, the alleged mastermind behind the drug operation. He was never tried for his alleged role in the drug ring because he fled. (www.newspapers.com)
Ultimately, its buyer was a Dutch man named Erik van Veenen. At that point in his life, he was living in Alaska, running a trading post and a hunting business.
After a ship purchase in Nova Scotia fell through, a lawyer involved with the failed transaction tipped him off about the Adeline-C.
After seeing the ship and the equipment on it, he figured it was worth a million dollars.
"So I fell in love with the boat and I bought it and I've regretted it ever since," said van Veenen, now 82 and living in Germany.
He believes he paid around $100,000 US for it.
Two people walk hand in hand on April 8, 2020, in Newport, R.I. The drug scheme was based out of the small coastal city. (Steven Senne/AP)
One day as he worked to get the ship ready to go back to Alaska, he pulled up the floorboards in the engine room, much like Gordon had done.

"I came across this big, blue logbook, all handwritten with the complete description of the journey of the boat: Amsterdam to Gibraltar to Cairo through the Suez Canal to Djibouti and then on past Singapore," said van Veenen.
Iran-Contra affair?

He believes the ship wasn't just into drug running, but was used for transporting weapons as part of the Iran-Contra affair, in which the U.S. made a deal to secretly sell weapons to Iran in exchange for the release of hostages being held by the Iranian-backed group Hezbollah in Lebanon.
While conducting interviews and reading through court documents and dozens of newspaper articles to research this story, the reporter did not come across any references to the Iran-Contra affair.
The Gesmer I, formerly the Adeline-C, is shown in St. John's Harbour in 1992. (Capt. Harry Stone/Maritime History Archive)

When van Veenen left Halifax, his plan was to sail the ship south along the Atlantic coastline, cross through the Panama Canal and then head north to Alaska, but financial troubles killed the plans. The Adeline-C was costly to run and a sale of his trading post soured, leaving him financially squeezed.
At some point, he'd changed the name of the ship to Thackeray C, in honour of his then wife.
Van Veenen said he posted the trawler for sale in a boating magazine, and the next buyer was based in Quebec.
By October 1984, the Adeline-C — now operating as the Thackeray C — was briefly accused of being the mother ship in a high-seas transfer of arms destined for use by the Irish Republican Army.

While an unidentified spokesperson for the Irish national police made that assertion to Gordon, a followup story a day later quoted a Canadian customs official who said the ship had been in Gaspé, Que., since July of that year.
FBI, IRS investigation

The year 1984 also marked the year that a task force involving the FBI, the Internal Revenue Service and the Drug Enforcement Administration started questioning suspects in Rhode Island about the drug operation, according to a 1988 Providence Journal article.

The investigation was aided by records obtained by police in Guernsey, an island in the English Channel, which contained "almost a diary of the whole operation," detailing names, dates, costs and expected profits, the newspaper reported.
The alleged mastermind behind the fraud was a Rhode Island resident named Robert Christopher (Chris) Murray.
How the money behind the drug operation was obtained

Accounts vary, but he obtained at least $10 million US in loans from the Guernsey branch of the First National Bank of Chicago. Murray used yachts owned by people well known "among the yachting fraternity in Rhode Island" as collateral, the Chicago Tribune reported in 1986.
The pitch was that the money would be used to distribute mortgages to clients who would buy and refit luxury yachts.

However, the Chicago Tribune reported that the notary public who vouched for the yacht owners and notarized financial statements did not exist, according to the federal government. Rather, it was believed the signatures belonged to Murray. The people who owned the supposed assets were fictitious.
In reality, the money was for the drug operation and the only boats purchased would be four mother ships in Holland, of which one never left the shipyard.
Of the three vessels that took part in the scheme, the Adeline-C was dubbed "the most mysterious ship of all," according to a 1984 Providence Journal article.
Journalist Rob Gordon, shown in a 2007 CBC News report, learned about the Adeline-C while working as a newspaper reporter in 1981. (CBC)

Before it was purchased for the drug operation, it was known as the Hilda H. It was purchased in Holland for 423,370 Swiss francs — about $219,000 US — on April 13, 1981. It then underwent some retrofitting to have state-of-the-art equipment installed that would prove beneficial in running drugs.

Newspaper accounts covering the drug operation predominantly focus on the roles of the other ships — the Caroline C and the Sea Scout — as the ports they visited were well documented and some of their smuggling was thwarted by authorities.
It's unclear where the Adeline-C picked up its drugs, with Lebanon and Thailand listed in varying newspaper accounts.
How the Adeline-C ended up in Halifax
But once it returned to North America, the Adeline-C met up at Georges Bank off Nova Scotia to unload roughly 12,000 pounds of marijuana, according to a 1986 Chicago Tribune article.
While half was transferred to one ship, the newspaper said the remainder of the drugs had to be dumped overboard when another ship, the Side Show, didn't show up.
Aerial view of Providence, R.I., on Aug. 1, 2019. Some of the court cases related to the drug ring were held here. (Eva Claire Hambach/AFP via Getty Images)

When the Adeline-C arrived in Halifax on Halloween 1981, the only cargo it contained was a rifle, a handgun and a load of teak that had been used to disguise the drugs, according to one of Gordon's stories.

In Rhode Island, about 18 people ended up indicted for their role in Murray's drug operation, and most were convicted, with the cases largely tried before the U.S. District Court in Providence, Rhode Island's capital, the Providence Journal-Bulletin reported.
As for the alleged mastermind, he was never brought before the courts because he couldn't be located.
Murray was wanted in Illinois, North Carolina and Rhode Island for bank fraud, drug smuggling and income tax evasion, according to a 1988 Providence Journal article.
His last known address was in Guadeloupe in the Caribbean, but he later fled to Spain and lived under an assumed name, the newspaper reported.
This Nov. 20, 2011, photo shows the West Indies island of Guadeloupe. Chris Murray's last known address was on this island. (Jean Michel Andre/AFP via Getty Images)
But Murray didn't live a quiet life. He rented a Spanish villa and drove three cars, including a Porsche.
It was in a car, a white Ford, where Murray's life came to an end in 1987. He'd been shot three times and his burning vehicle was found in a grove of eucalyptus trees.
Fingerprints taken from the body and processed by an FBI lab in Washington later confirmed his identity, the Providence Journal reported.
People sunbathe on the beach of Torremolinos, Spain, on July 20, 2015. It was in this community where Chris Murray was found slain in 1987. (Jorge Guerrero/AFP via Getty Images)
The Adeline-C is still alive, but it goes by the name of Gesmer I, according to various ship tracking websites. At the time of writing, it was in Dominica in the Caribbean.
Looking back on the Adeline-C's time in Halifax, Gordon thinks about other ships.
"Back around that time, there was an enormous amount of drug smuggling ... tons and tons of dope from all sorts of directions was arriving here," he said.
"And that ship, because it was abandoned, because it was downtown Halifax, it sort of stuck out. But it certainly wouldn't have been the only ship that did that."

articles.title: Quiboloy counsel says Cendaña went beyond 'permitted commentary'
articles.summary: The counsel of detained preacher Apollo Quiboloy thumbed down Akbayan party-list Representative Percival "Perci" Cendaña free speech defense against the libel and cyber libel complaint that the…

blocks.text: Published October 31, 2026 4:34pm

The counsel of detained preacher Apollo Quiboloy thumbed down Akbayan party-list Representative Percival "Perci" Cendaña free speech defense against the libel and cyber libel complaint that the religious leader filed against the lawmaker.
Quiboloy, through his legal counsel Ferdinand Topacio, filed the complaint against Cendaña, Mamamayang Liberal party-list Representative Leila de Lima, and Senator Risa Hontiveros last September.
"The statements of Mr. Cendaña went beyond the bounds of permitted commentary, and clearly crossed the line into criminal defamation," Topacio said.
"We will prove malice in view of a long history of ill-will against Pastor Quiboloy, and a long-running intention to malign his good name," he added.
Topacio accused Cendaña of singling out Quiboloy for a selfish political agenda.
On Friday, Cendaña filed his counter-affidavit regarding the libel and cyber libel complaint that Quiboloy's camp filed against him.
The complaint stemmed from a radio interview, wherein Cendaña supposedly issued statements such as:
"Nakita naman natin kung papaano isa-isa 'yung mga witnesses tinatakot at hinaharass nila para bumaligtad, 'no? At kahit 'yung mga biktima, tinakot at hinarass nila para hindi ituloy ang laban."
(We have seen how witnesses were threatened and harassed to change their statements. Even the victims were threatened and harassed to discourage them from pursuing their cases.)

The lawmaker issued the comments in relation to the various charges that the pastor was facing, including qualified human trafficking, child abuse, and sex trafficking in both the United States and the Philippines.
Washington has formally sought to extradite Quiboloy from the Philippines to face justice in the US.
In his affidavit, Cendaña cited free speech enshrined in Article III, Section 4 of the 1987 Constitution.

"The complainant has not established the elements necessary to bring my statements outside the protection afforded to good faith public commentary under the Constitution and applicable jurisprudence," Cendaña said. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: The races that will decide control of the US Senate
articles.summary: Democrats are now competitive in states Donald Trump won handily in 2024, even as Republicans seek to capture Democratic-held seats of their own

blocks.text: WASHINGTON, DC, USA – Democrats need a net gain of at least four seats in November’s midterm elections to wrest control of the US Senate from Republicans, with voter discontent over President Donald Trump, the Iran war and rising prices putting races in once-solidly Republican states into play.

Republicans hold a 53-47 majority, and a Democratic takeover looked unlikely at the start of the year. But Democrats are now competitive in states Trump won handily in 2024, even as Republicans seek to capture Democratic-held seats of their own.
Here are the races that could determine control of the Senate:
Alaska
Republican Senator Dan Sullivan is up for reelection against Democratic former US Representative Mary Peltola and an outsider who shares Sullivan’s name.

Alaska allows voters to rank their top picks rather than choosing a single candidate. Voters will have four choices, including Sullivan, Peltola, and the other Dan Sullivan, a candidate Republicans have called a decoy in what they believe is a Democratic effort to confuse voters.
Trump’s midterm travel this month included a stop in Alaska.

Peltola has outraised Sullivan through October, $33 million to nearly $14 million. But Sullivan reported having more campaign cash, $5.1 million to Peltola’s $3.2 million, and Republicans have outspent Democrats, $42 million to $38 million.
Trump won Alaska by 13 points in 2024, but recent opinion polls show Peltola narrowly leading Sullivan.
Iowa
Trump’s unpopularity, tariffs and the Iran war have put Republicans on defense in Iowa, where Trump won by 13 points in 2024.

Republican US Senator Joni Ernst’s decision not to seek reelection has made this an open-seat contest between Republican US Representative Ashley Hinson and Democratic state Representative Josh Turek, a two-time Paralympic gold medalist.

Hinson has called for an “immediate end” to the Iran war and said Iowans should not have to pay higher fuel or grocery prices as a result of it. However, she has repeatedly voted against resolutions in Congress calling for an end to the war.
Turek has outraised Hinson, $20 million to $14 million. But Hinson reported $3 million more cash on hand through September, and Republicans have outspent Democrats, $81 million to $70 million.
Recent polls show Hinson with a narrow lead.
Kansas

The political environment has shifted in favor of Democrats so much that Kansas is now in play. Republicans have diverted resources from North Carolina to shore up US Senator Roger Marshall, who in recent weeks has condemned the activity of Immigration and Customs Enforcement in his state.

Trump won Kansas by 16 points in 2024, but the state has twice elected Democratic Governor Laura Kelly. And Republican leaders have acknowledged the race is competitive and closer than they would like it to be.

Marshall’s opponent is Adam Hamilton, founding pastor of a Methodist megachurch. Hamilton has outraised Marshall, $14 million to $6 million, and reported more cash on hand, $3.2 million to $922,000, through September.
In a reversal of the usual pattern, Democratic groups have outspent Republicans in Kansas, $28 million to $22 million.
The last time Kansas voters elected a Democrat to the US Senate was 1932. Most recent polls show Hamilton leading narrowly.
Maine
Democrats’ top pickup opportunity to begin the cycle was in Maine, the lone state where a Republican incumbent is up for reelection in a state Trump lost in 2024.
Senator Susan Collins and her Democratic opponent, former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson, were both joined on the campaign trail by big-name supporters last week.

Collins stumped with former US Senator Joe Manchin, a West Virginia independent who left the Democratic Party in 2024, while Jackson held a town hall with US Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York.

Manchin’s joint appearance with Collins came after the senator distanced herself from Trump at a debate earlier this month, when Collins — who voted to convict Trump after he was impeached following the January 6, 2021, assault on the US Capitol — acknowledged that she isn’t the president’s favorite senator and said he wouldn’t be coming to Maine.

Democrats say Collins only votes against Trump when it doesn’t matter — such as when she voted against a sweeping tax-cut package last year after backing it in a procedural vote. Democrats also hope voters will hold her accountable for helping confirm Brett Kavanaugh to the US Supreme Court, which led to the overturning of a federal right to abortion.

Democrats, however, have their own drama. The party’s original nominee, progressive oysterman Graham Platner, was pressured into withdrawing following sexual assault allegations, forcing the state party to scramble for a new candidate. Platner denied the allegations.

Jackson, another progressive, emerged as Platner’s replacement, but he has drawn criticism for his treatment of women. He has said publicly he doesn’t regret telling Collins to “shut up” at a recent debate. Jackson’s female allies publicly defended his character and legislative record last week, when the Maine Women’s Lobby endorsed him over Collins.

Jackson has outraised Collins by more than $1.6 million despite not entering the race until July. But Collins has a $1.1 million advantage in cash on hand as of mid-October. Republican groups have outspent Democrats, $76 million to $40 million.
Recent polls show Jackson with a narrow lead or tied.
North Carolina
Republicans appear to have conceded North Carolina, where even Trump has suggested the Democrat will win.
At a campaign rally last week in Greenville, Trump told supporters it was “crazy” that former Governor Roy Cooper, a Democrat, was going to be their next senator.
Trump won North Carolina by 3 points in 2024, but Republican Senator Thom Tillis’ retirement made this year’s Senate race an open contest.

Trump recruited former Republican National Committee Chairman Michael Whatley to succeed Tillis, but the ex-party official has been unable to compete with Cooper’s fundraising, and Republican allies who invested heavily in holding North Carolina have begun shifting their focus to other states.
Cooper has raised $50 million and has $9 million in the bank. Whatley has raised $14 million and has just $900,000 on hand through mid-October.
Recent polls have Cooper leading by double digits.
Ohio
Democrat Sherrod Brown is seeking to return to the Senate after losing his seat in 2024, and working-class frustration with the Iran war and rising prices may be giving him a tailwind.

This time, Brown faces US Senator Jon Husted, who was appointed to the Senate to replace US Vice President JD Vance when Vance left the Senate for the White House. The winner of the special election will be on the ballot again in 2028 for a full six-year term.

The Ohio race has become one of the most expensive Senate contests in the nation. Republican and Democratic outside groups have each spent nine figures on the race, with Republicans investing $232 million and Democrats pouring in $118 million.

Brown has more than tripled Husted’s fundraising through October 14, bringing in $68 million to Husted’s nearly $20 million. Both campaigns reported having a little more than $4 million to spend as of mid-October.
Recent polls show Brown leading by 3 to 5 points.
Texas
No Democrat has won statewide in Texas since 1994. James Talarico, a state representative, could break the streak.
Talarico faces Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton in the big, conservative-leaning state that has dashed Democratic hopes repeatedly in recent years.

Trump won Texas by nearly 14 points in 2024. Yet Republican outside groups have already spent $300 million to hold the seat after runoff voters nominated the scandal-plagued Paxton over incumbent Republican US Senator John Cornyn. Trump endorsed Paxton even though Cornyn was widely believed to have an easier path to victory.
Leaked audio has exposed daylight between Trump and Paxton, who privately told donors that the president’s midterm convention hurt his campaign.

Democratic groups have spent $76 million on this race. But Talarico’s campaign has outraised Paxton’s by $110 million and reported $9.6 million more in its campaign coffers as of September 30. Paxton’s donors include billionaire Elon Musk, who lives in Texas and has relocated SpaceX, Tesla, X, ​and other businesses there. Musk has given $158 million to a Republican super PAC to invest in Paxton’s race.
Recent polls show Talarico narrowly leading or tied.
Georgia

Georgia was one of two key pickup opportunities for Republicans at the beginning of the election cycle, as Trump won the state by 2 percentage points in 2024. But Republican US Representative Mike Collins has struggled to gain traction against Democratic US Senator Jon Ossoff, a potential 2028 presidential candidate.
Ossoff has outraised Collins by nearly $126 million through October 14 and began mid-October with $15.1 million in his war chest compared to Collins’ $1.1 million.
Polls have consistently shown Ossoff leading, and Democrats narrowly lead Republicans in outside spending, $19 million to $17.9 million.
Michigan

Republicans are more hopeful about flipping an open seat in Michigan, especially after the Democratic establishment didn’t get its pick. Progressive outsider Abdul El-Sayed narrowly defeated moderate US Representative Haley Stevens during the primary, putting him on a collision course with Republican Mike Rogers, a former US representative, in what could be the tightest race for a Democratic-held Senate seat this year.
Trump and former President Barack Obama campaigned in Michigan over the weekend.

A pro-Israel super PAC has spent at least $493,000 against El-Sayed, a follow-up to its $30 million effort to stop him from winning the Democratic nomination. The super PAC could spend as much as $9 million in the general election.
El-Sayed’s allies have also stepped up, with US Senator Bernie Sanders, an independent from Vermont, and Ocasio-Cortez each putting $1 million behind his campaign.
El-Sayed has raised $45 million through September, more than double Rogers’ nearly $21 million. But Rogers began October with more on hand, $6.5 million to $3.8 million.
Republicans have poured $136 million into the Senate race in Michigan, where Democrats have spent more than $70 million.
Most recent polls show El-Sayed with a narrow lead.
New Hampshire
Democrats are defending another open seat in New Hampshire, though this is a state then-presidential candidate Kamala Harris won by nearly 3 points in 2024.
Democratic US Representative Chris Pappas is running against former US Senator John Sununu, who was ousted by Democrat Jeanne Shaheen in 2008. Shaheen is retiring.

Sununu benefits from a famous last name. His brother Chris was governor until last year, and his father — also named John — was a governor and White House chief of staff for President George H.W. Bush.
Pappas has raised four times as much as Sununu, $24 million to $6 million. Pappas has a modest $200,000 cash advantage, but Republicans have spent $37 million in the race to Democrats’ $20 million.
Pappas has maintained a consistent polling lead of 5 to 8 points in recent surveys. – Rappler.com

articles.title: 'No one is safe' as Ebola outbreak surges to more than 10,000 cases, Africa's top doctor warns Canada
articles.summary: Africa's top doctor, who has called Canada home since 2013, tells CBC News there could be "massive" cross-border spread of Ebola in the months ahead as he calls for more international support.

image.caption: Dr. Jean Kaseya, director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, at an emergency meeting of African ministers in late October amid a devastating outbreak of Ebola that's gripped central Africa for most of 2026. (Dr. Jean Kaseya/Africa CDC/X)

blocks.text: Health·Exclusive
Africa's top doctor, who has called Canada home since 2013, tells CBC News there could be "massive" cross-border spread of Ebola in the months ahead as he calls for more international support.
African health official tells CBC News there may be 'massive' cross-border spread, calls on Canada for support

As the world's fastest-growing outbreak of Ebola hit more than 10,000 confirmed cases this week, Africa's top doctor warned there could be "massive" spread into additional countries — and even other continents — unless countries such as Canada offer more support.

"No one is safe today," said Dr. Jean Kaseya, director-general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), in an interview with CBC News from Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, on Friday.
"We are calling on all African countries to increase the level of preparedness. But we're also calling our Western countries, especially Canada, because Canada is where my heart is."

Kaseya is from Kinshasa, the capital of the Democratic Republic of Congo, and has led Africa CDC for the past three years. But he has called Canada home since 2013. He told CBC News he has been living apart from his family — his three children attend university in Toronto, and his wife remains in Laval, Que. — as he works to end an unprecedented crisis that began in his home country.
He singled out Canada as an ally to African health officials, though he said more can still be done.

"This is my message to Canadians: No fear, no panic, but take it seriously, and even talk to your parliamentarians, talk to other people you know, if they can provide more support for this outbreak," he told CBC News.
"I really want to be back home to celebrate with my family, but we need to stop this outbreak before doing that."
Death toll surpasses 5,000

Kaseya's comments follow a grim new milestone in this year's Ebola outbreak. Confirmed cases in the Democratic Republic of Congo have surpassed 10,000, while the latest report from the country's public health institute shows the death toll has surpassed 5,000.
The outbreak was first declared in mid-May, but scientists suspect the Bundibugyo strain of the virus had been spreading undetected for months in some of Congo's most remote regions.

items: Ebola cases top 10,000 in Democratic Republic of Congo, as countries race to stop spread
Nigeria Ebola patient flown to Switzerland, Congo health worker killed as 4 countries deal with outbreak

blocks.text: Ongoing conflict, public distrust and the lack of an approved treatment or vaccine for the Bundibugyo strain have further complicated efforts to contain the outbreak.

It is now the country's largest-ever outbreak and the fastest-growing and second-largest Ebola outbreak ever recorded — behind only the West Africa Ebola crisis, which infected more than 28,000 people, mainly across Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone, from 2014 to 2016.
"If this outbreak [continues] like that, with the same magnitude, in one year we'll have more than what West Africa had in two years and a half," Kaseya said.
"But it won't be just a few countries. It will be more countries. It can also affect some other continents."
A much smaller number of infections have already appeared in neighbouring countries, including Uganda, Kenya, and most recently in Nigeria, which reported its first Ebola infection in a decade.
That patient, the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat, was flown to Switzerland for treatment on Monday, the latest in a series of patients evacuated to European countries since the outbreak began.

items: Fears of a pan-African Ebola crisis growing as fourth country reports first case
1 in 4 Ebola deaths are children in Democratic Republic of Congo's worst outbreak

blocks.text: Kaseya said imported infections could continue as teams on the ground struggle to slow community transmission in new areas of Congo.
The risk to Canada remains low, he added, though he implored Canadian officials to "move from low to zero by supporting [Africa] to stop the outbreak where it is currently."
Ebola outbreak now deadliest in Congo’s history
Canada offered $8M to Ebola fight

Canada committed $8 million to the Ebola response in May, including $2 million for Africa CDC to accelerate surveillance and strengthen biosecurity measures. In late July, Health Canada also authorized Moderna to launch a clinical trial of its vaccine targeting the Bundibugyo virus.

The federal government also introduced temporary border measures aimed at reducing the risk of Ebola entering and spreading in Canada, including outbreak alerts issued for Kenya and Nigeria in October.

"The Government of Canada will continue to monitor the situation closely and may adjust these measures, as appropriate, based on evolving evidence and the epidemiological situation both in Canada and internationally," the Public Health Agency of Canada told CBC News in a statement this week.

items: Suspected Ebola case at Montreal hospital turns out to be a false alarm
Canada extends Ebola travel restrictions for another 30 days

blocks.text: Alongside those official efforts, Canadian research teams are also working behind the scenes to study this once-rare form of Ebola.

University of Winnipeg microbiologist Jason Kindrachuk said Canadian and Congolese scientists have sequenced more than 1,000 genomes to date, offering insights into how the virus is behaving and whether existing vaccines may offer cross-protection for the Bundibugyo strain.
But he stressed there are "finite resources" for that collaborative, cross-border work.
Congolese students in Montreal separated from loved ones due to Canada travel restrictions
Canadian scientists 'scramble' for research funding

"We're trying to scramble with funds from whatever sources we have to be able to keep things like genome sequencing alive, to keep testing alive … so I think at some point we need to see bigger investment, and certainly sustained investment, from the high-income areas of the world," Kindrachuk said.
"I think there's a real need for Canada and other countries to step up."

Kaseya praised Canada's efforts to date, including the close collaboration between African and Canadian health officials, but agreed that the threat of Ebola could persist for months without broader support to end the crisis.

"We'll continue to work hard to keep Canada safe — we'll do our best to keep all other countries in the world safe — but … if we do not provide support, we cannot guarantee that all of us will be safe," he said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Lauren Pelley is a senior health and medical reporter for CBC News. She's a two-time RNAO Media Award winner for in-depth health reporting in 2020 and 2022, a silver medallist for best editorial newsletter at the 2024 Digital Publishing Awards, and a 2024 Covering Climate Now award winner in the health category. Contact her at: lauren.pelley@cbc.ca.

articles.title: How to tell whether your lithium batteries are a fire risk — and what to do if they are
articles.summary: We've heard a lot about how dangerous lithium battery fires are, but most of us also keep and charge smartphones, e-bikes and other lithium battery devices at home. Do we actually need to worry? Are…

image.caption: Experts warn consumers to watch out for the warning signs of a damaged battery that could start a fire in devices such as cellphones or power banks. (Daniel Krason/Shutterstock)

blocks.text: We've heard a lot about how dangerous hot, fast-moving lithium battery fires are and their rising number — more than 1,500 in communities across Canada last year.
But most of us also keep and charge smartphones, power banks, e-bikes, vacuum cleaners, drills and lots of other lithium battery devices at home without any issues.
So are all the fire warnings overblown? Are some kinds safer than others? Can batteries really go from safe to risky? What are the warning signs? And what should you be doing about this?
How safe are lithium batteries really?
Experts generally agree that overall, lithium batteries are very safe.

Vinny Gupta, assistant professor of fire safety engineering at the University of Waterloo, notes that more than 10 billion battery cells are now manufactured every year. "And we typically only hear about safety issues in just a few of them."

The problem is when the systems fail and they do catch fire, it's "quite dramatic," acknowledged Gupta, who does research that involves intentionally making them fail and catch fire to study their fire risk.
Safety measures typically built into consumer lithium batteries include temperature sensors, pressure relief valves to vent potentially flammable gases and systems to prevent overcharging.
So do you really need to take measures like watching them as they charge and unplugging them as soon as they're done charging, as firefighters advise?
Regina fire chief gives reminder to check charging devices
It's true that the battery should automatically stop charging.
But experts note that a battery that has been safe all along can become a fire risk at some point.
How can a lithium battery that was safe become a fire risk?

David Giles, CEO of TempAlert, a Halifax company that sells heat-sensing battery-monitoring stickers, said even if people are using batteries as intended, they can become damaged and therefore hazardous.
That could be due to a defect. Or it could be due to an event, such as an e-bike or e-scooter collision.
He says that when you drop your phone, you may notice if you crack the screen. "But you also may have done other internal damage that might not show up right away" — including damaging the battery.
TempAlert makes heat-sensitive stickers that change from black to yellow at 60 C, indicating a problem with your battery. (TempAlert)
Heat, such as from charging your battery in the sun, can also cause damage.

Gupta said one of the most common ways to cause a battery to fail is by overcharging it. Typically, batteries are designed to prevent that, but some are more poorly designed than others, and the risk increases if they're tampered with or paired with the wrong charger.

Giles says that's easy to do, since most have connectors that fit into many devices. But he warns they may be designed for different voltages. The wrong charger "could be ramming, you know, 80, 90 volts into a battery only designed for 40. That's when you start having a major problem."
Repeatedly charging and recharging a battery over time can also eventually cause it to wear out and fail.
When that happens, does the battery catch on fire right away?
Here's the good news — usually no.

"Batteries don't just go into thermal runaway instantly," Giles said. Thermal runaway is a term for when a battery starts to rapidly self-heat, generating more heat and creating a feedback loop that can lead to a fire. "It progressively gets worse and worse."
Lithium batteries are found in many devices, including e-bikes, and most are safe. (Grant Linton/CBC)

When a battery first starts failing, it may feel hot to touch while charging — Gupta says that's "the earliest indication" that something is wrong. At that point, it will usually cool when you unplug it.
Giles said that may happen repeatedly before it stays hot even after being unplugged.
So how much time do you really have before you have a dangerous fire?
"To be honest, we don't really know," Gupta said, as it depends on what is going on inside the battery and the self-heating process is exponential once underway.
Giles said it could take days or weeks of charging and use, or it could take just 20 minutes.
What to do when a lithium battery is on fire
Are some kinds of lithium batteries less dangerous from a fire safety perspective?
The short answer is no.
The two most popular lithium battery chemistries are NMC (nickel manganese cobalt) and LFP (lithium iron phosphate), which have different materials in their cathodes.
Several readers wrote in to suggest that LFP is less combustible and prone to overheating.
But in Gupta's opinion, "It's hard to really say if one chemistry is safer than [the] other … there are trade-offs."

It's true that LFP is less energy dense and goes into thermal runaway at a higher temperature (about 235 C, compared with 200 C for NMC). It also ejects fewer solid fragments of battery when overheated — but more gas, Gupta said: "And that gas is often laden with both toxic and flammable products."
So, how do you stay safe?
Buy batteries with Canadian safety certifications such as CSA, cUL, cETL on the charger. Make sure you use the correct charger with your battery, even if another one fits in the charging port.
These are the kinds of certification marks you should look for on your battery charger, according to the Government of Canada lithium-ion battery safety website. (Health Canada)

Keep an eye on your charging battery and its environment. Charge your device or battery on a hard, non-flammable surface (not on a couch or bed), where you can see it. Gupta recommends not putting the device in the path that you would need to use to escape in case of a fire incident.
Know the danger signs of a damaged battery. They include feeling too hot, swelling, bad smells, gas or smoke.
There are some devices that can help identify these signs, such as:

items: TempAlert or other temperature-sensitive stickers that you can apply to the battery.
Heat detectors or alarms. Reader Adrian Hill of Crystal Beach, Ont., said he purchased one of these that he installed above the spot where he charges his e-bike.
A carbon monoxide detector. Gupta said many lithium batteries release carbon monoxide when overheated.

blocks.text: Know what to do if your battery overheats. Unplug it and get it to a safe, non-flammable place (such as outdoors, a sink or a bucket of sand) if possible. Don't try to charge it again, even if it cools, Giles says.
This is Call2Recycle's kit for dealing with damaged, defective or recalled lithium batteries at hazardous waste facilities. (Call2Recycle)

If it cools down, you can take it to a technician or hazardous waste disposal site. Do not put it in the trash. Call2Recycle has more detailed information on dealing with damaged, defective and recalled batteries.
If the battery continues getting hotter or releases gas or smoke, you're really in the danger zone.
"If you smell anything, that's bad," Gupta said. "You should leave and call the fire department."

Lithium batteries are around us everywhere and that's not going to change any time soon, he added. For the most part they're safe, but "it's important for people to be aware of the fact that they can fail and there are very simple things we can do that go a long way towards improving our personal safety."

articles.title: As a Nigerian, I thought Canadians had free health care. Then I became a pharmacist here
articles.summary: When Atai Okokon moved to Calgary from Nigeria, she was surprised to see that Canadians struggle to pay for medications in much the same way as Nigerians.

image.caption: As a pharmacist who worked in Nigeria and now calls Canada home, Atai Okokon did not expect to see her patients in Calgary struggle to pay for life-saving medications like she did in her home country. (Ola Ajayi)

blocks.text: Canada·First Person
When Atai Okokon moved to Calgary from Nigeria, she was surprised to see that Canadians struggle to pay for medications in much the same way as Nigerians.
As a patient and a pharmacist, I've found prescription drug costs can be a difficult pill to swallow
This First Person is the experience of Atai Okokon, who lives in Calgary. For more information about CBC's First Person stories, please see the FAQ.
I asked the woman at the pharmacy counter how she would like to pay for her child’s asthma inhaler.
"Does my insurance no longer work?" she asked in a whisper, her voice shaky and unsure. "I was laid off and I am not sure how long my employer coverage would last."
I tried putting it through a second time.
"I am sorry, ma’am. The coverage has been terminated."
She brought out her credit card to pay. It was declined. She hesitated for a bit, turned out her purse to see if she had enough cash, but she was $2 short. The tears rolled freely down her cheeks.
Her son needed his medication, but she couldn't afford it.

It wasn't the first time I experienced this. I had seen it in Nigeria, where I had trained and worked as a pharmacist. I had witnessed people become bankrupt, and some die, because they could not afford life-saving medication. I had provided samples, paid for medicines from my meagre salary, offered less expensive alternatives and discontinued medications that may not have been necessary to lower their expenses.
But I did not expect to see it in Canada.
Okokon worked as a pharmacist in Nigeria before moving to Canada. (Submitted by Atai Okokon)

In 2012, I accepted a full scholarship to study global health at Oxford University in the U.K., leaving the counter for the classroom. It was there I first heard about the inverse care law — the concept that those with the most needs often have the least access to care. I assumed it mostly applied in “poorer” countries. I was surprised to learn that countries can spend so much on health care and yet their citizens struggle to pay for the services. North America featured prominently in these discussions and Canada stood out as a country that had made universal health care work.

Eight years after I graduated, I moved to Calgary. I had admired and loved Canada from afar and as a health-care professional, I was excited to practise in a country where I believed anyone — no matter how much they earned or where they lived — could access most health-care services without thinking of the cost.

items: Trump’s push to cut pharma costs could drive up drug prices in Canada

blocks.text: I had a child after I moved to Canada and throughout my pregnancy, I did not spend a dime on routine tests, scans and specialist visits. I was unemployed but never worried about the cost of childbirth or what I would do if there were complications.
Okokon, left, with her mother Ekanem, in 2013 at a lunch at Oxford University for graduates and their families. (Submitted by Atai Okokon)

But that's also when I realized that getting medications was a different ball game. Outside the hospital, for the most part, medications are not free. I had terrible nausea in my first trimester. I woke up with it and, like a shadow, it stayed with me the whole day. The doctor prescribed medication but when I went to the pharmacy and heard the cost, I decided to find other ways to cope with the nausea.
“It will only last 12 weeks,” I told myself.
I was in the process of getting licensed as a pharmacist in Alberta and I did not want my husband, the sole provider at that time, to carry that extra financial burden.

items: His cancer drug costs $90,000/month. Doctors say it’s greed

blocks.text: That plan did not work. My nausea became worse and my husband bought a month’s worth of medication. I felt so guilty about the cost that I stretched it out, taking it only on the worst days, and said nothing to my husband. My doctor had also prescribed iron pills, as my levels were quite low, and a kind pharmacist gave me samples when I explained my financial situation.
Okokon with her family in Calgary in 2025. From left to right: her son Tomiwa, Okokon, her husband David and daughter, Toyosi. (Submitted by Atai Okokon)
One in five Canadians do not have drug insurance coverage and have to pay for their medication. I was one of them.

And so was the woman standing in front of me at the pharmacy counter. Her sniff jolted me back to reality. She had lost her job, and with it, her coverage. She now had to bear the cost of the inhaler her child needed. Luckily, we had some samples in the pharmacy and I gave her one.

She sighed in relief and through tears, told me the money she had with her would now go towards scraping together something for dinner. It was a déjà vu moment for me. I might as well have been behind the counter in Nigeria.
On the day Okokon took her citizenship oath in December 2024, her colleagues at her pharmacy in Calgary threw her a surprise party with cake and decorations. (Submitted by Atai Okokon)

Today, something similar happens on almost every shift. I find myself substituting, adapting, de-prescribing or troubleshooting insurance claims so that my patients can access the medicines they need. Just like I did in Nigeria.

I have experienced the health-care system of the country I now call home both as a patient and a practitioner and it’s made me realize a prescription is only a piece of paper when a patient cannot afford their medicines.
Do you have a compelling personal story that can bring understanding or help others? We want to hear from you. Here's more info on how to pitch to us.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Atai Okokon is a pharmacist, who lives in Calgary with her husband and two children. Her work has appeared in The New York Times' Tiny Love Stories and Pharmacy Practice + Business Magazine.

articles.title: This Texas midterm race has huge stakes, both for Donald Trump and the country
articles.summary: There's no U.S. midterm election with more at stake than the battle between Republican Ken Paxton and Democrat James Talarico to become the next senator for Texas. The outcome could determine which…

image.caption: U.S. President Donald Trump welcomes Ken Paxton, the Republican candidate for U.S. Senate in Texas, at a campaign rally in Lubbock, Texas, on Tuesday. (Annie Rice/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: In the U.S. midterm elections on Tuesday, no race has more at stake than the battle to become the next senator for Texas.

The contest between Republican Ken Paxton and Democrat James Talarico matters for Americans across the U.S., as the outcome could determine which party holds a majority in the Senate for the remainder of Donald Trump’s presidency.
"If we lose Texas, we're going to lose the country," Paxton has told the Republican faithful at numerous campaign rallies.
The stakes are particularly significant for Trump, since all the reasons the Republicans risk losing in Texas trace directly back to him.
Trump pointedly inserted himself into the Texas race from the start by endorsing the scandal-ridden Paxton to become the Republican candidate over long-serving incumbent Sen. John Cornyn.

Paxton's sketchy ethical record, high prices for gas and diesel triggered by Trump's war on Iran and heavy-handed Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) tactics are all driving what appears to be a dramatic shift in voter sentiment.
Is the razor-thin Texas Senate race a referendum on Trump?

No Texas Democrat has been elected to the U.S. Senate since 1988, the year before Talarico was born. Despite that history, and despite Trump carrying Texas by 13 percentage points just two years ago, polling averages suggest a Democrat win this time is a distinct possibility.

Paxton's campaign is based on low taxes, cracking down on illegal immigration and supporting Trump's agenda. Talarico's key themes include stopping cuts to health-care funding, imposing term limits on members of Congress and shifting the tax burden from the middle class to corporations and the wealthy.
'Most corrupt politician in Texas'
Both candidates have described the consequences of the election in monumental terms, frequently depicting their opponent as extreme.
The race "isn't just red versus blue," Paxton told a recent rally in the Dallas suburb of Allen. "It's the America our founders gave us versus something they would never recognize.”
"Ken Paxton is everything that's wrong with our politics," countered Talarico later that same day at a rally in Fort Worth. "We are running against the most corrupt politician in Texas."

The corruption cloud hanging over Paxton, the state's attorney general since 2015, includes a grand jury indictment for securities fraud and impeachment in the Texas House for abusing his office to help a political donor. (The fraud charge was eventually dropped after he struck a plea deal, and the Texas Senate declined to convict following his impeachment.)

Voters attend a joint midterm election rally in Weslaco, Tex. on Oct. 25 for three Democratic Party candidates: James Talarico for the U.S. Senate, Bobby Pulido for the U.S. House and Gina Hinojosa for state governor. (Michael Gonzalez/The Associated Press)
Paxton casts Talarico — a former teacher and Presbyterian seminarian who has served in the state legislature since 2019 — as a dangerous, leftist radical.

"A vote for James Talarico is not just a vote for his radical agenda," Paxton told the Allen rally. "It's a vote for every dangerous idea that Democrats across the country are putting forward right now.”
Paxton's backers go even further in their rhetoric.
'We cannot let evil win'
Lydia Elizondo, the Republican running for district attorney in the South Texas county of Hidalgo County, introduced Paxton at a rally last week.
"We cannot let evil win," Elizondo told the crowd. "That evil has a name, and its name is James Talarico."

items: Cross Country Checkup is asking: How will the U.S. midterm elections affect you? What questions do you have? Leave your comment here and we may read it or call you back for Sunday's show

blocks.text: One tangible sign of the high stakes: The Senate race in Texas is poised to become the single-most expensive non-presidential campaign in U.S. history.

Spending on advertising by the candidates, parties and corporate-funded political action committees since the Texas primaries began has surpassed $500 million US, according to data compiled by the firm AdImpact.
Trump hits rally circuit in last big push before U.S. midterms
Much of that spending has been bankrolled by one rich Texas resident who also happens to be the wealthiest man on Earth.
Two of Elon Musk's political action committees have funneled more than $210 million US to help the Paxton campaign, according to election finance filings.
The Musk-funded ads are primarily aimed at motivating Republicans to vote by invoking culture-war fears about the consequences of a Talarico win.

One ad claims Talarico wants "taxpayer-funded sex-change surgeries on kids." Another claims he backs "putting parents in jail if they do not support surgically transitioning their children." Talarico has rejected the accusations as lies.

items: These midterm races will decide who controls U.S. Congress for the rest of Trump's presidency

blocks.text: The Democrat has in turn made Musk's investments in the Paxton campaign part of his argument to voters.
"Elon Musk is trying to buy this Senate seat," Talarico said as the Fort Worth crowd booed the name of the SpaceX and Tesla CEO.
James Talarico, the Democrat candidate for U.S. Senate in Texas, speaks at a campaign rally in Fort Worth on Oct. 19. (Mike Crawley/CBC)
"But on November 3rd, we will deliver a crystal-clear message to the world's first trillionaire. We will let Elon Musk know that Texas is not for sale."
Early turnout in Texas leans Democrat
Advance turnout figures provide some evidence the Democrats' messaging may be working more effectively than the Republicans'.

During the first week of early voting in Texas, people who'd previously voted in a Democratic Party primary slightly outnumbered those who'd voted in a Republican primary, a scenario that a Republican political consultant described as unprecedented.

At a polling station in the South Texas city of Edinburg, first-time voter Laysha Chavez said the key factor driving her decision was the way ICE deportations have separated families who've lived in the U.S. for many years.

items: Why the Hispanic vote could sway the outcome of the U.S. midterm elections

blocks.text: "Seeing that happen really breaks my heart because you never know who it could be next. It could be your friend; it could someone close to you," Chavez, a biology student, told CBC News.
There's a range of polling evidence suggesting that Hispanic voters in Texas, who swung toward Trump in record numbers in 2024, have soured on Republicans in 2026.
Also in Edinburg last week, Paxton drew around 100 people to an evening rally, including Ruben Martinez, who said he supports the Republican Party in part for how it deals with illegal immigration.

"It's like, right now here, we're waiting in line to get in," Martinez told CBC News outside the venue. "So it's not fair that somebody just comes out of nowhere and goes straight to the door and maybe fills up the last seat."
'I'm a Talafreako'

While polling suggests pocketbook issues such as the price of gas and diesel are top of mind for midterm voters, those who back either Paxton or Talarico often bring up values as the chief motivator of their support.
Daniel Mitchell attended the Talarico rally in Fort Worth wearing a black T-shirt with the words "I'm a Talafreako," co-opting the derisive nickname that Trump and others have used for the Democrat.
"I think what [Talarico] is doing for Texas is great, how he presents an idea that we can have a change that uplifts everyone," Mitchell told CBC News.

Mitchell's view of the Republican candidate? "Paxton's a fraud," he said. "Just down to his personal life and the policies he's supporting, you can tell that he sells out for whatever makes him happiest in the moment."
After Paxton's rally in the Dallas suburb of Allen, supporters wrote messages on his campaign bus. (Mike Crawley/CBC)
Paxton's personal life came under public scrutiny last year when his wife, a Texas state senator, filed for divorce, citing "biblical grounds" and accusing him of adultery.
Neither that nor the corruption allegations sway the Christians who are among Paxton's most ardent backers.
At Paxton's rally in Allen, attendees wrote messages of support on the campaign bus, many on Christian themes.
Mardi Day, a resident of nearby Plano, chose "Blessed is the nation whose God is the Lord" as her message.
"I believe that's how the United States is going to stay a strong nation, by following Jesus Christ and our Constitution," Day told CBC News.

items: Your guide to the U.S. midterms, and why they're crucial for Donald Trump

blocks.text: Another rally attendee, Gloria Jones, said her top political priority is undoing what she called a "massive immigration problem" from Arab countries.
"How are we going to get rid of all these radical Muslims?" Jones said. "They want to practise Sharia, they need to go back to their country and practise there."

Steve Ceh is a pastor at Solomon's Porch Ministries in New Braunfels, Tex., and a member of Pastors for Paxton, a group of 27 Christian leaders who endorsed the Republican candidate. (Mike Crawley/CBC)

Steve Ceh, pastor of Solomon's Porch Ministries in New Braunfels, a city of 120,000 near San Antonio, is one of 27 Pastors for Paxton, a statewide group of Christian leaders praying for the Republican candidate.

"Every man that runs and every woman that runs is a flawed person," Ceh said when asked by CBC News to describe Paxton's positive traits. "So we look beyond the personality of that person and we vote policy, and he is directly in line with Christian values."
Ceh criticizes Talarico for what he calls a "severe leftist ideology" that can't co-exist with biblical principles.
"In Texas, when you start to threaten people's beliefs, values, they're going to go out and vote," he said. "[Talarico] will not win in Texas. I'm not even worried about it."

items: Why the war in Iran might cost Trump and the Republicans at the ballot box

blocks.text: Trump, however, is worried enough about it that he has travelled to four cities in Texas since Oct. 1 to urge the MAGA faithful to get behind Paxton and raising the spectre that Democrat control of Congress would mean "communists" in power.
"You have to vote for Ken," Trump told a rally in Corpus Christi on Tuesday. "Otherwise, all of the great things we've done are going to change very quickly."

articles.title: Bat boxes were supposed to be a safe haven for bats. So why are they killing them?
articles.summary: Manmade homes meant to protect bats from the elements can become deadly in a heat wave, with reports worldwide of mass casualties in an animal population already under threat. But a few tweaks to the…

image.caption: Female bats like the Yuma myotis, pictured here, prefer to roost in artificial bat boxes that have a "Goldilocks zone" temperature of between 35 C and 41 C. But scientists say climate change is driving up temperatures inside homes too high, causing them to become deadly. (credit: John Saremba)

blocks.text: LISTEN | There’s a bat housing crisis and the solutions are adorable :
What on Earth?25:02There’s a bat housing crisis and the solutions are adorable
At ƛ̓éxətəm Regional Park in Port Coquitlam, just outside Vancouver, sits an unusual housing complex of tall wooden structures, with narrow little openings.
The sole tenants? Roughly 800 female bats.

Mothers, daughters and grandmothers return to the bat boxes summer after summer to give birth and raise the young. For more than a decade, bat enthusiast John Saremba has helped care for the colony, maintaining the artificial roosts designed to shelter the animals from environmental threats.

“They’re incredibly tender, wonderful mothers,” Saremba told CBC’s What on Earth? host, Johanna Wagstaffe. “In fact, if a female bat is having problems with pregnancy, the other bats will rub her tummy.”

items: Rabid bat found in Burlington, Ont., health officials say

blocks.text: That show of tenderness made his discovery in July 2018 all the more heartbreaking; he arrived at the boxes for a routine check and found 65 dead bats.
“We came out here and I was just devastated,” he said. “I really didn’t know what to do.”

The very boxes meant to protect the bats can become deadly, scientists say, as climate change fuels more frequent and intense heat waves. The boxes can then trap heat inside, exposing the animals to extreme temperatures.

That doesn’t mean we should abandon bat boxes — bats are already under threat due to disease and habitat loss — but as global temperatures keep rising, conservationists say the boxes need a few tweaks.

A view looking straight up into one of the bat boxes on site at ƛ̓éxətəm Regional Park in Coquitlam, B.C, which contains about 400 bats in just one of the very large boxes at the time. (Submitted by John Saremba)
What exactly happened in 2018?

It wasn’t the first time the colony experienced dangerously high temperatures; the bats had survived a heatwave a month before the fatalities. So what was different this time? And if conditions had become unbearable, why didn’t they simply fly away?
Leah Rensel, a wildlife biology PhD candidate at the University of Montana, was studying the Port Coquitlam bats when the die-off occurred.
“The temperatures inside the bat boxes had exceeded, I believe it’s 44 C, which is lethal for the species,” Rensel said.

Rensel suspects the bats’ fiercely protective maternal instincts was the reason they stayed, noting the colony was likely going through parturition in July 2018, a time when the female bats gather to give birth.
“[The babies] are really small … so the bats had these vulnerable pups and they didn’t want to leave the roost, even though the conditions were too hot.”

Though expectant mothers seek out warm spots — so they can devote themselves to giving birth, nursing their young and hunting insects instead of temperature regulation, there’s a limit to how much heat they can handle.
“I call it the Goldilocks zone,” Rensel said, which falls between 35 C and 41 C for the little brown bat and the Yuma Myotis bat.
“So it's not too hot and it’s not too cold … so if you’re a bat in a maternity colony and you find a roost that hits that most of the time, that’s golden.”
But these little wooden boxes can heat up quickly, particularly when they’re painted black and placed in direct sunlight, as the Port Coquitlam boxes were.
A cluster of bat boxes housing female Little Brown and Yuma Myotis bats in Səhətləm Regional Park in Port Coquitlam. (Submitted by John Saremba)
And the combination of higher temperatures and the stuffy conditions inside the boxes led to humidity, which is especially harmful to the inhabitants.

“What climate change is doing is essentially increasing the temperature component of their microclimate,” said Cori Lausen, director of bat conservation with the Wildlife Conservation Society Canada and Rensel’s thesis adviser.
“When you bring temperature and humidity together, that’s heat stress,” she said, noting that bats don’t sweat, which makes it harder for them to cool down.
Why bats are in danger
Bats are under threat from more than just heat.

Worldwide, habitat loss and forest fragmentation have reduced the availability of natural roosting sites and the insect-rich habitats bats rely on for food. In North America, the fungal disease known as white-nose syndrome has decimated their populations.
Of the world’s nearly 1,400 known bat species, 25 are considered critically endangered, 87 endangered and 110 vulnerable, according to the International Union for Conservation of Nature.

A world without, or with significantly fewer, bats could devastate ecosystems, because the animals perform natural pest control, suppressing insect populations that can ravage forests or farmers’ fields, according to a 2019 paper published in the Biodiversity and Conversation journal.
In tropical and subtropical forests, bats disperse seeds through their droppings, an important role in regeneration.

And the consequences of losing these fanged creatures may even extend further: one peer-reviewed study even found that where bat populations died off, pesticide use jumped — and that, in turn, increased infant mortality rates.
Bats have a housing crisis. And it's getting worse
So, what’s the solution?
The answer, Lausen says, is not to scrap bat boxes but to use more of them.
“Never take away a box, never change a box,” she said. “Add boxes around your property, for example, to give them more options.”
She recommends placing boxes less than 100 metres apart so that bats can easily switch roosts if they need to warm up or cool down.
“Get a nice collection of bat boxes going: different sizes, different styles, different solar radiation.”

That could include boxes with different types of venting or different paint colours, which can affect how much heat the bats absorb, Lausen says. She adds that an “absolute minimum” of three bat boxes should be installed on each property.

Another option is a “bat condo,” Lausen said, complete with different spaces, so the animals can move between microclimates without having to leave the roost, much like an old attic where city bats traditionally made their homes.

The first bat "mini-condo" designed to hold 1,000 bats built in a regional park in Metro Vancouver. In a bat condo, bats can move between different microclimates without having to leave the roost. (Submitted by John Saremba)
In B.C., Saremba has been experimenting with the old bat houses and making new ones. He’s added shading to the old boxes using white blankets and building emergency exits out of PVC pipes.
Following those changes, bat deaths stopped.
And he’s also built a mini condo designed to mimic an attic, giving bats more room, more temperatures and humidity levels to choose from.
It even includes somewhere for the youngsters to practise flying.
“It’s like a teenager learning to drive,” Saremba explained. “You don’t go right on the highway first thing, no, you go on the side roads.”
